News.title: In-N-Out shooter, 24, is named after killing three and injuring seven in horrific drive-thru massacre
News.content:
THE gunman who killed three people at an In-N-Out drive-thru in Idaho has been named.

Chad Williams, 24, went on the horror rampage at the burger chain in Twin Falls before turning the gun on himself.



Terrifying footage showed Williams storm a shopping complex armed with a camouflaged AR-15-style rifle and let off a barrage of shots.

He killed three people, including a beloved employee, and injured seven others.



Two were left in critical condition, three others were described as stable, and two more have been discharged.

Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said Williams acted alone.

He praised a brave bystander armed with a handgun and off-duty officer who both fired at Williams during the incident.

Hicks said: “We believe their actions helped drive the suspect away from the scene, preventing further casualties.”

In a statement on Sunday, In-N-Out President Lynsi Snyder paid tribute to a “beautiful” employee who died in the tragedy.

She wrote: “My heart is broken, my chest is heavy, my eyes burn from the tears I’ve shed.



“We lost one of our beautiful Associates tonight. She was taking care of our most important asset – our customers, and her life was taken by a disgusting human who doesn’t value the lives of others or his own.

“He shot both on our property and off, and ended his life shortly after he took the precious lives of our Associate and Customers, innocent people who never saw it coming.”

The only victim to be identified thus far is Terry Dudley.



The company that he works for, North Star Taxi, said he has “a very long road ahead of him.”

Terry was charging his Tesla when he was shot in the back twice, according to a GoFundMe page.

A statement on the fundraiser read: “Our community experienced the kind of tragedy that changes lives forever.

“A senseless act of violence took the lives of innocent people, left many others critically injured, and shattered countless families in an instant.

“Our hearts are with every victim and every loved one who is now facing unimaginable grief and uncertainty.



“In a matter of moments, an ordinary day became a nightmare that no family should ever have to endure.”

The page, which was set up to help “tenacious, compassionate, kind hearted” Terry, has raised more than $8,000 so far.

Police found Williams’ body in an area near the restaurant.

Bullets began ringing out at around 3pm local time, with shocking footage showing dozens of people fleeing for their lives.

Williams drove up to the chain’s drive-thru before exiting a white vehicle and retrieving a rifle from the trunk.



Wearing a black T-shirt and blue trousers, he was seen walking through the car park before shooting through a Tesla‘s windscreen.

Someone in an In-N-Out uniform was later filmed dragging a person, also uniformed, bleeding from a gunshot wound in her chest across the parking lot.

Twin Falls resident Haley Dodaro, 43, was having lunch in In-N-Out with her mum when she saw people running across the street.

“People were running out crying and screaming”, she said.

Officials were still working on notifying the family members of victims.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Apart from Terry, names, ages and other details of those wounded in the shooting have not been released.

The FBI confirmed it would be assisting in the ongoing investigation.

News.title: Why John Healey must avoid becoming the second Healey to send Britain’s finances off the rails
News.content:
HISTORY has a habit of coming back to haunt our politicians.

Fifty years after Denis ­Healey’s policies plunged ­Britain into economic turmoil, the nation’s finances now lie in the hands of another Chancellor called Healey.



Like his bushy-browed predecessor, John Healey faces strikingly similar challenges — stagnant growth, high inflation and rocketing oil prices.

But his mission could not be simpler: Don’t repeat the catastrophic mistakes that pushed Britain to the brink of bankruptcy half a century ago.



In 86 days’ time, he will give us the clearest indication of whether he has learned the lessons of history when he delivers the first Budget for Andy Burnham’s new government.

The Yorkshireman must utilise his blunt honesty and frugality to confront the harsh economic realities facing us.

His first tasks will be to force big-spending ministers to tighten their belts, tame the out-of-control welfare bill and rebuild our worn-out defences.

With an extra £13billion a year required to meet our Nato commitments, he will have to convince Labour MPs of the need to divert cash from benefits to bombs.

There is only one piece of advice from his former office-holder that John Healey should heed.

It’s a well-known phrase coined by Denis which goes: “The first rule of holes — when you are in one, stop digging.”



Unfortunately, Denis Healey didn’t follow his own advice. He was a “Silly Billy”, as TV mimic Mike Yarwood would say.

Inflation was at 15 per cent when Denis was appointed Chancellor in 1974.

Within a year, it hit 27 per cent — one of the highest rates in the developed world.

The excessive wage demands of militant trade unions, coupled with relentless pandering to Labour’s hard Left only made matters worse.

But it was his tax and spend instincts which turned crisis into catastrophe.



Vowing to squeeze the rich “until the pips squeak”, Denis Healey increased income tax to a historic peak of 83 per cent, with tax on investment income hitting 98 per cent.

It scared off investors and led to the brain drain of senior doctors and scientists, while cultural icons such as the Rolling Stones and Sir Rod Stewart became tax exiles.

Despite soaking the rich, he was still spending billions more than he received in taxes, and 50 years ago next month the chickens came home to roost.



On September 28, 1976, Denis Healey was sipping a G&T in the VIP lounge at Heathrow on his way to the annual meeting of the International Monetary Fund, in Manila, when he received an urgent message from the Treasury.

Officials told him financial investors were selling the Pound because they feared its value would drop even further.

He abandoned the flight and rushed back to the office. Days later, he went cap in hand to the IMF for a £2.2billion bailout — about £20.5billion in today’s money.

It was the largest request it had received at that time.

The severe restrictions attached to the loan infuriated the unions and the Labour Left and set the stage for the Winter of Discontent of 1978-79, when widespread strike action led to fuel and food shortages, the dead left unburied and rubbish piled high in the streets.



It took two years of free market economics under Margaret Thatcher to restore Britain’s economic balance.

That’s why, after two weeks in the job, John Healey should take a break from Treasury spreadsheets and glance at the history books. He shares the same name, the same party and a similar massive headache to Denis.

But he can’t afford to make the same mistakes as his namesake fellow Yorkshire MP.

His first duty will be to lay down the law to Cabinet colleagues, backed by Burnham, that there is no new money for any spending pledges. This means reining in the people-pleasing Prime Minister and his unfunded giveaways, too.

Our new PM’s 86p-a-week cut on household energy bills, £2 cap on bus fares and help for pub and music venues has already landed the Chancellor with a combined bill of £1.5billion.



Some estimates put the cost of Mr Burnham’s policy proposals at £96billion — equivalent to £4,300 in extra tax for every family.

Mr Healey has to break the Labour cycle of promise, borrow and spend.

He must show a clear path to stop £3trillion of government debt rising and for it eventually to fall, control inflation and turbocharge economic growth.



That means getting a grip on the bloated welfare budget and banning large, unfunded spending increases.

The simple truth is one that politicians hate to hear.

You can’t keep spending money you haven’t earned.

You can’t tax businesses into creating jobs.

And you can’t borrow your way to prosperity.



The wealth has to come first.

If John Healey bears that in mind, he might avoid becoming the second Healey remembered for sending Britain’s finances off the rails.

ANDY BURNHAM showed solidarity with President Zelensky by wearing a black T-shirt and jacket for his meeting with the Ukrainian leader.

I wonder whether he’ll have the nerve to dress down when he finally gets an audience with Donald Trump.



TONY BLAIR famously announced that his three priorities for government were “education, education and education”.

But it seems the job of running our schools is less of a prize and more like the ministerial equivalent of detention.

After removing Bridget Phillipson from the post of Education Secretary, Andy Burnham offered the job to Ed Miliband’s brother, David, along with a seat in the Lords.

He politely declined.

Burnham then turned to Rachel Reeves, ­suggesting she might take it as a ­consolation prize after being axed as ­Chancellor. She passed, too.



Only at the third attempt did Labour’s ­deputy leader Lucy Powell agree to take on the brief.

But even then she wasn’t ­punching the air, as she had been hoping to land something bigger – Deputy PM, ­perhaps.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

That’s four noses put out of joint over what was once a plum Cabinet job.

Or, as Pink Floyd almost put it: We don’t need no Education Secretary.

News.title: Labour blasted after 160k businesses close in six months under weight of National Insurance hikes & extra red tape
News.content:
LABOUR has been blasted after 160,415 businesses closed in six months under the full weight of National Insurance hikes and extra red tape.

And business creation is at one of the lowest levels in a decade.



Ex-Chancellor Rachel Reeves’s £25billion tax grab made it more expensive to hire staff, while boosts to workers’ rights and the minimum wage were also said to have been factors.

Business openings in the first six months of the year stood at 157,980 — lower than during Covid, and at anytime since the first half of 2023.



Straight after the pandemic, the figure peaked at 193,245.

Shadow Chancellor Mel Stride told The Sun: “Labour don’t understand business.



“Their new regulations and higher taxes are destroying jobs and punishing the businesses that drive our economy.”

Shadow Business Secretary Andrew Griffith said some entrepreneurs had fled the country and others were now thinking twice before making a move.

He added: “The drought of new businesses opening in Britain is every bit as barren as the dry weather.”

The Lib Dems analysed official figures to reveal the business crisis.



The party wants a new deal with Europe, claiming it would cut regulations.

Economic spokesperson Daisy Cooper said: “Too many budding entrepreneurs will look at the Government’s crushing jobs tax and anti-growth agenda and be put off even trying to get their business off the ground.”

Britain’s economy shrank in April amid the Iran War, continuing to have an impact on energy prices in particulary. It grew by 0.1 per cent in May, according to the ONS.

News.title: Taxpayers have forked out enough for promises on migrant boats — they want to see results
News.content:
Show us results

IN the past decade, Britain has handed over £1billion to France as an incentive to stop the migrant boats.

But what have taxpayers got for their money?



Since 2018, more than 200,000 have crossed the Channel in flimsy dinghies — enough to populate Portsmouth — while French police simply shrugged their shoulders and looked on.

You’d be forgiven for thinking they had been told not to try too hard because they’re glad to see the back of them.



The more money they get the less they do to intercept boats in shallow water.

Barely a third of attempted crossings have been thwarted by French police since a lucrative three-year funding deal was signed in April.



The number of migrants arriving by small boats has topped 2,000 in the two weeks since Andy Burnham became PM.

Last Wednesday, 752 landed, the highest number in a single day this year.

We now learn it costs £8,000 for every migrant they stop — most of whom probably hop on the next boat out anyway.

The money would be better spent on a proper deterrent like reviving the Rwanda deportation scheme — sending Labour’s open borders backbenchers into meltdown in the process.



Uncontrolled migration is having a devastating impact on wages and will make British workers £2,500 a year worse off by 2031, according to Tory analysis.

Sooner or later Mr Burnham is going to have to confront the thorny issue head-on.

He won’t solve the problem by talking about buses or his favourite pub snacks on social media or telling us that “much more needs to be done”.

It’s two weeks since he entered No10 on a pledge to restore hope in politics.

Taxpayers have forked out enough for promises. They want to see results.



Tin eared

THE shocking scenes in Ceuta should be a wake-up call for world leaders.

Some 60,000 migrants entered the tiny Spanish territory from Morocco, in Europe’s biggest ever border breach.

It left 72 people dead and caused alarm among national leaders. But not so Spain’s PM.

As a sea search for bodies continued, Pedro Sanchez left for a two-week holiday with his wife in Lanzarote.

In a callous disregard for the victims, he took to social media to share his soundtrack of music by Madonna, Charli XCX and the Rolling Stones.



Europe’s border crisis demands serious leadership — not a playlist.

Get to business

BRITISH business is stuck in a vicious circle of high taxes and sluggish growth.

New ventures are starting up at the lowest rate in a decade.

More than 160,000 firms closed last year after crippling Labour National Insurance hikes.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

In 12 weeks’ time, new Chancellor John Healey can turn his first Budget into a lifeline for business.



By undoing the damage inflicted by his predecessor.

News.title: Railway station just a stone’s throw from Del Boy’s famous flat to produce Britain’s first-ever station wine
News.content:
BRITAIN’S wine industry has shown it is on track – after the nation’s strangest vineyard sprung up at an urban railway station close to Del Boy’s south London manor.

Chateau Denmark Hill – at the station in Camberwell – will be sticking the cork in their white wine from their 22 Bacchus vines, grown metres from the busy tracks.



It will make it the first wine to be produced at a railway station in the UK – and a sign of Britain’s changing climate as most the nation basks in yet another heatwave.

And the tiny vineyard is less than two miles from Del Boy and Rodney’s fictional Only Fools and Horses flat in Peckham where he would often exclaim: “Chateauneuf du Pape.”



Commuters are expected to be able to enjoy vin du pays when the wine is ready to be uncorked as early as next year.

Local Keith Griffiths, 41, a copywriter said: “I walked past without noticing it, then spotted it from the signs – and now cannot wait to try it.



“It’s amazing to have a little vineyard in Camberwell and is a great use of space.

“I supposed it is also one benefit of warming temperatures.

“It is the sort of entrepreneurial spirit that would make Del Boy proud.”

Winemakers at the station – next to busy King’s Hospital and in one of the capital’s most hectic areas – wrote on their Instagram: “This year will be our first wine producing year at the station.”



In another post, they added: “The dream of sipping a glass of wine, grown right here in Camberwell, is becoming a reality… making history as they work on the first ever vineyard in a UK station.”

Camberwell is a densely populated area just two miles south of central London with former inhabitants including ex-England football ace Jadon Sancho, comedian Jenny Éclair and ex PM Boris Johnson and his wife Carrie.

Rail firm GTR – the nation’s largest railway franchise which owns Southern, Thameslink, Great Northern and Gatwick Express – has helped fund the vineyard.

The project is being run by the Camberwell society, who have named it ‘Chateau Denmark Hill Station’.

Winemakers reclaimed a tiny bank just two metres from the busy station platform and planted 22 Bacchus vines.



They have all now budded wine and are ready to be harvested.

A new sign proudly announces itself as “the first ever vineyard at a UK station”.

Wine-making is one of the UK’s fastest-growing new industries with over 1,100 active sites nationwide due to warmer summer weather.

Around 16.5million bottles of wine are produced across the country every year with most being made in Kent, Sussex and Hampshire – with many bottles of sparkling wine rivalling the best from France’s acclaimed champagne region.

News.title: Afghan murder suspect ‘was cleaner in building where Brit found dead in suitcase was staying’ in Athens
News.content:
AN AFGHAN suspect arrested over the death of a Brit woman was reportedly a cleaner in the building where she was staying.

Elisabeth Ross, 38, was found stuffed inside a suitcase at an abandoned building in central Athens two weeks ago.



After a major manhunt, Greek cops said they had detained a 26-year-old Afghan man “for intentional homicide, robbery and violation of the law [regarding] weapons”.

The possibility Elisabeth was suffocated is being “seriously contemplated” given the lack of evident injuries on her body, a well placed source told the Sun.



Police found a replica pistol and a knife in a raid of the suspect‘s home, which is a ten-minute walk from the derelict block where Elisabeth’s body was found.

He was reportedly identified on CCTV using her credit cards to withdraw money from ATMs.



The suspect claimed the Scotswoman was already dead when he found her, but police have been working on the theory that Elisabeth was killed in the flat.

George Kalliakmanis, the president of the Attica Police Officers’ Union, told The Times: “[The suspect] and his wife worked as the cleaners of the building where Elisabeth lived.



“He allegedly killed her, took her bank card, and put her body in a suitcase or a box. He then transported it to the abandoned building using a trolley.

“Once there, he realised the suitcase he had used would likely contain his fingerprints, so he transferred the body into a second suitcase, trying to be more careful to avoid leaving prints.”

But cops were still able to find fingerprints and track the suspect down to Arachova, a mountain village in central Greece.



Elisabeth’s phone was used to send messages and mislead her loved ones until her identity was made public on July 29.

Her dad, a lawyer from Edinburgh, said he received texts for up to two weeks after her death.

Messages sent to family and friends claimed that she needed to take some time for herself and wanted to be alone for a while.

A Facebook post announcing that she was going to travel to Turkey was made on July 24, six days after her body was found, according to the Mail.

Elisabeth arrived in the Greek capital on a flight from Edinburgh on June 26.



A Greek couple who Elisabeth was staying with in Keratsini told cops she was going to stay with some Americans she knew in Kypseli.

But cops later revealed that they believed she used it as a cover story to visit the homeless community in central Athens without worrying her friends.

Elisabeth, known as Lisa, was reportedly seen chatting to homeless people close to an abandoned car park where they take drugs, drink and sleep rough.

She was a regular traveller to Greece and volunteered for One Heart – a charity which provides medical help for refugees from Afghanistan and Iran.

Her aunt, Anne Bangham, described her as a “beautiful loving and kind young lady”.



Greek authorities said her cause of death could be revealed in “days” as they fast-track crucial tests.

Tests on blood, urine and vital organ tissues will be key to determine if foul play was involved.

The Foreign and Commonwealth Office said earlier: “Our thoughts are with Elisabeth’s family during this difficult time.

“We are providing consular support and are in contact with the local authorities.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

A Police Scotland spokesperson said: “We are aware of the death of a Scottish woman in Athens and are liaising with authorities in Greece.



“Officers are providing support to her family in Scotland.”

News.title: Three people injured after ceiling collapses on dance floor at packed nightclub in Brit hols hotspot
News.content:
THREE people have been injured after a nightclub ceiling collapsed onto a packed dance floor at a British holiday hotspot.

Tourists were plunged into chaos when part of the ceiling came crashing down inside the newly opened Ave María nightclub in Torremolinos, on Spain’s Costa del Sol.



Horrifying footage shows revellers scrambling for the exits as panic erupted, with some seen shouting and others crying amid the mayhem.

Three people were rushed to hospital after being struck by falling debris.



The injured were two women, aged 28 and 31, and a 31-year-old man.

The trio were taken to the University Clinical Hospital of Malaga after the terrifying incident in the early hours of Sunday morning.



Their injuries are not yet known, nor have their nationalities been confirmed.

The packed club was in full swing when its decorative false ceiling suddenly gave way just before 1am.

A huge chunk of decorative cornice also came crashing down onto the dance floor, sending shockwaves through the packed venue.

Witnesses in the Plaza de la Nogalera raised the alarm after seeing part of the roof collapse without warning.



Others inside the nightclub were rapidly evacuated as fears grew that more of the structure could come crashing down.

Firefighters from the Provincial Consortium of Malaga raced to the scene alongside several Torremolinos Local Police patrols.

Crews secured the stricken area, checked for structural damage and worked to rule out the terrifying possibility of another collapse.

Police also cordoned off the area to clear the way for emergency crews and prevent crowds gathering around the danger zone.

The 061 Health Emergency Centre sent an ambulance, with paramedics assessing the injured before rushing all three to hospital.



All three were reportedly conscious and stable when they were admitted, although no medical reports detailing the severity of their injuries have been released.

The nightclub has since been sealed off as a precaution while technical reports are carried out by Torremolinos council and the Junta de Andalucía.

The collapse has also raised fresh questions over safety at entertainment venues during the height of the tourist season.

Ave María only opened its doors on June 3 and had quickly become a popular nightlife spot in Torremolinos.

The Plaza de la Nogalera is a bustling pedestrian area packed with bars, terraces and nightclubs that draws thousands of residents and tourists every weekend.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Now investigators are probing how a venue opened less than two months ago suffered such a shocking structural failure.

Officers will also examine whether the nightclub met all the necessary technical requirements when it opened.

News.title: Pointless French cops are billing us £8,000 for every migrant they stop… as another 2,000 arrive since Burnham became PM
News.content:
USELESS French cops were last night accused of ripping off UK taxpayers as it emerged Britain has been billed an estimated £8,000 for every migrant they actually stop.

Police in Calais have halted fewer illegals this year but are still set to rake in £1billion from border agreements.



Robert Bates, at the Centre for Migration Control, told The Sun: “The French are laughing at us. It is clear they have no real interest in ending the Channel crisis.”

Yesterday PM Andy Burnham pledged to crack down on the crisis on a visit to Dover.



The Premier, who has seen 2,000 migrants cross since he entered No 10 last month, vowed to bring back control of Britain’s borders but offered no specific plan.

Sun analysis of Home Office data reveals that since May 2024, 50,903 migrants have been prevented from crossing from Northern France.



Over the 27-month period, the UK has spent and allocated up to £411.5million on deals with France.

It includes an estimated £73.5million for this April to July under the terms of a deal signed under ex-PM Sir Keir Starmer in April.

It means for every person stopped from reaching British shores, taxpayers have footed a bill of £8,084.

Our funding estimate includes parts of the £476million deal signed by Tory ex-PM Rishi Sunak in 2023, and a new £662million agreement finalised this year.



Some £161million is results- dependent, meaning France may not get the full sum if they continue to fail to stop crossings.

Mr Bates added: “The French police cannot be relied on, refusing to stop boats in shallow water and standing by as hundreds depart from the shore. Those migrants that are stopped from crossing simply try again at a later date.”

Further Sun research shows police in Northern France are ­performing worse in 2026 than in 2025.

Between this January and the end of July, 34.8 per cent of attempted crossings were successfully halted.

That is down from 39 per cent for the same months in 2025, although total crossings were significantly higher then.



On Saturday, The Sun watched people-smugglers launch boats from beaches as kids played nearby.

Our pictures show up to 100 migrants in life jackets walking to an inflatable dinghy in Neufchâtel-Hardelot.

It picked up around 80 would-be asylum seekers at 4pm, while around 20 who could not fit in the dinghy trudged back to town.



Some 326 arrived here on Saturday as police appeared to do nothing to halt the migrants’ journey.

France counts arrests, dinghy captures and finds of smugglers’ gear — such as boats and life vests — as “preventions”.

But many who are stopped try again days or weeks later.

Updated rules mean “taxi boats” can be intercepted at sea.

But French cop unions are instructing members to stick to guidelines and stand back as soon as dinghies are in the water.



Some weeks have seen a total surrender by beach patrols.

Between June 15 and 21, 1,912 migrants arrived in the UK, while French officers stopped just 800.

During one week in late March, officers stopped only 39 people while 272 successfully launched.

Between July 19 and 26 — the week Mr Burnham became PM — 881 migrants arrived compared to 504 prevented.

Yesterday the PM insisted real progress was being made as he spoke to Interim Chief Coastguard John Craig and Duncan Capps, Border Security Commander.



Mr Burnham told reporters at the Border Force HQ near Dover: “Although this is the peak period for crossings, overall the number of crossings is down, the number of removals of people is up.

“So, there is progress, but we both recognise that we need to do more. The public don’t like the idea that the border looks like it’s not controlled. We need to bring back that control, but also we need to offer support for people who genuinely need it.

“It’s about changing the whole approach. There’s more to be done.”



During the visit Mr Burnham was shown a small boat which 96 migrants had used in May, plus a surveillance drone used to detect boat activity.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said she was “laser-light focused” on the issue on a visit to the National Crime Agency’s offices in Stratford, East London.

And she pointed out she has doubled the number of immigration crime officers from 376 to 791.

But Tory Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said if the Government was serious about controlling borders, it would accept the Conservatives’ plan to exit the European Convention on Human Rights.

Last Wednesday marked the busiest day for boat crossings this year, with 752 migrants arriving.



The provisional total for the year so far is 14,526. Two more boats arrived early yesterday.

Crossings are lower than the number recorded by this time last year, when 25,436 had made the journey, and down 14 per cent on the same period in 2024.

Home Office sources said they did not recognise the £411.5million figure.

They said only £342million has actually been paid so far under the terms of Britain’s Sandhurst arrangements with Paris.

Even at that rate, the cost would still be more than £6,700 per migrant.



A Home Office spokesman said: “This Government is bearing down on crossings, with removals of migrants at record levels, and asylum claims down by 12 per cent.

“The Home Secretary has signed a landmark payments-by-results deal with France to boost enforcement on beaches, strengthen intelligence-led disruption activity and put people-smugglers behind bars.

“The deal is delivering more officers, enhanced surveillance and tougher action against the criminal gangs behind these crossings. This has helped to seize more than 1,100 boats and engines that could have facilitated over 72,000 crossings, while preventing more than 46,000 attempted Channel crossings since the Election.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Meanwhile, Reform have committed to using the Navy to sweep up boats and return them to France or Belgium, saying the plan is backed by retired officers and Marines.

The party’s home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf warned: “To those with no right to enter Britain, our border will be impenetrable.”

News.title: 'Prince Harry and King Charles' public reunion would show even deep wounds can heal'
News.content:
'Prince Harry and King Charles' public reunion would show even deep wounds can heal'

Prince Harry, known as the Duke of Sussex, could soon appear in public together for the first time in years, which would signal a major shift in relations between the pair

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

A visible reunion between Prince Harry and the King at next year’s Invictus Games would carry meaning far beyond royal ceremony. Father and son have not been seen sharing any warmth in public since the Queen’s funeral in 2022. Harry attended his father’s coronation the following year, but there was no interaction between them, and he left soon afterwards. Since then, much has been said, written and regretted as the family’s rift has played out before the world. Yet beneath the titles, bitterness and endless headlines, they remain a father and son who, like any family, surely want to get along and find their way back to each other. Invictus, built on courage, recovery and refusing to give up, would be a fitting place for that healing to be seen. An appearance together in Birmingham would show that even deep wounds can mend, and could mark the moment reconciliation finally moves from private hope to public reality for them both.

‌



Fuellish crime

Once again, Donald Trump threatened Iran with death and destruction, only to pull back at the eleventh hour. But his reckless brinkmanship drove up oil prices, leaving motorists to pay at the pumps. Petrol now costs 160p a litre and diesel 179p. Fuel thefts from forecourts have risen by a fifth, with nearly £200,000 stolen every day. More drivers are filling up and speeding away, while repeat offenders pile pressure on retailers facing higher costs, staff abuse and threats. However hard household budgets are squeezed, theft can never be excused. Offenders must face justice. But while Trump keeps claiming peace is close, his boasts offer little reassurance. This reckless war must end before more lives, livelihoods and family finances are wrecked.

Little Britain

Russell Valentin crossed the Atlantic and discovered Britain’s greatest health craze: smaller portions, fewer mystery chemicals and plenty of walking. Nine stone later, he is living proof our food can work wonders. It turns out Britain’s secret weapon was decent grub, smaller servings and the long walk home each night.

News.title: Ross Kemp and Gary Lineker lead push to get Britain talking across divides
News.content:
Ross Kemp and Gary Lineker lead push to get Britain talking across divides

At a time of fraught political tensions and division in communities, a host of big names are backing a push to take the country back from extremists, and to build bridges not walls

Famous faces want you to join the National Conversation

Famous faces - including Ross Kemp, Gary Lineker and Delia Smith - have urged people to focus on the things we share as part of a project to bring the nation together.

‌



At a time of fraught political tensions and division in communities, a host of big names are backing a push to take the country back from extremists on all sides, and to build bridges not walls.

‌



The National Conversation, launched earlier this year, is compiling views from the public on how their community and this country should look, and what it means to be British.

‌



In a voice note for the project, EastEnders legend Ross said: “I think we're a great country. That doesn't mean we've got everything right. We haven't. And you know what? We won't.

Why The Mirror is launching Britain Talks with UK more divided than ever - and how you can take part READ MORE :

View 2 Images Ross Kemp led calls for the public to share their vision for Britain's future (Image: Ken McKay/ITV/REX/Shutterstock)

"But I think we do share values, ideas, and even eccentricities that mean we fight for the underdog, stand up for fairness on what is right.

‌



"It's what drove us to stand against the Nazis in our finest hour but it was also what made us look after our neighbours in Covid.”

His sentiments were echoed by TV star Gary, who said: “What is it that holds us together when social media and politics is trying to tear us apart? You see it in stadiums every weekend: different people cheering for the same thing.

"I think our country can be a bit more like that where we don't focus on our differences, but on what we are building together, where we are going.”

‌



View 2 Images Gary Lineker said he wanted to see the country focused on 'what we are building together' (Image: PA)

Chef Delia said: “What I would dearly love for my country and for the world is just one word, and that's unity.

"If we could all join forces so that it's us who are making all the decisions and running things, I think the world and our country would be a better place.”

‌



Actor Eddie Marsan said in his voice note: “I want a country where, in the words of Jo Cox, we realise that we have more in common than what divides us and we see ourselves in the other. We see ourselves in the more vulnerable, the dispossessed, the poor.”

And playwright James Graham added: "I just wish we could find ways and make more effort together to sometimes put ourselves in each other's literal company so that better, healthier, more reasonable conversations and more surprising conversations can happen."

Former Cabinet Minister Sir Sajid Javid, who co-chairs the Independent Commission on Community and Cohesion, said: “We often talk about what unites us as a country - this is the first serious attempt to actually map it out.

Article continues below

"Tens of thousands of people have already participated so make sure you don’t miss your chance to share your experience and to have your voice heard. ”

The Mirror is relaunching our ground-breaking ‘Britain Talks’ project in September, which will carry on from where the National Conversation ends. Using technology pioneered by our partners, Die Zeit in Germany, we will match you to someone who sees the world differently.

Mirror readers, and anyone who wants to step away from division, are urged to sign up here.

News.title: Five Mohamed Al-Fayed sex abuse survivors were victims of human trafficking
News.content:
Five Mohamed Al-Fayed sex abuse survivors were victims of human trafficking

One woman reported being recruited into a false role within Harrods, while two were hired for legitimate roles and selected for abuse "off the shop floor"

View 4 Images Mohamed Al-Fayed is at the centre of a trafficking investigation (Image: Daniel Hambury/PA Wire)

At least five survivors of sexual abuse at the hands of billionaire Harrods owner Mohamed Al-Fayed were victims of human trafficking.

Their experiences include international and domestic trafficking, as well as trafficking within the Harrods building itself. One survivor reported being recruited into a false role within Harrods, while two others were hired for legitimate roles and then selected for abuse off the shop floor.

Another survivor worked as a domestic worker for a member of the Fayed family after being recruited via a letting agency. Their cases date back to the nineties, while the most recent took place after Harrods was sold in 2010.

All five survivors have received conclusive grounds decisions from the National Referral Mechanism (NRM) that they are victims of modern slavery, after being referred by the charity Unseen UK. The NRM is the framework for identifying victims of modern slavery in the UK, including human trafficking, forced labour and servitude.

View 4 Images Mohamed Al-Fayed is at the centre of allegations over claims he trafficked women at Harrods (Image: BBC)

Commonwealth Games star trades Team Scotland for NHS doctor scrubs READ MORE :

Police, Border Force, the National Crime Agency and local authorities must offer an NRM referral to any adult they have reasonable grounds to believe may be a victim of modern slavery.

Charities like Unseen, the Salvation Army, Bernardo’s and the Refugee Council are also able to make referrals as non-statutory first responders.

In April, Rachel Louw had received a positive conclusive grounds decision, after reporting abuse suffered at the hands of Mohamed Al-Fayed and his late brother Salah, who died in 2010.

Since then, all four members of an advocacy group for Al-Fayed survivors called No One Above have received conclusive grounds decisions that they are victims of modern slavery.

Justine, Elizabeth, Margo and Isabella are not their real names but used to protect their identities. Justine worked at Harrods for more than three years in the nineties, and was trafficked and abused during this time.

She said: “It’s not something I realised was happening to me at the time, so it’s all part of this journey that we're on now in reliving this experience, and actually really understanding what happened to us, which is very difficult.

"But it’s a really significant thing, getting that decision, seeing it in writing that you were a victim of modern slavery and trafficking is very… it’s really shocking to read.”

View 4 Images Mohamed Al-Fayed pictured outside the London High Court in 2007 (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Justine said the Home Office had confirmed that survivors were victims of human trafficking and that the scope of experiences are wide.

They range from domestic to international trafficking, from those who worked at Harrods to those not involved with Harrods at all. She said this is very significant, because Harrods’ position has been that the abuse was just the actions of “one bad man”, and that there is nothing they can do now he is dead. Justine said: “These decisions illustrate that that is not the case at all.” Elizabeth was also a Harrods employee and received a conclusive grounds decision that she was a victim of modern slavery in May. She insisted that the victims were recruited, exploited and silenced and were all trafficked. She said: “Everybody connected with this case is a trafficking victim, because it was all one system. “You can’t say that victim A wasn’t trafficked and victim B was.

“I think there’s this persistent misunderstanding, possibly within the Metropolitan Police themselves, which is scary, that trafficking only involves being moved across international borders. “There have been positive conclusive grounds trafficking decisions in cases where the trafficking occurred within the Harrods building.” Margo was a domestic worker for Fayed after the sale of Harrods, and was recruited via a letting agency. She received a positive conclusive grounds decision that she was a victim of human trafficking in July. Margo had not felt like a victim of trafficking “because really I didn’t know what trafficking was, especially domestic trafficking”. She said the trafficking network went “so beyond Harrods”. “This was Balnagown, it was Saint-Tropez, it was Fayair, it was Fulham Football Club. “Everywhere he went he had enablers, and everywhere he went he had the capacity to abuse. All of his residences, all of his businesses,” she added.

View 4 Images Harrods Department store in London, once owned by Mohamed Al-Fayed (Image: SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images)

Margo did not originally come forward because she did not work at Harrods. She added: “There has just been so much emphasis put on Harrods to the point where I believe that there are so many more victims that haven’t come forward because they believe that it’s solely a Harrods issue. “I know of one other Hyde Park Residence victim, but there has to be hundreds more somewhere.” Isabella worked in the chairman’s office at Harrods in 2001. She received her conclusive grounds decision that she was a victim of trafficking in May. She said: “I think one thing that the public doesn’t understand is they think this was one bad man, but he couldn’t have done what he did without Harrods processing women to him and silencing them afterwards. “And it wasn’t just Harrods, obviously. It was any entity that Al-Fayed owned or had control of. “It was his yachts, his aviation business, the Ritz Paris, his properties all over France and Monaco, it went as far as the States and the UAE – anywhere that man touched.” It was not just Mohamed Al-Fayed either, she said, but “a wider network of perpetrators”. Isabella added: “We are not aware of any negative decisions in this case, and there have now been many self-initiated referrals through Unseen.”

Article continues below

Under UK law, human trafficking is defined by the 2015 Modern Slavery Act as a person arranging or facilitating the travel of another person with a view to that person being exploited, including for sexual purposes. It applies to movement into, out of, or within the UK, and victim consent is irrelevant. More than 400 allegations of sexual misconduct have been made against Al-Fayed, dating between 1977 and 2014, including sexual assault, rape, sexual exploitation and human trafficking. The Met Police are investigating at least 156 victims who contacted them directly, including 21 who came forward before Al-Fayed’s death in 2023 at the age of 94. The investigation, known as Operation Cornpoppy, is looking at people who may have facilitated or enabled his crimes. Four people have been questioned to date, 19 months after the investigation opened. The Home Office has been approached for comment

News.title: Drivers have stolen nearly £200,000 of fuel from UK forecourts every day since Iran war began
News.content:
Drivers have stolen nearly £200,000 of fuel from UK forecourts every day since Iran war began

An estimated daily average of £194,000-worth of petrol is stolen across Britain every day following the Iran war price surge, new data shows - that's 20 per cent more than before

View 4 Images Fuel theft is on the increase, statistics show (Image: Getty Images)

An average of nearly £200,000 of fuel has been swiped from ­forecourts every day since the start of the Iran oil crisis.

‌



Fuel theft prevention company ­Forecourt Eye said thefts soared by 20% in the five months after the conflict began on February 28, compared with the preceding five months.

‌



The increase in pump prices driven by the war means the value of stolen fuel rose by 48% in that period, reaching an estimated daily average of £194,000 across 8,359 forecourts.

‌



For first-time offenders, there was a 23% increase in incidents and a 26% rise in the volume of fuel stolen, compared with 17% and 20% ­respectively among repeat offenders.

View 4 Images A brazen thief fills fuel into plastic containers at a petrol station in Kent (Image: Forecourt Eye/PA Wire)

The figures are based on reports by a representative sample of 550 forecourts.

‌



They include drive-offs, when there is no attempt to pay, and no-means-of-payment incidents, when a customer fills up and claims they have no way to pay. The average price of a litre of petrol climbed to 160p on Friday.

That was about 27p more than before the conflict, and represented a three-and-a-half year high. The average price of diesel is about 37p per litre higher than prior to the war, at 179p.

Forecourt Eye is offering free access to crime reporting technology to its customers, which it said will make it easier to record fuel thefts, shop crime and other illegal incidents.

‌



View 4 Images Ben Lawrence says the thefts are no longer mainly carried out by people involved in other crimes (Image: Barnett Creative/PA Wire)

Users will also have the option of joining a live facial recognition network run by Facewatch to alert them to known offenders. Forecourt Eye managing director, Michelle Henchoz, said: “As offending becomes more organised and more sophisticated, operators need joined-up technology that helps them protect both their forecourt and their convenience store.”

Gordon Balmer, ­executive director of the Petrol Retailers ­Association, which ­represents independent forecourts, said its members are “reporting increasing levels of abuse and aggression towards colleagues who are simply doing their jobs and have no influence over the price displayed on the forecourt”.

‌



View 4 Images Prices have risen dramatically since Donald Trump's war with Iran (Image: Getty IMages)

He added: “Bringing together ­technologies that help retailers prevent crime, manage incidents and support police investigations is a positive step for the industry.”

Ben Lawrence, a director at Lawrences Garages, which owns five petrol stations in Norfolk and ­Hampshire, said fuel thefts were ­historically often carried out by people involved in other crimes. But rises in the cost of living mean this is no longer the case.

Article continues below

He said there is a “misconception” that all forecourts featuring branding from energy giants such as BP and Shell are operated by those companies, rather than smaller businesses.

So some drivers believe it “doesn’t matter” when they fail to pay.

He said: “It does matter to us. When someone drives off after taking fuel worth £80-£90, it’s hitting us, not the oil companies. We’ve already purchased it.”

News.title: More than one in 10 households do not plan to follow the hosepipe ban as UK plunged into drought
News.content:
More than one in 10 households do not plan to follow the hosepipe ban as UK plunged into drought

Around 40% of the UK households have been hit with a hosepipe ban but a new survey has suggested some people will not follow the restriction with just 49% supporting the ban

View 3 Images Stock image of a person using a hosepipe in their garden (Image: Getty Images/Image Source)

A staggering one in 10 households do not intend to follow the hosepipe bans enforced in their areas after droughts were announced across large parts of the nation, according to a survey.

‌



The UK has been hit with four heatwaves so far this year, with temperatures toping a staggering 35C. Some parts of the UK recorded just 1mm of rainfall in July, with millions of households being hit with hosepipe bans across the country. Despite this, a new survey suggested around 11% of households living within a ban area do not intend to follow the restriction.

‌



Around 5% of people said they did not yet know if they would stick to the ban, a YouGov poll of more than 4,200 adults found.

‌



Met Office confirms July is driest on record as heatwaves plunge UK into drought READ MORE :

View 3 Images Dry grass around Chesterton Windmill in Warwickshire, on Sunday (Image: Jacob King/PA Wire)

The poll also revealed what people would do if they saw next-door using a hosepipe when they shouldn't. Some 10% of householders said they would report a neighbour using a hose in their garden while a ban was in place and 71% said they would not, with the remainder unsure.

Seven water companies have introduced the restrictions – officially known as a "Temporary Use Ban" – affecting 23 million customers, or around 40% of England's population. These companies are: Affinity Water, Anglian Water, Cambridge Water, Southern Water, South East Water, Thames Water and South West Water.

‌



View 3 Images Dry grass at Kensington Palace Gardens in London, on Friday (Image: Aaron Chown/PA Wire)

The poll suggested the public was split on the overall measure with just half of households (49%) saying they supported a hosepipe ban in their local area, while 35% said they opposed the restrictions. A significant number of people said they believed those on a meter should be able to use as much water as they needed because they were paying for it.

Other reasons given by people polled for ignoring a ban were concerns about fruit and vegetables going to waste because they were too difficult to water with a watering can. Another reason was to help wildlife in the garden.

‌



Some people raged about water companies and the price of their bills, with one person saying: "I pay an extortionate amount for my water. It is not my problem that water companies would rather give their CEOs ridiculous amounts of money instead of building new reservoirs."

Households in ban areas are able to use a watering can and can use a hosepipe to water food crops at home or in an allotment, when a can is not an easy option. Drip irrigation systems are also allowed as long as it is fitted with a timer and pressure-reducing valve and delivers water directly to the soil rather than spraying it into the air.

The bans come as almost a third of England – including parts of the South East, Midlands and North West – languish in "prolonged dry weather" status, with only the North East and Yorkshire still seeing "normal" conditions for the time of year.

Article continues below

A Water UK spokeswoman said: “We are incredibly grateful to customers for doing their bit to protect our environment and preserve our water supplies. Some parts of the country have seen demand for water rise by more than a third.

"Water companies are working round the clock fixing leaks, moving water across regions and running treatment works flat out to keep supplies flowing, and we urge all customers to use water wisely."

An Environment Agency spokeswoman said: "A hosepipe can use 1,000 litres an hour – which is more than a family-of-four will use in a day. These short-term bans allow companies to conserve their supplies as we don't know when this drought will end."

News.title: Boy, 3, rushed to hospital with serious injuries after being hit by van at campsite
News.content:
Boy, 3, rushed to hospital with serious injuries after being hit by van at campsite

The boy was rushed to hospital in an air ambulance after the collision took place on the family run-campsite and is currently being treated for serious injuries

View 2 Images A three year-old boy has been seriously injured in a collision at a campsite (Image: Red House Farm)

A three-year old boy has been seriously injured after being hit by a van at a UK campsite.

‌



The toddler was rushed to hospital in an air ambulance from Red House Farm in Earnley, near Chichester after the incident on Saturday.

‌



Police were called by witnesses at around 7.30pm.

‌



Sussex Police have said that no arrests have been made and an investigation is underway.

The boy is being treated for serious injuries.

View 2 Images Sussex Police were called to the scene (Image: DAILY RECORD)

‌



Witnesses said the air ambulance was at the scene of the campsite on Bookers Lane at around 9pm, according to the Mail.

A spokesperson for Sussex Police said: "Emergency services responded to a collision at a campsite in Bookers Lane, Earnley, Chichester, at around 7.30pm on Saturday, August 1.

"A three-year-old boy was injured after he was involved in a collision with a van and he was taken to hospital for treatment.

‌



"No arrests were made and police are investigating the circumstances."

Red House Farm is a family-run campsite just three miles from West Wittering Beach in Chichester.

It is a small site with ten pitches for caravans and motorhomes and 20 spots for tents.

Article continues below

It also has four 'luxury glamping pods' on site.

News.title: Parts of UK to roast in 34C heat as temperatures 'rapidly rise' and health alert issued
News.content:
Parts of UK to roast in 34C heat as temperatures 'rapidly rise' and health alert issued

The soaring temperatures come as half of England and the whole of Wales are already in drought, with fire crews battling multiple blazes across the UK

View 3 Images A drought has been declared across half of England and all of Wales (Image: Vuk Valcic/SOPA Images/Shutterstock)

Parts of the UK will once again be hit by scorching temperatures that could reach up to 34C, making it hotter than popular holiday destinations like Santorini or Barcelona.

‌



"Hot and very humid air" will be imported into Monday in southern England, with temperatures "rapidly" rising into the mid-30s. This resulted in fresh yellow and amber heat health warnings being issued for England by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

‌



Met Office meteorologist Tom Morgan said: "Many parts of England and Wales will see plenty of sunshine and once again the temperatures will rapidly rise in that strong August sunshine so turning into an increasingly humid and very hot day in the south east of England in particular, where temperatures may well approach the mid-30s.

‌



"Tropical nights on Tuesday as well in the south as temperatures will remain above 20 in some places."

Mr Morgan added that, while parts of Northern Ireland and Scotland will experience some rain on Monday, England and Wales "will stay largely dry, with some clear spells, and a much more uncomfortable night for sleeping compared to last night".

View 3 Images Met Office meteorologist Tom Morgan said the high temperatures will also make sleeping uncomfortable (Image: Met Office)

‌



Tomorrow, popular holiday destinations like Barcelona and Santorini will see lower temperatures compared to parts of southern England. These are forecast to peak at 30C and 26C, respectively.

The East Midlands, East of England, London and South East of England will all be covered by a UKHSA amber heat health warning from 9am tomorrow until 9am on Wednesday. This means "significant impacts are likely across health and social care services due to the high temperatures".

View 3 Images Temperatures will peak on Monday afternoon (Image: Met Office)

‌



These include a rise in deaths, particularly among the elderly and those with health conditions, increased demand on health and social care services and indoor environments overheating. The North West, Yorkshire and the Humber, West Midlands and South West are covered by a yellow heat health warning for the same period of time.

This means significant impacts are "possible" across health and social care services. The Met Office forecast for Monday reads: "Rain affecting much of Scotland on Monday, some heavy.

"Scattered showers across Northern Ireland and other western areas, though most of England and Wales fine with some hot sunshine. Humid." Earlier this week, the Government announced half of England is now in drought.

Article continues below

The seven areas are East Anglia, Hertfordshire and the whole of London, Thames Valley, Hampshire & the Isle of Wight, Devon & Cornwall, the West Midlands and Wessex. The whole of Wales is also in drought.

News.title: UK weather maps show exact time violent thunderstorms to abruptly end heatwave
News.content:
UK weather maps show exact time violent thunderstorms to abruptly end heatwave

The relentless high pressure - which led to a 27.8C high on Saturday in Surrey - could come to an end within the next few days with spells of heavy rain and even thunderstorms

View 4 Images Thunderstorms are on the way for some with heavy rain also possible (Image: Getty Images)

These striking weather maps show when thunderstorms will bring weeks of scorching sunshine to an abrupt halt.

‌



Many Brits will briefly say goodbye to the dry summer for a few hours at least this week, with rain bringing sweet relief to millions. Several counties across the country saw less than 1mm of rainfall in July, with more than half of England and the entirety of Wales officially in drought.

‌



The UK has been hit with four heatwaves so far in 2026, with wildfires causing devastation in Suffolk, the New Forest, Hampshire, Berkshire, Oxfordshire and Dorset. But a large amount of rain could be on its way in the days ahead for some as weather forecasters at Ventusky detail the areas where conditions will switch. It uses data provided by meteorologists at Metdesk.

‌



View 4 Images The outlook at 4am on Tuesday morning

UK wildfires cause devastation to rare wildlife habitats that could take 25 years to recover READ MORE :

Met Office names 29 areas facing heavy rain on Monday – see full list READ MORE :

On Tuesday, an area of low pressure will extend across the UK from the south west, bringing a spell of potentially heavy rain to parts of the north with showers in the south.

This will also bring warmer and more humid air back across England and Wales, with 30C likely to be exceeded again for some. Some areas are expected to experience thunderstorms, with maps showing that at around 4am parts of Northern Ireland possibly seeing thunderstorms. Cumbria and the Northeast of England could also see flashes of thunder as well as heavy showers, with an area of low pressure also covering much of Scotland.

‌



By 7am, the rain moves down to north Wales, with storms also expected in parts of the Northwest of England. The soggy start to Tuesday will be felt in part of the Midlands and as far south as as Devon and Hampshire.

View 4 Images By 7am, more heavy rain is on the way

The 10am maps show thunderstorms could be felt in parts of Cumbria and again in Scotland as rain moves over the east of the England, with areas in Berkshire and Birmingham predicted to see some rainfall. By 4pm, the storms could return across the Irish sea, with data showing Belfast could be struck with storms.

‌



No official weather warning for rain or thunderstorms are in place at this time.

Met Office Chief Forecaster Chris Bulmer said: “A change in weather type early next week will see warmer conditions return across England and Wales but in contrast to much of the summer, this will be associated with showers or perhaps thunderstorms for some places.

"However, some parts of the south will only see small amounts of rain. It will stay cooler in the north with the potential for heavy rain to build up, especially over parts of Scotland.”

‌



View 4 Images Thunderstorms will continue until after 10am

The UK Health Security Agency has heat alerts in place for several areas from Sunday, August 2 until Wednesday August 5 at 9am.

The UK has been experiencing skyrocketing temperatures throughout the day and night, with extreme heat sweeping through the nation. Conditions this summer have resulted in record-breaking temperatures and three heatwaves.

Article continues below

But maps for August 10 show huge blue patches covering parts as far as the Scottish Highlands and as far south as Cornwall.

A large chunk of England will also experience wet conditions, with the heaviest rain across the North and the Midlands. Parts of Wales will see light rain, as well as the south, though most of the region will escape the rain by evening. Temperatures are also expected to be moderate potentially ranging in the mid-10s.

News.title: Burnham pledges to be 'relentless' in curbing small boat crossings
News.content:
Andy Burnham has pledged his government will be "relentless" in curbing the number of people arriving in the UK on small boats.

The prime minister said progress had been made and the government was "changing the whole approach", with enforcement officers tackling people-smuggling gangs doubled on both sides of the Channel.

"People want to see this issue addressed," he said in Dover, adding: "We also need to build a system that offers safe routes for people as well, because that also takes away the selling point of the gangs."

The Conservatives said that Labour had not delivered on its promises on migration, while Reform UK said it would deploy the Royal Navy to ward off crossings.

Political discussions around the UK's policies on illegal migration have resurfaced since tens of thousands of migrants swam into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta on Thursday.

Burnham noted that 98% of the people who swam to the African territory had been returned to Morocco - which he said had dealt with the immediate issue.

But he added: "There's a broader issue about the Schengen area and our relationship with it, and of course, I would want to be in regular dialogue with the EU on those issues."

His comments came shortly after the Home Office announced that the number of National Crime Agency (NCA) officers tackling smuggling gangs facilitating small boat crossings had risen to almost 800 from 376 at the start of 2025.

Burnham said there had been a similar doubling of French officers.

Asked whether he wanted to change the tone of the debate around small boats, he said that he wanted to "deal with the issue rather than play politics with the issue".

He added: "The public don't like the idea that the border looks like it's not controlled. We need to bring back that control. But also we need to offer support for people who genuinely need it."

News.title: Ariana Grande to take a break from public life amid 'endless' scrutiny
News.content:
Ariana Grande is to withdraw from public appearances and will no longer star in an upcoming musical production in London when she ends her Eternal Sunshine tour next month.

A representative for the US singer, 33, told People magazine that she "will be taking a step back from visibility" when the tour ends, after her appearances led to "endless, ongoing public scrutiny".

The company behind a revival of Stephen Sondheim's Sunday in the Park with George, due to play at the Barbican in 2027, confirmed that she would no longer be part of the production and had its "complete understanding and support".

Grande's physical appearance and health have been a topic of speculation in recent years.

This speculation has increased since the release of her latest album, Petal, two days ago and her appearance in promotional material for it.

Her representative stressed to People that Grande looked forward to finishing her tour "on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny".

They added: "She performs a very physical show, and there is a lot of athleticism involved. She performs healthily and successfully at a very high level night after night."

The tour's last show is slated for 1 September in London.

The Thank U, Next and 7 Rings singer was billed to appear alongside her Wicked co-star, British actor Jonathan Bailey, in the new production of Sondheim's critically acclaimed 1984 musical.

A representative for Empire Street Productions confirmed to the BBC that the musical would go ahead without Grande.

"Following this evening's announcement from Ariana Grande's team, we can confirm that she has decided to step back from Sunday in the Park with George," they said.

"We know this cannot have been an easy decision, and she makes it with our complete understanding and support. We wish her nothing but the best."

A replacement for Grande in the West End revival of the Pulitzer Prizeâwinning musical has not yet been named.

The BBC has approached Grande's representatives.

Scrutiny surrounding Grande's appearance was brought back to the limelight after the release of a music video for her latest single, Petal, from an album of the same name.

In the music video, Grande plays a performer who is repeatedly told in auditions that she is "not good enough", is "desperate" and that she "should get some work done" then that she has "too much work done." The character eventually takes a chainsaw to the critics.

News.title: Prolonged drought could cause shortage of some foods, farmers' union head says
News.content:
Bradshaw also suggested farmers should be given tax breaks to build water storage systems on their land to prepare for the years ahead.

"We have taken our food supply for granted for far too long," he added.

"Those other countries around the world that we currently rely on to produce our food and vegetables, their climates are changing as well.

"It does feel like there is going be some shortages of [food] products", Bradshaw told Radio 4's Broadcasting House.

In a message to Prime Minister Andy Burnham, he said: "Let's draw a line in the sand and make sure we prioritise domestic food production to deliver growth across the UK."

After a wet and mild start to the year, it has been exceptionally dry hot and dry with a succession of heatwaves across the UK.

The combination of low rainfall and prolonged heat has quickly depleted water reserves in soils, vegetation and rivers.

While droughts can occur naturally, climate change is making weather patterns more erratic, and heatwaves more frequent and intense.

Scientists say there is a greater risk of droughts happening as a result, and of them being more severe and longer-lasting when they do.

The Met Office reports that England saw just 5.6mm of rainfall up to 30 July â just 8% of its long-term meteorological average for the month and less than half of the previous record of 13.4mm set in 1911.

For Wales it was 7.9mm of rainfall, also 8% of its long-term average for the month and almost a third of the previous record of 22.6mm, again set in 1911.

Heat health alerts are in place across most of England until at least 09:00 BST on Wednesday.

Amber alerts indicate a rise in deaths of vulnerable people and increased demand on health services are likely, while yellow alerts indicate these are possible.

News.title: Man admits transporting Scottish woman's body in suitcase, Greek police say
News.content:
Greek police say a man has admitted transporting the body of a Scottish woman in a suitcase to an abandoned building.

Elisabeth-Jane Ross, 38, was found in the Kypseli district of Athens on 18 July, days after she was reported missing.

Local officers launched an investigation with cooperation from authorities in the US, the UK and Scotland, and now say they have arrested a 26-year-old man - the BBC understands he is from Afghanistan.

The force said he was brought to police headquarters on Thursday where he "confessed to his actions". He was arrested on suspicion of manslaughter, robbery and weapons offences, but the exact charges have yet to be finalised under the Greek legal system.

News.title: 'No guarantees' - joyful Glasgow cannot banish all Commonwealth Games doubts
News.content:
After Victoria withdrew in 2023, Glasgow answered the SOS call - and organisers say the past 11 days in the Scottish city have "exceeded all expectations".

Yes, there have been grumbles - including from those who have seen parking spaces outside their houses taken - and taxi drivers and shop owners the Games have passed by.

On the ground, though, this felt like a meaningful event.

Ticket sales of 434,000 were well down from 1.5 million for Birmingham 2022, but they were always going to be given the smaller venues for this scaled-back edition. It has been rare to enter a venue and not find a joyful, engaged crowd.

There was plenty of excitement for fans, too - Josh Kerr's golden homecoming at Scotstoun, Angharad Evans making the swimming pool floors shake, and Neil Fachie's emotional victory on his return to the Sir Chris Hoy Velodrome.

They also celebrated Jamaica's seismic netball win over Australia. Live sport rarely fails to deliver.

But a nagging question has remained throughout: is anyone else watching?

Big names such as Kerr and Adam Ramsay-Peaty - with his emotional reaction to taking bronze in the pool - broke out of this Glaswegian bubble, but what else?

Organisers said their social media views passed those of Birmingham within the opening few days and highlighted record-breaking television figures in Australia and New Zealand, where the Games were free-to-air.

Still, without that same coverage in the UK, these Games have - at times - drifted by.

Glasgow 2026 was also hurt by the absence or late withdrawal of big-name competitors, particularly in athletics, which missed Keely Hodgkinson, Katarina Johnson-Thompson and Dina Asher-Smith.

The Games' differing relevance between sports was again clear - for netball, this remains the pinnacle and is treated as such; for others, it is a stepping stone. Many narratives focused on the "next generation".

Eighteen-year-old Jersey swimmer Filip Nowacki was perhaps the most exciting name to emerge, but gymnasts Ruby Evans (Wales) and Reuben Ward (Scotland) and England track cyclist Henry Hobbs, who won two golds and a bronze, were others.

Swimmer Faye Rogers impressively brought her success at the Paralympics back to Glasgow with gold in the pool - and then competed in the non-para event as well.

Cyclist Emma Finucane turned her three Olympic medals in Paris into four Commonwealth golds in Glasgow.

All will have their eyes on Los Angeles in 2028.

News.title: Massive Attack respond after Singapore ban over Palestine display
News.content:
Massive Attack have said they were "surprised and disappointed" by their treatment by Singaporean authorities after expressing pro-Palestine sentiments during a performance in the city-state.

The group wrote on Instagram on Sunday that its members were "detained by the police, isolated and separately questioned", with some subject to hotel room searches and temporary passport confiscation.

The band's two members held up a Palestinian flag during its 29 July show there and shouted "free Palestine" alongside members of the audience.

Singapore, which has stringent rules on public speech and assembly, subsequently said it had indefinitely banned Massive Attack from returning to the country.

A police spokeswoman told the BBC on Friday that the two band members would not be allowed to re-enter Singapore and were barred from performing there.

Robert Del Naja and Grant Marshall were "given stern warnings" concerning alleged offences under two laws that restrict the public display of foreign flags and regulate political expressions at public events.

Massive Attack said that before the show and again at the end "large sections of the auditorium organically led chants of 'Free Palestine', presumably aware but undeterred that this spontaneous expression alone could violate their government's censorship laws".

The band did not address the ban directly, but described the situation as a "surreal experience" and said they "did not imagine that merely holding up the flag of a sovereign state recognised by 157 countries would violate any law".

They added that they were "proud to have made the impromptu expression" with fans in Singapore, who "clearly felt a moral imperative to show solidarity with the people of Palestine".

Massive Attack are known for openly expressing their political stance on a range of issues, including the war in Gaza.

Del Naja was arrested earlier this year on suspicion of showing support for the proscribed organisation Palestine Action during a protest in London.

The 61-year-old sat among hundreds of fellow demonstrators with a sign that read "I Oppose Genocide, I Support Palestine Action".

Singapore has taken a strong stance on public statements on the Israel-Gaza war, with authorities in the multicultural country insisting this was necessary to preserve racial and social harmony.

The home affairs ministry put out a statement in 2023 advising against "the public display and wearing of articles" in relation to the Israel-Gaza war, including foreign national emblems.

Massive Attack are currently on a world tour, with performances next week in Australia following the end of its Asia leg.

The BBC has contacted the Singaporean police for comment.

News.title: Three in hospital after fire and crush at festival in London
News.content:
Three people were taken to hospital after a fire and crush at the entrance of a festival.

Organisers of Ghana Party in the Park, also known as Shattafest UK, at Copthall Playing Fields in Barnet, London, said the event was stopped following a "major incident" at about 18:00 BST on Saturday.

The Metropolitan Police said a fire had started near the gates, which meant they were closed temporarily.

A crowd built up, and there was a surge when the gates reopened, it said.

Organisers said the decision to end the festival was made on health and safety grounds.

They said in a statement the day had been "one of the most difficult" in the event's history and called what happened "deeply upsetting".

News.title: The change that may help you get a mortgage as a first-time buyer
News.content:
If you're working towards buying your first home you might feel like everything is stacked against you - but recent changes could help you get a mortgage.

It hard to save for a deposit when the cost of living is so high, the average house price is nearly Â£300,000, external and interest rates on new mortgages are rising.

However, a rule change and more flexible lending mean first-time buyers can now borrow up to six, or at the most, seven times what you earn in a year.

This means mortgages will be within reach for more people but it is a shift that comes with some risk so here's what you need to know.

News.title: Body of mountaineer Nirmal Purja recovered after Pakistan avalanche
News.content:
Prince William said he was "truly saddened to hear of the tragic death" of Purja, who he said "served with distinction" as a soldier before "becoming one of the greatest mountaineers".

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said in a post on X: "Incredibly sad to learn of the passing of Nirmal (Nims) Purja and those he was climbing with.

"He was an inspirational man who served in our Armed Forces for many years - and whose incredible mountaineering adventures are known the world over."

Naila Kiani, a spokesperson for the Alpine Club of Pakistan which is involved in the rescue efforts, told BBC's Newshour programme on Saturday that her organisation feared all members of the group were dead, and that Purja had led many expeditions she was on.

Praising his leadership skills, she described him as a "very experienced climber and fearless".

Teams in Pakistan have been searching for the climbers on the world's 12th-highest summit since Thursday's avalanche on the 8,047m (26,400ft) peak in the Karakoram range.

The multinational climbing group was being led by Purja. Also known as Nims, he rose to prominence in 2019 when he climbed all 14 of the world's mountains with peaks above 8,000m in 189 days - smashing the previous record by more than seven years.

He became widely known following a Netflix documentary chronicling his journey, 14 Peaks: Nothing Is Impossible, released two years later.

At the time, he said: "It has been a gruelling but humbling six months, and I hope to have proven that anything is possible with some determination, self-belief and positivity."

Purja served in the British military for 16 years, 10 of which were spent in the special forces, and he was awarded an MBE by the late Queen in 2018 for his achievement in extreme high-altitude mountaineering.

Purja, who lived with his wife and three-year-old daughter in Hampshire in southern England, said he was also the first Gurkha to climb Everest while serving in the British military.

In his last post on X, published on Monday, he said he had not intended to climb Broad Peak.

"Initially, the plan was to climb just G2," Purja wrote, referring to Gasherbrum II, another peak in the Karakoram mountain range.

But right before he set off for Pakistan, he realised if he also managed to climb Broad Peak while he was there, he would have only one more mountain to conquer before becoming the "first person in history to climb all 14 eight-thousanders twice. Without oxygen."

An eight-thousander is a mountain that rises more than 8,000m above sea level.

"This wasn't planned," Purja wrote. "But opportunities don't scream: they whisper to those already working in silence."

"Broad Peak, I ask for nothing but safe passage up and back down. I take zero mountains for granted," he wrote.

Broad Peak is regarded as one of the more challenging mountains for climbers. The first successful ascent was in 1957, when an Austrian expedition reached the summit.

Since then, many more have climbed the mountain, but dozens have lost their lives.

One of Broad Peak's deadliest years was 2013, when at least six fatalities were recorded.

News.title: Teenager dies after 'medical episode' at Kendal Calling festival in Cumbria
News.content:
A teenage girl died at the Kendal Calling festival in the early hours of the morning, police have said.

The 17-year-old suffered a medical episode at about 02:15 BST and was pronounced dead at the scene, according to Cumbria Police. The force asked people not to speculate about the circumstances of the incident.

It added officers were looking into the circumstances and wanted to speak to anyone who was in the area of the Calling Out tent and the Big Wheel around the time of the girl's death.

A spokesperson said: "Officers are particularly keen to speak with a group of women who alerted first responders to the girl after becoming concerned for her welfare."

They said the girl's family had been informed and were being supported by specialist officers.

The force asked people not to speculate, saying it could have a "significant impact" on the family and friends involved.

"We would ask that the investigation be allowed to take its course."

News.title: Ballot paper for Clacton by-election is longest in British electoral history
News.content:
The longest ballot paper in British political history is costing four times as much to print than regular ballot papers, the local council has said.

The list for the Clacton parliamentary by-election, which was prompted by the resignation of Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, is 90cm (3ft) long.

When people unfold the paper, they will find it is longer than most adults' arms.

Tendring District Council chief executive Ian Davidson - who is the acting returning officer for the by-election in the Essex constituency - said organising the vote had been "manic".

People have already started returning postal votes to town hall and most registered voters will go to polling stations on 13 August.

Davidson said: "We've logistically been looking at the size of the ballot paper, how we fold it to get it into the envelope so we can send it out to our postal voters [and] how we manage the polling stations."

News.title: Four arrested over hate crime attack on ship crew
News.content:
Three men have been arrested on suspicion of attempted murder after a Filipino crew member of a cargo ship was attacked in what police described as a hate crime.
