Where you can fish along the Costanera

The classic spot is the Costanera Norte, the public riverfront promenade running along the Río de la Plata. Shore fishing here is a long-standing local tradition, tolerated on the open city waterfront.

The scene is social as much as sporting. Regulars stake out favourite railings, share bait tips and treat the promenade as an extension of the neighbourhood, especially at weekends.

Not every stretch of waterfront is open, though. The Reserva Ecológica Costanera Sur, the wetland reserve on the southern side, prohibits fishing within its boundaries, and that rule is enforced.

Between the reserve and the northern promenade, the accessible fishing is really about the public shoreline, where the river opens out wide enough to feel more like a coast than a city river.

Timing shapes the experience more than any single spot. Dawn and dusk draw the most dedicated anglers, while the middle of the day tends to belong to walkers, cyclists and families sharing the same promenade.

The width of the river here is striking. On a clear day the far bank is barely visible, and the horizon of open water gives the northern promenade an almost seaside character rare in a capital city.

Licences: city shoreline versus provincial waters

On the CABA shoreline you do not need a city fishing licence to cast from the Costanera. That is a large part of why the spot is so accessible to newcomers and casual anglers alike.

The picture changes the moment you move into Buenos Aires province. Provincial waters require a licence under Ley 11477, and enforcement is a real possibility rather than a formality to be ignored.

If you plan to fish beyond the city, sort the paperwork first. The line between tolerated city shoreline and regulated provincial water is not always obvious from the bank, so err towards compliance.

The distinction is jurisdictional rather than cosmetic. The city of Buenos Aires and the surrounding province set their own rules, and the same river can carry different requirements depending on which side of that line you stand.

For visitors, the safe reading is simple: treat the city promenade as the easy, licence-free option, and assume anything further afield needs paperwork. When in doubt, ask locally before you cast.

What you are likely to catch

The Río de la Plata is surprisingly generous for an urban river. Common catches include pejerrey, boga, bagre, carpa and patí, with pejerrey the local favourite in the cooler months.

Species and success vary with season, water level and weather. Wind direction on the estuary can change the fishing dramatically from one day to the next, so two visits rarely feel the same.

For many regulars, the appeal is the ritual rather than the haul. A morning on the Costanera is about the river, the company and the wait as much as whatever ends up on the line.

Bait and technique shift with the target species. Regulars tailor their rigs to whatever is running, and a friendly question along the railing usually yields more useful advice than any guidebook.

Sábalo also features heavily in the river’s ecology, and it is the species that recurs most often in the contamination studies. That makes it a useful marker for why the eating question matters so much here.

Numbers can be deceptive on a slow morning, and blank sessions happen even for locals. Part of the appeal is reading the water and the weather, and part is simply patience on a bench beside the estuary.

The catch you should not eat

This is the spine of the whole subject. Studies by UNLP and provincial bodies have found PCBs in Río de la Plata fish above the guideline in Argentina’s Código Alimentario, and sábalo has been flagged as “no apto para consumo” — not fit for consumption.

The contamination story does not end with PCBs. A 2023 study reported record levels of glyphosate in sábalo and came with a public warning, underlining how much industrial and agricultural residue the basin carries.

The Riachuelo basin, which drains into the same system, has carried long-standing health advisories of its own. Decades of industrial discharge have left a legacy that fish accumulate in their tissue over time.

The uncomfortable takeaway is simple. The water may look inviting on a bright morning, but the fish sit at the end of a contaminated food chain, and ordinary cooking does not remove these contaminants.

Contaminants such as PCBs and glyphosate build up the food chain and lodge in fatty tissue, which is why long-lived and bottom-feeding species tend to carry the highest burdens. It is not a matter of one bad fish but of the whole system.

Advisories of this kind are not unique to Buenos Aires, as many industrialised river mouths carry them. But the combination of PCBs, glyphosate and the Riachuelo’s legacy makes the local case unusually well documented.

Why catch-and-release is the only sensible approach

Given the science, the responsible framing for Costanera fishing is catch-and-release. Enjoy the sport, photograph the fish if you like, and return it to the water rather than the frying pan.

Handling matters if release is the goal. Wet your hands, keep the fish in the water where possible, use barbless or de-barbed hooks and avoid long air exposure to give it the best chance of recovery.

Treating the activity as recreation rather than provisioning also sidesteps the health and legal grey areas entirely. There is nothing to inspect on a plate if there is no plate.

For the wider environmental backdrop, coverage of the Riachuelo clean-up explains why advisories along this river system have persisted for so long.

None of this need spoil the appeal. Anglers around the world increasingly fish for the experience alone, returning their catch, and the Costanera fits neatly into that ethic given what the science says about the water.

A landing net, forceps for hook removal and a damp cloth for handling all make release cleaner and kinder. Small kit choices add up to better survival odds for the fish you let go.

Gear, tides and etiquette on the waterfront

A basic surf or float set-up covers most Costanera fishing, and local tackle shops can point beginners to the right rig for pejerrey. Bring layers, because the riverfront wind bites in the cooler months.

The estuary is tidal and wind-driven rather than strongly currented, so water levels shift with the weather more than with a clock. Watching what the regulars do is the fastest way to read the conditions.

Etiquette is straightforward. Give other anglers space, take your litter and discarded line home, and keep clear of the reserve boundaries where fishing is prohibited; guides to the city’s green spaces map where those limits fall.

Safety on the bank deserves a thought too. Railings can be slick, the water is deeper and stronger than it looks, and keeping an eye on children near the edge is simply sensible.

Respecting the shared nature of the promenade goes a long way. This is public space used by many people at once, and anglers who stay tidy, quiet and considerate help keep the tradition welcome.

Before You Cast Where: The public Costanera Norte shoreline is open for shore fishing; the Reserva Ecologica Costanera Sur is off-limits. Licence: No CABA permit is needed on the city shoreline, but provincial waters require a licence under Ley 11477. Catch: Common species include pejerrey, boga, bagre, carpa and pati. Do not eat the fish: Studies found PCBs above the Codigo Alimentario limit and record glyphosate in sabalo, flagged unfit for consumption. Practice: Treat the whole outing as catch-and-release. Rules and advisories change; confirm with provincial authorities before fishing.

This is reporting, not travel advice. Confirm dates, prices and rules with official sources before booking.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a licence to fish on the Costanera? Not on the Buenos Aires city shoreline. Shore fishing from the public Costanera Norte is tolerated without a CABA licence, which is a big reason the spot is popular with casual anglers. The rules change once you move into Buenos Aires province, where a licence is required under Ley 11477 and enforcement is a real possibility. If you plan to fish beyond the city, arrange the paperwork first rather than assuming the city’s relaxed approach applies.

Can I eat what I catch in the Río de la Plata? No, and this is the most important point. Studies by UNLP and provincial bodies have found PCBs above the guideline in Argentina’s Código Alimentario, and sábalo has been flagged as ‘no apto para consumo’, meaning not fit for consumption. A 2023 study reported record glyphosate levels in sábalo with a public warning, and the Riachuelo basin carries long-standing advisories. Cooking does not remove these contaminants, so treat every fish as catch-and-release.

What fish live in this stretch of river? Common catches along the Costanera include pejerrey, boga, bagre, carpa and patí. Pejerrey is the local favourite, especially in the cooler months, though results vary with season, water level and wind. The Río de la Plata is a tidal estuary, so conditions shift with the weather more than with a fixed schedule. For many regulars the appeal is the ritual of a morning by the water rather than the size of the catch.

Where is fishing banned? Fishing is prohibited inside the Reserva Ecológica Costanera Sur, the protected wetland reserve on the southern side of the waterfront, and that ban is enforced. Elsewhere along the public Costanera Norte, shore fishing is tolerated on the city side. If you are unsure whether a stretch falls inside the reserve or within provincial jurisdiction, err towards caution, keep clear of marked boundaries and ask locals or park staff before casting a line.

Is it safe and legal for a visitor to fish here? Casting from the public city shoreline is legal and widely practised, and no CABA licence is needed there. The health risk lies in eating the catch, not the activity itself, so the sensible approach for visitors is strict catch-and-release. Bring layers for the riverfront wind, give other anglers space, and take home all litter and discarded line. Stay out of the ecological reserve, and arrange a provincial licence in advance if you intend to fish outside the city.

World.title: Costa Rica Reaches the Heart of the Romería on the Feast of La Negrita
World.content:
Today is the day the walking stops. August 2 is the feast of the Virgen de los Ángeles, the small dark stone image Costa Ricans call La Negrita, and it closes the Romería — the pilgrimage that has been filling the shoulder of every road into Cartago for the past week. If you were anywhere near the San José–Cartago corridor last night, you already know. If you slept through it, you will still feel the effects of it today.

As you may or may not know, tradition holds that on August 2, 1635, a young woman named Juana Pereira found a stone figure of the Virgin holding the infant Jesus on a rock near a spring outside Cartago. She took it home. It reappeared on the rock. A shrine went up around the spot, and the Basílica de Nuestra Señora de los Ángeles now stands over it — the rock itself sits in the crypt, and people still line up to touch it and fill bottles at the spring behind the church.

The Virgin was declared Costa Rica’s patron saint in 1824. Every year, people walk to her. The classic route runs about 22 kilometers (14 miles) from San José over the Ochomogo ridge, but walkers come from Guanacaste, Limón, the Southern Zone and the Northern Zone, some covering more than 280 kilometers (174 miles) over six or seven days.

Church estimates put participation near two million people across the period. Some finish the last stretch on their knees. This year carries an extra weight. It falls in the centenary of the Virgin’s pontifical coronation, which Pope Pius XI granted in April 1926, and the official program was built around that anniversary, running from July 23 through tomorrow.

The main event today is the solemn Mass at 9 a.m., celebrated outdoors on the plaza in front of the basilica rather than inside it, because nothing like the crowd would fit. Mario Enrique Quirós Quirós, the bishop of Cartago, presides. Civil and religious officials attend alongside pilgrims who have been sleeping in tents on the plaza and in the parks around it. In the evening, the Rosario de la Luz brings a candlelit rosary back to the same plaza.

If you are going, walk in. The three-block ring around the basilica is closed to vehicles, and only residents inside the perimeter can drive through it. Dress for cold and wet — Cartago sits at roughly 1,435 meters (4,708 feet) and this morning it is around 18°C (65°F) under heavy cloud, with a high near 21°C (70°F) and a real chance of rain by afternoon. Yesterday’s walkers got soaked and wind-blown by Tropical Wave 27, and the pattern has not fully cleared.

If you are trying to leave Cartago, move before mid-morning. The Cartago–San José train has been running without a break since 9 a.m. Saturday and stops at midday today, and it is the fastest way out while it lasts. Buses are the fallback: the temporary terminal at Plaza de la Soledad, a few blocks southwest of the basilica, runs until 10 a.m., while the regular downtown terminal reopens at 6 a.m., so there are two departure points this morning.

About 146 buses were authorized for the return, including 34 extra units on the main San José route, with direct services to Guadalupe, Desamparados, Heredia and Escazú. Expect lines anyway. Everyone finishes at roughly the same time, which is exactly the problem. If you are driving today, the restrictions come off in stages. Toll collection at the Tres Ríos plaza on the Florencio del Castillo resumed at 6 a.m. after twelve free hours overnight.

The ban on heavy trucks and hazardous-materials transport along Ruta 2 between Hacienda Vieja de Curridabat and the La Lima junction lifts at noon, as does the alcohol sales ban in the perimeter around the basilica. Traffic Police reinforced the Florencio del Castillo from 6 a.m. this morning, watching for speeding, illegal parking and drivers overcharging for rides. Assume pedestrians on the road well into the afternoon — the return trip is on foot for plenty of people too, and reversible lanes may be used between Cartago and San José depending on volume.

The support operation behind all of this stays in place. More than 500 Fuerza Pública officers and about 150 traffic officers have covered the route since Friday, backed by roughly 840 Red Cross volunteers and more than 145 emergency vehicles, a network of 25 health posts run by the Caja Costarricense de Seguro Social, and over 500 cameras along the pilgrim corridor from Cristo Rey in El Fierro through central Cartago. Most of what the Red Cross treats is not dramatic: blisters, muscle strain, dehydration, blood pressure trouble.

Last year nearly nine in ten cases traced back to physical overexertion, and the largest single group of patients was over 61. If you are walking today and your chest hurts, you are dizzy, or you cannot catch your breath, stop and find a post. Those are not part of the experience.

One more day follows. Tomorrow at 9 a.m., the image leaves the basilica in the procession known as La Pasada and travels to the Nuestra Señora del Carmen cathedral, where it stays until the first Sunday of September. The return trip in September is the one to mark on a calendar — families spend the pre-dawn hours laying carpets of dyed sawdust, flowers and seeds across the streets of central Cartago, and the procession walks over them and erases them.

Today is also a national holiday, though an unusual one. Under article 148 of the Labor Code, August 2 is a feriado de pago no obligatorio — everyone is entitled to the day off, but how it is paid depends on whether wages are calculated weekly, biweekly or monthly. It does not shift to another date, so falling on a Sunday this year means it passes largely unnoticed on the calendar even as it fills the roads.

World.title: Long term licenses and its role in harvesting Belize’s timber and forest resources in a sustainable manner
World.content:
Long term licenses and its role in harvesting Belize’s timber and forest resources in a sustainable manner

By Hugh O’Brien: “Safeguarding Belize’s forests through responsible harvesting, restoration and sustainable forest management”

Belize’s forests are undeniably among the country’s most valuable natural resources, providing a wide variety of timber and exotic woods, habitat for wildlife and endangered species, clean water for drinking, irrigation and other purposes, carbon storage/sequestration, and growing opportunities for tourism and recreation. Our nation’s forests are under severe pressure from agriculture expansion, inclusive of small-scale farming, cattle ranching and commercial grain production, the need for residential expansion particularly in the rural areas, and the unsustainable timber harvesting techniques practiced by the timber industry. The pressure has become so great that areas once set aside and protected as forest reserves have gradually been, and continues to be, chipped away. Sustainable management of our very valuable forests is essential to ensure that they continue to meet the needs of both present and future generations.

Sustainable forestry is often misunderstood. Many people assume that harvesting timber and conserving forests are opposing goals. They are not. When forests are managed scientifically, timber harvesting becomes one of the tools used to keep forests healthy, productive, and capable of providing the ecological, social, and economic benefits previously mentioned for generations to come.

In the mid 1990’s while teaching at the Belize College of Agriculture (BCA then now the Central Farm Campus of the University of Belize), I had the pleasure of taking my students each year on a field trip to the Mountain Pine Ridge Forest Reserve where we studied the different soils that formed from the granite and limestone formations in the area. On three (3) or (4) of those field trips, the BCA students and myself were pioneering witnesses to the launch of the 40-year cutting cycle for managing and harvesting pine trees in the Mountain Pine Ridge Forest Reserve. This 40-year rotation system of management was designed by some British forestry experts (I can’t remember their name) who were in the country at that time, and the then Chief Forest Officer Mr. Richard Belisle accompanied us on a couple of these field trips and explained how the scientific harvesting system was designed to work.

Up until today, the 40-year cutting cycle remains one of Belize’s most important forest management tools particularly for the Caribbean Pine. Rather than clear-cutting forests, only a portion (1/40th on an average) is harvested during each cycle, balancing timber production with biodiversity conservation and long-term forest health. Where scientific evidence shows faster growth rates, the cutting cycle may be adjusted by a certified forester.

Only mature trees that have reached the minimum cutting diameter, and are suitable for commercial use, are removed. The best, most vigorous and healthiest trees are selected to remain as mother or seed trees, hopefully producing much stronger offsprings for later harvest. The cutting cycle provides enough time for this tree species to mature and replace those that were removed. After harvesting sustainably, the area continues to be sustainably managed while the remaining trees grow and new seedlings develop.

Every harvest begins with a detailed forest inventory. Trained foresters assess the species, sizes, and abundance of trees before determining how much timber can be harvested sustainably. Roads and skid trails are carefully planned to minimize impacts on soils, waterways, and surrounding vegetation, and once harvesting is complete, the forest is monitored throughout its regeneration.

However, sustainable forestry does not mean simply harvesting a forest and leaving it alone for so many years. Pine ecosystems require continuous management and intervention. Wildfires, bark beetle infestations, hurricanes, invasive vegetation, and overcrowded stands all threaten the long-term health of the forest.

Another essential practice is thinning. Weaker, diseased, or overcrowded trees are selectively removed to reduce competition, allowing healthier trees to develop into high-quality timber. Many of the trees removed during thinning can be utilized for products such as fence posts rather than being left on the forest floor.

Prescribed burning is another essential management practice. Carefully planned and controlled fires reduce hazardous fuel loads, promote pine regeneration, recycle nutrients, and help prevent the catastrophic wildfires that have become increasingly common. (We will talk about prescribed burning in more detail in a future article.)

This system offers many environmental benefits. Because only selected trees are removed, most of the forest canopy remains intact, preserving habitats for birds, mammals, reptiles, insects, and other wildlife. The remaining vegetation helps prevent soil erosion, protects water quality in rivers and streams, and maintains the natural beauty of the landscape. The forest also continues to absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, helping to reduce the impacts of climate change.

The economic benefits are equally important. By allowing forests sufficient time to regenerate, Belize can maintain a continuous supply of valuable timber without exhausting its natural resources. This supports the forestry industry, creates employment opportunities, and provides income for local communities while ensuring that future generations will also benefit from healthy and productive forests. Sustainable harvesting also increases the value of Belize’s forest products by demonstrating that they are produced using environmentally responsible practices. Ideally, under a well-managed system, Belize should be able to supply the lumber market without having to rely on pine importation. While it may be easier to import and resell lumber, investing in the sustainable management of our forests is what ensures they continue to provide economic benefits for generations to come.

Although this management system has proven successful, it also faces several challenges. Illegal logging, forest fires, hurricanes, pests, diseases, and the effects of climate change can all damage forests before they complete their recovery period. Effective enforcement of forestry regulations, regular monitoring, scientific research, and community participation are therefore essential to ensure that the rotation cycle continues to achieve its objectives.

Sustainable forest management cannot be achieved through short-term thinking. It requires decades of planning, investment, monitoring, protection and restoration. For that reason, I am an advocate of dividing the country’s forest resources into a large enough number of management areas and using a transparent process to tender out the management of these areas. I am also an advocate of the issuance of long-term licenses as a tool to harvest and manage Belize’s timber resources in a sustainable manner. I am not an advocate of simply issuing a license to anyone for them to use as a tool to negotiate and sell the license. I am also not an advocate of issuing long term licenses to holders who are involved in illegal harvesting, bribing of public officials and constantly breaking the law.

Sustainable forestry management in the ‘Jewel’ is severely affected by accusations of corruption at various levels in the forestry department and allegations that party loyalists and close friends and families of senior public officials are receiving long term permits without having experience or demonstrating adequate ability to manage the forest on a long term basis. Decisions to approve or disapprove petty and other permits take far too long thereby complicating matters further. It is also no secret that there are hoards of illegal logging occurring across the country and that our forest resources are being depleted rapidly and that there are only a handful of examples of companies that are properly managing the portion of forest granted to them in their license. I pause to recognize two (2) such companies that I know who are doing so – the first is Programme for Belize operating in northern Belize and the other is Bulridge Company Ltd. operating in Central Belize.

The future of Belize’s forests will not be determined by how much timber we harvest today, but by how well we manage the forests that remain for generations to come.

World.title: San Jose Village woman slapped by partner, then punched and choked by his son
World.content:
San Jose Village woman slapped by partner, then punched and choked by his son

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A San Jose Village woman says a simple remark about a passing vendor brought a double assault down on her inside her own home, slapped by her common-law husband, then punched, choked, and struck from behind by his son, and a doctor has certified her injuries as harm.

According to the Belize Police Department, the 36-year-old domestic worker reported that on Saturday, August 1, 2026, at about midday, she was at home with her daughters, her common-law husband, and his son when a vendor passed by selling. Having no money herself, she asked her husband to check what was on offer.

His response, she reported, came in an upset tone, saying he did not want to see anybody. When she raised her hand in a dismissive motion and said to leave it then, the man approached her, told her she was no one to raise her hand like that, and slapped her twice across the face, causing pain.

The violence then multiplied. His son emerged from his room and threw a punch that missed her arm and struck the door behind her, according to her report. When she told him she can come anytime at the house, he punched her on the mouth and grabbed her tightly by the neck, and she struggled with him until one of her daughters intervened.

She stood and declared she would call for police assistance. As she moved to leave, the son grabbed her by the hand, releasing her only when his father told him to let her go. Even then, she reported, the son followed her as she left and hit her behind the head, causing pain.

Police recorded a statement from the woman, and medico-legal forms were issued and returned, with a doctor certifying her injuries as harm.

The police report does not indicate that anyone has been detained or charged at this time, and the matter awaits further action. The identities of those involved are being withheld.

To anyone facing violence at home, from a partner or any member of the household, help is available through the police and trusted support services. This woman’s decision to walk out and report, even as hands tried to stop her, is the step that puts the law on her side.

World.title: Bullets hidden in the wall: police clear another stash spot
World.content:
Bullets hidden in the wall: police clear another stash spot

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Police searching an abandoned house in Trial Farm Village have uncovered a dozen rounds of 9mm ammunition concealed inside an electrical box cemented into the wall, the second hidden ammunition cache cleared in the Orange Walk District in under two weeks.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Saturday, August 1, 2026, between 12:00 and 12:30 p.m., police personnel conducted a search of an abandoned house and lot in the Trial Farm area.

During the search of the house, an officer discovered a transparent bag containing a black box bearing the markings of a handgun ammunition brand, hidden inside an electrical box cemented into the wall. Further inspection of the box revealed twelve gold-coloured 9mm rounds.

No one was in the immediate area at the time of the discovery, and the ammunition was taken to the Trial Farm Police Station, where it was labelled and sealed as found property.

No arrests have been made, and the matter remains under police attention.

The find follows the discovery of 27 rounds of 9mm ammunition, a magazine, and suspected cannabis hidden under a sponge at an abandoned house on the Palmar Road just two weeks ago, and comes amid heightened attention on the 9mm calibre, which featured in the recent drive-by shooting on San Antonio Road. Police have drawn no connection between the found ammunition and any incident, but the pattern of live rounds stashed in the district’s empty buildings continues to concern.

Every cache cleared is ammunition that will never leave a barrel. Anyone with information on the stash is urged to contact the Trial Farm police or Crime Stoppers anonymously at 922.

World.title: One turn, one collision, and a case of he said, he said
World.content:
One turn, one collision, and a case of he said, he said

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A collision between an SUV and a motorcycle at an Orange Walk Town intersection has left the motorcycle rider with leg injuries and both vehicles damaged, and police are investigating with the question of fault still open.

According to the Belize Police Department, a 31-year-old manager reported that on Saturday, August 1, 2026, at about 11:05 a.m., he was driving a silver Mitsubishi Outlander SUV along Dunn Street, travelling from the direction of Cinderella Street toward St. Peter’s Street.

According to his report, as he intended to make a left turn onto St. Peter’s Street, a black motorcycle collided with the left portion of his vehicle. The impact scraped and dented the SUV’s driver and left rear passenger doors, broke the left rear view mirror, and broke and dislocated the fender running under the left rear passenger side. He also observed damage to the motorcycle, including a broken front wheel guard and a broken right-side fender near the fuel tank.

The scene was visited and processed by scenes of crime personnel, with a sketch plan drawn and measurements taken. The motorcycle rider, who was observed with abrasions to the right leg, was served medico-legal forms.

Police recorded a statement from the SUV driver, who is not accepting fault for the accident but has indicated he is willing to settle the matter through insurance. A statement is yet to be recorded from the other party involved, and until both accounts are in hand, the question of responsibility remains undetermined.

The matter is under investigation.

The collision adds another entry to a month in which motorcycles have featured heavily in the district’s road news, and it carries the timeless caution for every intersection: the turn and the through-rider must see each other, because when they meet instead, the rider always takes the worse of it.

World.title: Noisy motorcycle draws patrol’s attention, triple charge follows
World.content:
Noisy motorcycle draws patrol’s attention, triple charge follows

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The exhaust announced him before the paperwork could fail him. A loud motorcycle rolling through Guinea Grass on Friday night pulled a patrolling officer’s attention, and the stop that followed swept the board: expired licence, no insurance, no registration.

The Belize Police Department reports that the officer, on motorcycle patrol in the village at about 10:40 p.m. on Friday, July 31, 2026, noticed the noisy bike carrying a rider and passenger and caught up with it. The licence handed over had expired on June 5, 2026, a date that happens to be the rider’s own birthday, meaning the document died the day he turned twenty and rode on regardless.

The questions only went downhill from there. Insurance? None, by the rider’s own admission. Vehicle licence? Also none, the checks confirmed. Three offences, one caution, and a quiet trip to the Guinea Grass Sub Station.

There, the rider was identified as Randel Rafael Perrera, 20, a labourer of the village. Rights read, custody record signed, and the formal charges laid the same date: riding without third-party risk insurance, riding an unlicensed motorcycle, and riding without a valid driver’s licence. He answered the final caution with silence.

Bail was set at $500, with a 9:00 a.m. date at the Orange Walk Magistrate Court on Wednesday, August 5, where he will share the morning with another Guinea Grass rider, stopped by the very same officer just five minutes later on the very same patrol. One officer, one village, one night, two bikes, five charges.

The district’s two-week scoreboard now reads four riders and eleven charges over unpapered bikes, and Friday night added the lesson to remember: the loud pipe that turns heads turns the patrol’s head too, and it cannot outrun a paperwork check. Renew on the birthday, ride insured, and keep the noise for the horn.

World.title: Licensed rider, unlicensed bike: Guinea Grass teen charged
World.content:
Licensed rider, unlicensed bike: Guinea Grass teen charged

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): An 18-year-old Guinea Grass Village rider had his paperwork half right, and the missing half has earned him two traffic charges and a date at the Orange Walk Magistrate Court.

According to the Belize Police Department, on Friday, July 31, 2026, at about 10:45 p.m., an officer patrolling within Guinea Grass Village observed a person approaching who stopped upon seeing the police.

The officer approached and requested a driver’s licence, which the rider produced, and it was valid. The good news ended there. Asked for the insurance, the rider stated the motorcycle was not insured, and further checks revealed the motorcycle was not licensed either.

The rider was informed of the offences, driving a motor vehicle not insured with third-party risk insurance and driving an unlicensed motor vehicle, cautioned, and escorted to the Guinea Grass Sub Station.

There, he was identified as David Eliazar Efrain Perez, 18, of Guinea Grass Village. He was informed of his constitutional rights and voluntarily signed the custody record.

That same date, police formally arrested and charged Perez with both traffic offences. Cautioned once more, he chose to remain silent.

Bail was granted in the sum of $500, and he is to appear at the Orange Walk Magistrate Court at 9:00 a.m. on Wednesday, August 5, 2026.

The case is the third of its kind in under two weeks, following near-identical charges against riders in Belmopan and Orange Walk Town, as traffic enforcement keeps finding motorcycles on the road with paperwork running behind the wheels. The uninsured bike remains the quiet risk in every near-miss: when something goes wrong, there is no third-party cover for whoever gets hurt.

World.title: Government seeks $16 million loan to digitize civil service systems
World.content:
Government seeks $16 million loan to digitize civil service systems

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Government has taken a loan motion to the House of Representatives for 16 million dollars (8 million US) from the Inter-American Development Bank to support the civil service modernization project, an initiative covering digital transformation, data analytics and strengthened institutional capacity for human resource management. Government will contribute an additional 2 million dollars (1 million US) in counterpart resources, bringing the total investment to 18 million dollars (9 million US).

Leader of the Opposition Tracy Panton signaled support for the goal but pressed hard on accountability, setting the motion against a mounting borrowing tally. “The last time we were here, we approved over 53 million dollars in loan motions. Today by the time we get through this House meeting, we would have approved another 81 million dollars in loan motions,” she said. “Modernization is therefore a principle we support. The issue however is whether there are adequate safeguards in place and whether the Belizean people can be assured that this investment can deliver measurable results.”

Panton requested a copy of the detailed implementation plan and a breakdown of who and how the money will be spent, asking pointedly: “How much money will be allocated to technology and innovation. How much will be spent on consultants, how much is budgeted on software licensing fees, how much will actually be invested in training Belizean public officers, and how much of this 9 million US dollars will go towards project management and administrative costs.”

Minister of the Public Service Henry Charles Usher rose to defend the project’s necessity, citing three longstanding challenges. “Annual expenditures on personnel continue to exceed budget estimates, placing pressure on government finances,” he said, adding that “there are significant variances in compensation among similar job categories affecting consistency and equity,” issues he said had been discussed with public officers and the Public Service Union to build consensus.

The third weakness, Usher said, is the absence of integrated systems. “There is no integrated human resources system and that system is not even linked and we have to get it linked to the financial management information system so that these two digital systems can start communicating with each other and putting in the necessary guardrails.”

The motion forms part of a broader effort to control personnel costs, standardize compensation and digitize government operations. Breaking Belize News will follow the project’s implementation.

World.title: Belize City ranked second dirtiest in the Caribbean by travel influencer
World.content:
Belize City ranked second dirtiest in the Caribbean by travel influencer

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): One million views and counting. That is the audience for travel influencer Drew Binsky’s reel ranking the Caribbean’s dirtiest cities, with Belize City sitting at number two behind Georgetown, Guyana, and our canals cast in the starring role as what he called giant illegal trash cans overloaded with trash.

Mayor Bernard Wagner is having none of it. “No credible study or scientific method has been provided to support that ranking,” he responded, pointing to the City Council’s “robust garbage collection programme and cleanup” and insisting that when hotspots or informal dumpsites are identified, “we tackle them immediately.”

The mayor has a fair point. Binsky’s list is content, not science, no criteria, no data, no methodology, built by a creator with nine million followers who understands exactly what travels online. Call it clickbait and you would not be wrong.

But here is the uncomfortable part every Belize City resident already knows: he did not need a study to film those canals. The footage stings precisely because it is familiar. The canals have been the city’s open wound for generations, and no amount of pushback at a ranking changes what floats through them after a heavy rain.

So maybe both things are true at once. The ranking is unserious, and the problem it spotlighted is deadly serious. City Hall collects the garbage, but the garbage in the canals did not fall from the sky, it was thrown there, bag by bag, by residents. A cleanup programme can only outrun a littering culture for so long.

A million strangers have now seen our canals. The better question is what the people who live beside them, and the council that manages them, do next.

Be honest, Belize City: whose job is it to fix the canals, City Hall’s or ours? Sound off below.

World.title: Wheatley granted injunction barring IC charges until judicial review
World.content:
Andrew Wheatley

The Supreme Court has granted an injunction preventing the Integrity Commission (IC) from charging Cabinet Minister Dr Andrew Wheatley until the hearing and determination of an application by his lawyers for judicial review.

Wheatley had applied for leave to pursue judicial review against the IC’s recommendation that he be charged with illicit enrichment.

Observer Online understands that the Supreme Court on Friday granted Wheatley’s application, recommending that the judicial review be heard by a panel of three judges.

Before granting the injunction, presiding Judge Justice David Batts had suggested that the IC consider an undertaking not to charge Dr Wheatley until the hearing and determination of the judicial review.

The commission said it could not give an undertaking at this time. The judge then granted the injunction.

It is understood that the IC’s application for leave to appeal the ruling was denied.

The Integrity Commission had alleged that there is a disproportionality in Wheatley’s assets when compared to his income to the tune of $164 million.

Wheatley rejected the allegation and accused the IC of failing to take into consideration $168 million in rental income accumulated over a decade.

He is being represented by a high powered legal team including King’s Counsel Ransford Braham, Abe Dabdoub and Neco Pagon.

The Integrity Commission is being represented by King’s Counsel Kevin Powell.

World.title: DROUGHT ALERT!
World.content:
Principal Director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica, Evan Thompson gives the forecast for the island over the next few months during a press briefing Thursday afternoon.(Photo: Karl McLarty)

With projections from the Meteorological Service of Jamaica showing prolonged dry conditions stretching into October this year, Water, Environment and Climate Change Minister Matthew Samuda has put Jamaicans on alert for full prohibition orders for water usage, which he says will take effect on August 10 if the forecast remains unchanged or worsens.

The warning comes following a Thursday morning meeting of the Integrated Water Resources Management Council — a Cabinet subcommittee comprising all stakeholders in the water sector; academia; municipalities; and the ministries of agriculture, health and national security. That report was complemented by forecasts of the Met Service and assessments of the Water Resources Authority, according to Samuda.

Since earlier this year, nightly water restrictions and scheduled supply cuts have been implemented in vulnerable Corporate Area networks, such as Kingston 20, given the drought conditions.

Speaking during a media briefing at the Half-Way-Tree Road offices of his ministry to discuss the rainfall and drought conditions, Samuda said given the indications that there will be “a dry August, a dry September, and a dry October…it is clear and should be clear to all Jamaicans that conservation is indeed imperative at this stage”.

“We are first encouraging conservation, but being very clear that as at August 10th…if the situation has not changed — meaning if the Met Services evaluation of rainfall in July is as we suspect — that we will have continued declines in rainfall, and if the rolling three-month forecast has not changed, or has worsened, prohibition orders will come into effect,” Samuda said.

The water minister said those orders will be targeted at “irrigation and watering of gardens, lawns, grounds, and farms, filling or supplying of pools, and other things for domestic services”.

“Washing of cars, watering and washing of roadways, and any purpose that would require unusual or non-essential use of water would be prohibited,” Samuda added.

He emphasised that the announcement was not to be interpreted to mean “that the systems and the storage are at critical levels today, but the rainfall that would normally come at the end of August is not projected to be experienced”.

Pointing to the learning loss that has already resulted from the COVID-19 pandemic as well as weather events such as Hurricane Beryl, Tropical Storm Raphael, and Hurricane Melissa, the minister said every effort will be made to ensure that schools receive the support needed.

“We simply cannot afford water to contribute to learning loss in September. So we will take the measures that we absolutely need to ensure that we’re able to safeguard the opening of schools in September and not contribute to learning loss. So that needs to be understood. We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” Samuda stressed.

“We do hope that the situation will change, but with the information that we have, this is the best decision that we can make at this stage,” he added.

Speaking during the briefing, principal director of the Meteorological Service of Jamaica Evan Thompson said as at the end of June the parishes of St Elizabeth, St James, St Ann, and St Mary “were determined to be experiencing drought conditions”. He said the parishes of Manchester and St Catherine “were both basically on the borderline, in that they were just about moving toward drought conditions”.

“It’s most likely that having not experienced significant rainfall during the month of July, that situation would have been worsened. We should be seeing that drought conditions at least would have extended to these two parishes. That’s what we’re expecting to pick up after the month of July has ended, as we begin to gather and collate and compare our data,” Thompson told members of the media.

He noted that the projections did not mean there would be “no rainfall” at all for the island, but that “the number of incidents of rainfall will be fewer”, influenced by the El Nino phenomenon which has caused “lesser than normal amounts of rainfall and higher than normal temperatures” over the past few months.

“However, we could have a bulk of rainfall that is intense, and so we could have very small areas that experience maybe even flooding events in small areas as these systems develop and as they continue to affect us, but generally we will experience dry conditions,” Thompson explained further.

He cautioned that with the forecast for August showing “higher-than-normal temperatures right through the month” and “lower-than-normal rainfall”, Jamaicans should be on the lookout for “climate-induced bushfires”.

World.title: More for MSMEs
World.content:
WILLIAMS... it is a catalyst for the next era of public procurement in Jamaica.

ONLY about one per cent of the Government’s annual procurement spending currently reaches micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs), a disparity Finance Minister Fayval Williams says the upgraded Government of Jamaica Electronic Procurement portal (GOJEP 2.0) is intended to address. The platform will increase MSME access to public contracts.

Speaking during Thursday’s launch of the updated digital procurement portal, Williams said the modernised system eliminates outdated technical requirements, and creates more opportunities for local businesses to access a share of the Government’s roughly $470-billion annual procurement spend.

“Let me put the scale in perspective. Each year, the Government of Jamaica spends roughly US$3 billion — translated into Jamaican dollars, that’s about $470 billion, depending on the currency at any point in time – and this procures goods, services, and works from the private sector. This is close to, I think, about 13 per cent of our GDP (gross domestic product). And yet, of that enormous sum, only about one per cent reaches our micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises,” the minister pointed out.

“That imbalance is exactly what we are determined to correct so that more Jamaican businesses can share in the billions that Government spends each year, particularly as we rebuild in the wake of Hurricane Melissa. So every procurement decision carries real responsibility. It must inspire public confidence, deliver value for money, create economic opportunity, and make certain that every dollar entrusted to Government works harder for the people we serve,” she said during the event held at AC Hotel Kingston.

According to Williams, GOJEP 2.0 is an upgraded version of the Government’s online system for buying goods, works and services from the private sector. She explained that the remodelling of the digital portal will see the removal of outdated barriers, put in place stronger record keeping aimed at making the process faster and more transparent.

“It’s easier to use. You no longer need to install extra software just to submit a bid. You log in from any ordinary web browser on any device, including your phone. It’s better connected. The system now talks to other government systems, so the same information doesn’t have to be entered twice, it keeps a proper record digitally,” explained the minister.

“Every key decision made during evaluation is captured and tracked automatically instead of living in a paper file or in someone’s memory. It cuts duplicate paperwork for government staff, and it collects far better data on how long procurements take, how much competition is there, and how well our small business set-asides are working,” Williams added.

She also pointed out that bidders and buyers will now be able to follow opportunities that the government brings to market, and see who ultimately wins the work. Furthermore, she assured that GOJEP 2.0 was not the finished product, noting that upgrades will continue overtime.

“It is a catalyst for the next era of public procurement in Jamaica. And, over the next years, we will build a fully integrated end-to-end digital procurement system, one that connects planning, tendering, evaluation, contract management, supplier performance, and payment.

“Imagine in a year or two being able to open GOJEP and see the goods, works, and services that government intends to buy over the coming years. A business could then prepare, assess its capacity, build partnerships, secure certification, arrange financing, and position itself to compete. For our MSMEs especially, that advanced visibility can be the difference between watching from the sidelines and winning the work,” said the finance minister.

Meanwhile, Chief Public Procurement Policy Officer Jovell Barrett also highlighted the gap that exists for MSMEs, pointing out that of the 300,000 active businesses registered with the Companies Office of Jamaica, less than 10,000 unique people and entities are awarded government contracts each year.

“Government is one of the largest purchasers of goods, works and services. And so, the question that we have asked ourselves at the Office of Public Procurement Policy is how many Jamaican businesses see government as a potential customer? How many entrepreneurs look to the public procurement system as an opportunity? And perhaps most importantly, how many do not see public procurement as an opportunity — and if they don’t, why?” said Barrett.

He hailed Thursday’s launch of GOJEP 2.0 as an opportunity to ensure that every taxpaying Jamaican has a fair chance to participate in the public procurement process.

“That’s the vision that I have and that’s what I want to see as a Jamaican. Why? I want to see more Jamaicans participating in public procurement. When public procurement operates as I want to see it happen… small businesses, hundreds and thousands of them in each community, [will] become a mechanism through which public procurement will work best and will be able to develop our economy more. It becomes the instrument of change that Government really wants it to be. That is the power of public procurement,” he said.

World.title: Dexta Daps stays true
World.content:
Dexta Daps.

As thousands of patrons prepare to descend on Montego Bay for Dream Wknd, few performers arrive with the kind of anticipation that surrounds Dexta Daps.

Over the past decade the dancehall star has built one of the genre’s most devoted followings by staying true to the soulful, emotionally driven sound that first set him apart.

“Staying true to the vibe that started my career and keeping the music honest and relatable,” he says when asked about the secret to his longevity. “I evolve with the production sounds, but I don’t chase trends; solid melodies, real emotion, and a performance that connects with the audience is always the goal.”

In a genre that constantly reinvents itself, Dexta Daps has remained relevant by refining his craft rather than reinventing his identity. As production styles and audience tastes have evolved, he has focused on strengthening the qualities that first resonated with listeners.

His creative process, however, has never stood still.

“It’s ever-evolving,” he explains. “I’ve continued to sharpen my sense of arrangement and storytelling while balancing intimate, soulful moments with the dancehall energy.”

That balance has become one of his defining trademarks. Whether delivering emotionally charged ballads or high-energy dancehall records, he has demonstrated an ability to connect with audiences on multiple levels, creating music that feels both deeply personal and widely relatable.

As with any artiste whose career has spanned several years, thoughts inevitably turn to legacy. For Dexta Daps, the impact he leaves extends far beyond chart success or hit records.

“If fans only remembered one thing about my career years from now,” he says, “I’d want it to be that I gave people real, heartfelt music that resonated beyond the dance songs, music that felt honest and performances that stayed with them.”

That same commitment to delivering memorable performances is what fans can expect when he takes the stage at Dream Wknd, one of the Caribbean’s premier entertainment festivals, which runs from July 30-August 3 this year.

Sharing the stage with Dexta Daps at Dream’s Montego Bay debut are some of the biggest names in dancehall, including Alkaline, Tommy Lee, Govana, Shaneil Muir, Tifa, Elephant Man, General B, Jamal, Skeng, and Armanii, alongside a number of international acts.

“It’s always great to share the stage with so much talent,” he says. “It’s about representing the culture well and keeping the energy high for the crowd. I don’t take that for granted.”

While he remains tight-lipped about exactly what fans can expect, he hints that patrons should be prepared for something special.

“Always a few surprises,” he says with a laugh. “However, I can’t reveal them because then it wouldn’t be a surprise.”

Looking beyond the summer, Dexta Daps’s focus remains firmly on creating new music while continuing to expand his reach internationally.

“More music, working on an album,” he responds.

So, with new music, an album in the works, and another Dream Wknd appearance on the horizon, Dexta Daps is continuing to build a career rooted in authenticity, one heartfelt performance at a time.

World.title: DOLPHIN COVE’S US$2.5-M LIFT
World.content:
Visitors interact with dolphins at one of Dolphin Cove Limited’s Jamaican attractions. The company has added approximately US$2.53 million to its net book value following a revaluation of its Jamaican properties

DOLPHIN Cove Limited has added approximately US$2.533 million to its net book value after revaluing its Jamaican properties, an adjustment disclosed while its majority shareholder has agreed to sell its controlling stake and is seeking to add four directors.

Property Consultants Limited valued the group’s Jamaican land and buildings as at March 31, but its report reached Dolphin Cove’s board after the company had published its first-quarter financial statements.

The appraisal increases the carrying value of property, plant and equipment by approximately US$2.576 million. After adjustments to deferred taxation, the net increase in Dolphin Cove’s book value is approximately US$2.533 million.

Applied to the previously reported March figures, the adjustment would lift property, plant and equipment from approximately US$26.65 million to US$29.23 million and shareholders’ equity from US$27.39 million to approximately US$29.92 million, before any other second-quarter movements.

The increase is equivalent to approximately nine per cent of the equity Dolphin Cove reported at the end of March.

It is an accounting adjustment rather than new income or cash. Dolphin Cove said the revaluation has no effect on revenue, operating results or cash flow for the period.

The revised values will be reflected in the company’s financial statements for the six months ended June 30.

Dolphin Cove did not identify the individual Jamaican properties covered by the appraisal, disclose their separate values or say whether the updated figures were considered in the proposed sale of the company’s controlling stake.

The transaction under way is a sale of shares in Dolphin Cove rather than a direct sale of the properties.

World of Dolphins Inc agreed on July 9 to sell all 313,901,858 Dolphin Cove shares it owns to Global Attractions Limited, a Saint Lucia company incorporated in March. The shares represent 79.99 per cent of Dolphin Cove.

Neither the purchase price nor the expected completion date has been disclosed. Completion is subject to conditions, including arrangements for the refinancing and discharge of Dolphin Cove’s existing credit facility with Sagicor Bank Jamaica Limited. The beneficial owners of Global Attractions, its financing arrangements and its plans for Dolphin Cove also remain unknown.

The property adjustment has now been announced as World of Dolphins seeks to add four directors to the listed company’s board.

The majority shareholder has nominated Colin Kerr, Darys Estrella, Alberto Bergés González and Sylvain Dominici for election, according to a notice signed by World of Dolphins representative and Dolphin Cove director Steven Strom.

Dolphin Cove has not published biographies of the nominees, explained their connections to World of Dolphins or said whether any of them is associated with Global Attractions.

It also has not explained why the selling shareholder is seeking to expand the board before the ownership transaction is completed.

The nominations were scheduled for consideration at Dolphin Cove’s annual general meeting on Thursday, July 30, at The Courtleigh Hotel & Suites.

However, the chairman was expected to seek shareholders’ consent to adjourn the meeting to allow investors at least 14 days’ notice of the proposed appointments. The outcome was unavailable at press time.

If shareholders approve the adjournment, the resumed meeting would be held between August 13 and August 28. The exact date has not been announced.

Based on Dolphin Cove’s latest public disclosures, electing all four nominees would expand its five-member board to nine if the present directors remain in office.

World of Dolphins currently holds enough shares to determine the outcome of the elections if it votes its 79.99 per cent stake. That could change if the sale is completed or the voting rights are transferred before the adjourned meeting.

Once completed, the acquisition will trigger a mandatory offer allowing minority shareholders to sell their shares to the new controlling owner. The price and other terms have not been published.

Dolphin Cove said its properties in Saint Lucia and the Turks and Caicos Islands will also be revalued. It did not say when those appraisals would be completed or whether it expects them to increase or reduce the assets’ carrying values.

World.title: ‘He who has the gold’
World.content:
FIFA President Gianni Infantino (centre) addresses a round table press briefing at the end of the FIFA Executive Summit at the Montego Bay Convention Centre in St James in January 2018. Also pictured are Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) President Michael Ricketts (left) and Concacaf President Victor Montagliani.

Veteran administrator Tony James says FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s proposal to privatise world football is “underhanded”, but cautions that developing nations under severe financial stress will find the promised US$40-million payout nearly impossible to resist.

James, who led the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF) from 1985 to 1992 and has spent over 50 years working in football, offered a sharp critique of Infantino’s proposed FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE). Under the plan, FIFA aims to create a private commercial entity valued at US$20 billion (over $3 billion) to handle broadcasting, ticketing, sponsorship, and hospitality rights for competitions like the World Cup. Developed alongside JP Morgan, the strategy involves selling up to 21 per cent to private equity investors — led by Joshua Kushner’s firm, Thrive Eternal — to raise US$4.2 billion (roughly $665 billion) in upfront capital. Kushner is the brother of US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

To win over member nations, FIFA offered a substantial payout of increasing baseline development funding from US$10 million (over $1.5 billion) to US$20 million (over $3 billion) per nation for the 2027-2030 cycle. Associations could also access an additional US$20 million upfront through a new FIFA Fast Forward Programme for infrastructure, putting up to US$40 million on the table per country ahead of a September 19 deadline. Infantino, however, warned that member nations declining support would continue to receive the baseline.

While continental governing bodies have moved to block the move, James says that for smaller member associations, the financial reality takes precedence.

“It is underhanded, and the cynical view is being reinforced by the way it is being proposed now,” James told the Jamaica Observer on Thursday. “He who has the gold makes the rule. That’s how people perceive of it; that it’s the current way of the world. You’re trumping (pardon the pun) institutionalised good governance structures, integrity, etcetera. That’s what’s being put out in the public now.”

Despite the governance concerns, James says smaller associations operate in a vastly different financial reality than European giants.

“This US$40 million for each affiliate will have traction in all the poorer and developing countries,” he said. “The focus will be on CAF [Confederation of African Football], and Concacaf, which includes the Caribbean, but it’s also the poorer countries in Asia and UEFA.

“UEFA’s principled position is understandable, but it’s fortunate in having three financial platforms. One is the World Cup, like everybody else, and their teams are the top of the heap. Let us call them Category A teams because they’re the ones who are going to get most of the money. All of the rest of us are Category B and C teams that should get money, but not like the A teams.”

James’s comments come as global opposition to Infantino’s scheme reaches a boiling point. After an emergency meeting, Concacaf — the governing body for North America, Central America, and the Caribbean — unanimously voted down the proposed enterprise plan, joining European governing body UEFA in open revolt. Concacaf made its announcement moments after the Observer’s interview with James.

In its official statement, Concacaf mentioned severe procedural failures surrounding the proposal.

“During the meeting, the membership expressed deep concerns about the lack of due process surrounding the proposal, the artificially short deadline imposed, and the absence of any review or approval by the relevant FIFA governance bodies,” Concacaf said on its website. “In addition, the need for private equity investment to fund new and existing FIFA Forward programmes following the most profitable FIFA World Cup in history was questioned.”

Concacaf confirmed all 41 member associations rejected the deal after UEFA’s warning that it would pull its teams from FIFA competitions entirely.

“As a result of today’s discussion, no UEFA national teams will participate in any FIFA competition for so long as these proposals remain alive, unless this proposal has been abandoned in its entirety and binding assurances have been given that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” UEFA said on its website on Thursday.

Despite Concacaf’s joint rejection, local sentiments reflect exactly what James described.

JFF President Michael Ricketts rejected all of the Observer’s calls to him seeking a comment, and declined to respond to questions posed on WhatsApp.

However, while speaking to Nationwide Sports, he struck a far more open tone regarding the commercial structure.

“I have not discussed it with my directors, but my personal feeling is that, on the face of it, I really don’t think that anything is wrong with it,” Ricketts said. “It’s workable. But the big problem I’m having is the — for want of a better word — non-transparent way in which it was done. We would’ve spent so much time together with the leadership of FIFA before, during, and after the World Cup, and we were never apprised of these discussions, and this would bring to the fore some level of non-transparency.”

Ricketts’s pragmatic view is tied directly to local circumstances. He told the Observer in an interview on July 14 that the JFF is strapped for cash after a costly, unsuccessful World Cup qualifying campaign. He also said in that interview that he would fully support Infantino’s plan to expand the World Cup to 64 teams as early as the 2030 tournament as it would provide a greater chance of qualification for Jamaica.

A US$40-million windfall would completely alter local operations. Furthermore, with Jamaica actively bidding to co-host the 2031 Women’s World Cup with the US, Mexico, and Costa Rica, maintaining good relations with FIFA ahead of Infantino’s re-election bid in March remains a practical priority.

While acknowledging the lifelines that FIFA funds provide, James warned that dumping millions into unprepared administrative set-ups brings serious risks.

“Regrettably, I don’t think most developing countries have an administrative structure to deal with this kind of money. They don’t,” he said. “You also have to ask, given our system, how much of this US$40 million would actually reach football development, because human nature says when you have money, it’s about a source of power, greed, corruption, football politics, and that syphons off the money.”

And on whether Infantino’s tactics amount to using FIFA’s massive wealth to secure political survival ahead of the upcoming presidential vote, James gave a blunt assessment of how the global game operates.

“He has been a disgrace,” James said. “But in a new world where the golden rule applies, when he hits FIFA and hits the politics, what do you think they’re going to say to him? When he tells them how much he has earned off this World Cup, that the vision was his, the planning was his, what he has had to do, ‘Listen, we had problems here and there, but at the end of the day, look at what I have done for you. Look at what FIFA has done for you. Who are you going to vote for?’ What do you think is going to be the response? It’s all about performance. Let’s face it, he has performed.”

World.title: 2026 Isuzu D-MAX: Built to last
World.content:
The durability, reliability, and ability shown through the history of the Isuzu D-MAX pickup continues in 2026. (Photo: Rory Daley)

Isuzu has long been one of the darlings of the commercial vehicle sector, having built a reputation for durability, reliability, and longevity over its long history.

The D-MAX pickup is endowed with these characteristics, and for 2026 continues to be so.

EXTERIOR

The four-door cab pickup is based mostly on function rather than form. Redesigned from the ground up, Isuzu calls it their ‘Spirit of Truck’ DNA, giving the D-MAX a masculine and no-nonsense look from its wide stance and wedge-shaped body lines. However, function over form still rules, and the D-MAX uses aerodynamic integration of the lower body to boost fuel efficiency and reduce wind noise. For those wanting style, up to 18-inch wheels can be had.

INTERIOR

Inside the new spacious cabin it reflects the working nature of the D-MAX. There’s a quality impression and the presence of durability to the cabin. There’s a mixture of hard-wearing plastics, with soft-touch materials at the main points of user contact. Ergonomics is a key word, with simple large buttons for the main functions to be accessed with ease under all conditions, and feel like they’ll be working for years to come.

Storage is plentiful for those who have to work. The deep centre console will swallow important gear, as will the dual gloveboxes. Cup holders and door pockets that all can hold a 1.5-litre bottle further contribute to the ability to hold personal cargo. The D-MAX has redesigned seats with improved internal materials for higher comfort, and better lateral support to increase occupant, especially driver, comfort.

The infotainment is similarly focused, using USB-C for smartphone-run connectivity and services.

ON THE ROAD

Powered by a 3-litre turbodiesel, the D-MAX is not lacking in this area. With 190bhp and 332lb/ft of torque, it manages to be both frugal and powerful. This is because there is tons of low-end torque to effortlessly pull the D-MAX along in the situations it’s built to operate in.

Boost response is good, and it rarely has to be taken into the higher rpms for more power. On road, this keeps engine noise and vibration low so as not to upset passengers in the cabin, meaning a strong case for prolonged on-road use.

But the D-MAX didn’t get its reputation for its on-road manners. Off-road, it has the ability to match the class leaders, because it’s all under the skin with a chassis boasting greater torsional and longitudinal rigidity. The same suspension that smooths out rough roads and can deal with highway travel can easily handle tough terrain with or without payload.

Rookie or professional, the D-MAX gives confidence in challenging situations, delivering up to 800 millimetres of wading depth, 30 degrees of approach angle, 22.9 degrees of breakover, and 24.2 degrees of departure angle. Being equipped with 2WD, 4WD, and 4WD Low, plus a rear differential, few things can slow, even stop, the D-MAX on a trail.

VERDICT

The D-MAX retains the ethos of the Isuzu brand. There’s a reason the company is a commercial equipment manufacturing powerhouse, and that all is installed into their flagship pickup. The durability, reliability, and ability shown through the history of the D-MAX pickup continue without question. 2026 adds some key updates and refinements to keep it a top contender.

World.title: Choppers collide, killing 2, as fires and foreboding grip Greece
World.content:
Another three Greek firefighters died last Wednesday while tackling wildfires in Crete and on the Peloponnese, a rugged peninsula in southern Greece.

While a fire that has been burning since Friday around Porto Germeno on the Gulf of Corinth some 60 ​kilometers northwest of Athens has subsided, on Saturday the flames crossed a mountain to the south, fanned by strong winds of up to 130 kilometers per hour, and reached the settlement of Veniza closer to the capital. According to initial estimates, the fire has destroyed around 200 houses in the area.

On Sunday flames spread rapidly through western Attica, a region that encompasses Athens, threatening communities and an industrial district outside Megara, about 30 kilometers from the capital. Speaking on state TV Ert, the president of the firefighters’ federation, Nikos Lavranos, described it as a “huge front” and a “black blanket covering an area of around [25 acres].”

Dozens of settlements have been evacuated, and firefighters are focusing on preventing the flames from advancing toward Megara, pop. 30,000. Greece’s firefighting service said more than 2,500 people had been evacuated in western Attica by late Sunday afternoon.

“Unfortunately, we have uncontrolled fires in far too many areas. As soon as the fire brigade arrives at one spot, just as the fire is being brought under control, it flares up again in another spot,” Megara Mayor Panagiotis Margetis told Open TV.

Firefighters were also fighting another blaze in the Peloponnese on Sunday as well as on the island of Cephalonia in the Ionian Sea between Greece and Italy. More than 500 firefighters have been deployed across Greece.

World.title: Hungary faces energy crunch as drought shuts down Paks nuclear plant, PM says
World.content:
“Due to the further drop in the Danube’s water level,” Magyar wrote Saturday, “tomorrow it will be completely shut down for the first time in 44 years."

The Soviet-built Paks facility remains the backbone of the country’s power system. The loss of output has triggered national energy-saving measures and offers of support from regional neighbors.

A prolonged outage would cripple Hungary’s electricity supply at a time when temperatures are forecast to rise above 40 degrees Celsius in Budapest next week amid an ongoing heatwave and drought across Europe.

Magyar warned the shutdown could trigger an emergency at a time of high summer demand: “An energy crisis situation may arise from Monday. Coordinated steps and self-restraint will be needed to avoid more severe consequences.”

The government has urged households and businesses to reduce electricity consumption during peak hours between 5 p.m. and 10 p.m., calling on people to limit their use of air conditioning and washing machines. Authorities have also prepared an emergency plan to temporarily restrict consumption at industrial facilities on a rotating basis, while increasing output from other power plants.

The European Commission said Friday it was closely monitoring the situation and was prepared to convene an emergency meeting of its Electricity Coordination Group over the Paks shutdown.

World.title: Trump cancels strikes on Iran, says deal imminent
World.content:
Donald Trump speaks during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland, on July 31, 2026. | Aaron Schwartz/ AFP via Getty Images

Tehran has not responded to the U.S. president’s announcement and has not confirmed an agreement to end the Middle East conflict has been reached.

U.S. President Donald Trump said late Saturday that he was canceling planned strikes on Iran pending a rapid agreement with Tehran to end the conflict in the Middle East.

“We have just been asked by Iran, and other Middle Eastern Countries, to hold off any attack in that the perimeters of a deal has been agreed to,” Trump announced in a post on Truth Social.

He said the agreement would include the “Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT” and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat.” Trump added that Israel supported his commitment to pause strikes, contingent on “being able to rapidly make a DEAL.”

World.title: Ceuta crisis: 22 EU leaders gang up against Spain’s Sánchez over his migration policy
World.content:
In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, European Council President António Costa and Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, the 22 leaders made direct reference to the need for EU-level cooperation on policies such as Madrid’s migrant regularization scheme.

“We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration, by coordinating our action, strengthening our external borders and addressing all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularization of [a] very large number of irregular migrants,” the leaders wrote.

Madrid has pushed back against the claim that the country’s regularization scheme triggered the crisis in Ceuta, and has pointed out that none of the people who illegally entered the exclave would be eligible to benefit from the measure.

“This process is based on very specific conditions, such as proof of residency in Spain before January 1, 2026, and having resided in Spain for five consecutive months at the time of application,” said a spokesperson for the Spanish foreign ministry. Moreover, the deadline for filing applications for the scheme, which was launched in April, was in June.

But those explanations have not appeared to sway the EU leaders who signed the letter to Costa, Von der Leyen and Martin.

“We cannot allow uncontrolled mass crossings, the instrumentalisation of migration or other hybrid threats to create the perception that illegal entry into the European Union is possible. That a migrant’s illegal entry can turn into legal stay,” they went on.
