The figures also showed there were 125 registered trainers in Tasmania, but a quarter of those do not have a dog registered to them, and 40 per cent of the greyhounds were registered to just 10 trainers.

A greyhound racing ban came into effect in New Zealand on Saturday, with chartered flights bringing up to 150 dogs from New Zealand to Australia where they will be able to keep racing.

Jeremy Rockliff says legislation to ban greyhound racing in Tasmania will allow for an "orderly transition". (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The Tasmanian government said it did not expect any New Zealand dogs to come to Tasmania given the impending ban.

Even without the legislation, Mr Rockliff has indicated the government would still end the industry by stopping its funding when the current deed expires in 2029.

But he said the legislation would provide for an "orderly transition to support animal welfare, support the dogs and support the industry".

Questions over cost

Labor's racing spokesperson, Dean Winter, on Saturday reaffirmed his party's opposition to banning greyhound racing.

Mr Winter also said it was unclear how much the phasing out of greyhound racing would cost.

"What is the compensation going to be, how much is it going to cost Tasmania's budget that is already in all sorts of trouble," he said.

Anti-greyhound racing campaigners protested outside Labor's state conference in April. (ABC News: Mitch Woolnough)

The government has budgeted $4.6 million for "greyhound racing transition" over the next four years, but Labor has concerns the cost of rehoming greyhounds will cost far more than that.

"To my knowledge the only modelling that's been done is for 1,000 greyhounds and if you were to rehome them under the model that New Zealand's taken, it would cost Tasmanian taxpayers around $40 million," Mr Winter said.

Mr Rockliff said "the figures put forward by the national greyhound industry and indeed Dean Winter are fanciful".

"We will work with the industry, we have a budget that has been outlined in terms of compensation and transition."

World.title: Cooperation critical for 'future growth' is key message at mining forum
World.content:
As its name would suggest, the Diggers and Dealers Mining Forum brings together opposing sides of Australia's resources sector, those at the coalface carrying a shovel and financial backers with a briefcase.

As industry heavyweights descend on Kalgoorlie-Boulder for the 35th edition of the famous conference, bars and boardrooms in the historic gold mining city will be filled for three days as many a deal gets done.

But one company that will not be spotted on the sidelines is the taxpayer-backed Iluka Resources, which is building a $1.8 billion rare earths refinery in WA's Midwest.

Dan McGrath says about 90 per cent of the world's rare earths are supplied by China. (ABC Perth: Glyn Jones)

As Iluka's head of rare earths, Dan McGrath, explained, the company shakes hands on deals in private, out of necessity.

"We've got a lot of discussions ongoing with a lot of parties, but all of those discussions are confidential because right now those supply chains rely on rare earths from China," he said.

"Discussions may result in the risk of China cutting off the supply between now and when our rare earths are available next year, so we keep those discussions very confidential."

First deal of many

In June, the Perth-headquartered Iluka signed its first offtake deal with an unnamed global car maker to supply magnet rare earth oxides from 2028.

The $US155 million ($220 million) deal is set to underpin the first four years of operations at Iluka's Eneabba refinery, which is about 60 per cent built near the small farming community about 280 kilometres north of Perth.

Once commissioned, the plant will churn out products like neodymium, praseodymium, terbium and dysprosium, which are critical in the manufacture of high-tech magnets found in electric vehicles, wind turbines and weaponry.

The $1.8 billion Eneabba rare earths refinery is on track for commissioning next year. (Supplied: Iluka Resources)

Critical mineral supply chains, but particularly rare earths, have become a focal point for many Western governments in recent years.

In the case of the Eneabba refinery, the project is backed by a $1.65 billion loan from the federal government's Critical Minerals Facility.

Mr McGrath said Australia's relationship with the United States was a critical component moving forward.

Anthony Albanese and Donald Trump signed an $8.5 billion rare earth minerals agreement in 2025. (Getty Images: Anna Moneymaker)

"The world needs more rare earths and those manufacturing supply chains are currently captive to the whim of the Chinese government, which has had a tendency over the years to weaponise the rare earths supply chain," he said.

"Australia and other like-minded and economically liberal nations realise that their own domestic, sovereign manufacturing capacity needs a source of rare earths that's outside of China.

"We're not just talking to the US, we're talking to European, Japanese and other countries all over the globe."

Trade being 'weaponised'

The growing geopolitical tensions were reflected in July when the federal government signed an agreement to supply more uranium to India.

India's High Commissioner to Australia, Canberra-based Nagesh Singh, said ongoing cooperation among nations would be vital in lifting living standards in his country.

Nagesh Singh wants more collaboration between like-minded countries on critical minerals. (ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas)

During a brief stopover in Kalgoorlie-Boulder on Thursday, Mr Singh toured the $800 million Kalgoorlie refinery owned by the Gina Rinehart-backed Lynas Rare Earths.

"I am not naming any countries but trade, resources are being weaponised … so like-minded countries who share common geopolitical objectives are coming together the world over," he said.

"You'll see more and more cooperation happening. It's going to be a very critical area for future growth, not just for India and Australia, but the rest of the world.

"These specific minerals should be democratised, everyone should have access without the threat of denial."

World.title: Ex-NRL player reveals drug offers during crippling gambling addiction
World.content:
A former professional rugby league player says gambling company employees offered to secure him illicit drugs to "strengthen" their relationship when he was in the grips of a financially crippling wagering addiction.

Luke Bateman, 31, who had losses of "tens of thousands of dollars a month" at the peak of his problem gambling, will give evidence about his personal experience at a Senate inquiry into the federal government's legislation to restrict gambling ads in Canberra on Monday.

Luke Bateman reveals depths of gambling habit Luke Bateman was 19 and living out his NRL dream, but a gambling addiction saw him retire from sport $250,000 in debt.

The two-day inquiry is due to hear from medical experts and welfare charities urging Labor to strengthen its proposal, while the gambling industry has argued against tougher measures.

Bateman, who played in the NRL for the Canberra Raiders and is now a social media influencer with a two-book deal to author his own fantasy series, last month told Australian Story how he survived his gambling addiction and was now advocating for an end to so-called gambling inducements.

Members of the crossbench, opposition and some backbench government MPs are also backing this push, while last month delegates at Labor's national conference voted to include a commitment to tackle inducements in the party's policy platform.

The government's legislation proposes restrictions on TV gambling ads between 6am and 8:30pm and on radio during school pick-up and drop-off times, as well as an opt-out system for online ads.

'Relentless' gambling inducements take their toll

Bateman previously held multiple online wagering accounts across several companies and said as a high-spending punter he was assigned account managers as a personalised point of contact.

He said these managers would seek to build a rapport with him, offering gambling inducements, like bonus bets, and invitations to exclusive events with travel, hotels, food and alcohol all paid for.

Bateman said the promotion of inducements was "relentless". (Australian Story: Tom Hancock)

"They enter into this knowing that the reason that they are creating a friendship with you is to encourage you to bet with them and to continue to lose lots and lots of money," he said.

"They are not doing it out of any duty of care."

Bateman described the promotion of inducements as "relentless".

"I was a racing punter. Obviously Saturdays are your main race days, so every Friday I would receive a message of, 'Hello, this is your exclusive offer for tomorrow,'" he said.

"That would happen every single week."

Drugs offered in bid to build personal relationships

Bateman has also alleged there were "multiple times" when after accepting an invitation to an interstate event he would be contacted by his gambling account manager, offering to arrange access to illicit drugs.

"The week of the event, they'd sort of send you a message and be like, 'Hey mate, you know, do you want any … drugs on the weekend?'" he said.

" If you're going to Melbourne, they're like, 'Hey mate … if you need a couple of bags, let us know and we'll have it organised for you, and we'll get it to you.' "

Bateman said these offers were not made in any "official" capacity on behalf of the wagering companies, but he believed it was a "tactic" to "strengthen friendships and bonds" with his account manager.

"That obviously … came with the expectation that then I would continue to gamble with their company specifically, and nobody else," he said.

"Creating a sense of trust, creating a sense of friendship, absolutely came with the underlying desire to make sure that you lost all of your money with them.

Bateman played for the Canberra Raiders from 2015 to 2020. (Getty Images: Mark Nolan)

Bateman said illicit drugs were a part of the "sporting, partying male culture in general" that was "part and parcel" with the "racing, sporting drinking sort of scene".

"That was happening in all areas of life," he said.

"I was also like a very happy and willing participant of this. No-one was forcing me to do this.

" But I was also 21, very young, very vulnerable and these men [working for the gambling companies] were older, in positions of power … I would say really exploiting that vulnerability and youthful naivety. "

Inducements make it hard to 'break away'

Bateman said when he was losing tens of thousands of dollars, his account managers did not offer help, seek to verify what his earnings were or indicate he should seek support.

Instead, he said there were times after a "big loss" he would be contacted with a bonus bet offer where the company would tip in an additional amount of funds to gamble with.

Gambling advertising crackdown The Albanese government will target social media influencers and individuals who promote gambling on social media as part of its proposed laws.

"When someone reaches out to you and offers you … this really attractive deal to do it again, it's so motivating to re-enter gambling," he said.

Bateman said the inducements were also "incredibly triggering" when he was trying to "break away" from the patterns, people and places linked to his addiction.

Despite his experience, Bateman said he had a lot of "grace" for the account managers who were just doing their job.

"I'm not going to sit here and say that these people are completely evil, but the industry creates the opportunity for this to happen," he said.

" These people are really just existing inside of the vacuum created by lack of regulation. "

Bateman said he would like to see the government remove promotions and inducements sent by text, email or phone call, whether as a mass-marketing campaign or through personalised account managers.

"Removing those direct contacts and those direct promotions and inducements would be incredibly helpful," he said.

"It's not [about] trying to stop anyone from having a bet.

"What we're trying to stop is the relentless targeting of vulnerable individuals."

Under Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, Labor is pushing forward with its gambling reform. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Labor stands by 'strongest-ever' reforms

A spokesperson for the federal government said Labor was focused on implementing its proposal, described as the "strongest-ever" reforms to tackle gambling harms.

"Among these measures is a strengthening of BetStop, the national register that allows people who don't want to place a bet or get inducements to opt out," they said.

"There are also existing restrictions on gambling companies for inducements, including that direct marketing may only be sent to customers who have provided their consent to receive them."

This Liberal took his teacher to gambling anonymous When Liberal backbencher Simon Kennedy was a teenager, one of his high school teachers asked to borrow money for his gambling addiction. He says he ended up accompanying the teacher to Gamblers Anonymous meetings.

But Liberal MP Simon Kennedy said the gambling industry had shown self-regulation did not work despite the government leaving "predatory gambling inducements out of its reforms".

"Labor's own national conference has recognised the problem," he said.

"Now the prime minister needs to show the same leadership."

In submissions to the Senate inquiry, St Vincent de Paul Society CEO Toby O'Connor also said "stronger action" was needed, while the Royal Australasian College of Physicians called for an end to online gambling advertising.

Meanwhile, peak industry body Responsible Wagering Australia (RWA) has said Labor's proposal will "materially reduce funding for broadcasting, sport and racing" and argued the measures went "further than required" to meet the government's objectives.

"This will reduce funding flowing to sport, local clubs, community programs and racing," the RWA submission said.

RWA said illegal offshore gambling was a growing "threat" and argued reforms should be "carefully calibrated" to avoid pushing consumers toward these markets that were "beyond the reach of the very protections Australia has established to keep them safe".

World.title: Citizenship rule takes effect amid spike in Qld gun licence applications
World.content:
New restrictions on who can own guns in Queensland come into effect today, amid a spike in new applications to register weapons.

The latest figures from Queensland Police show a 21 per cent rise in firearm licence applications in March 2026, a month after Premier David Crisafulli announced reforms in the wake of the Bondi Beach terror attack.

Several provisions of the act relating to antisemitism are already in effect, but from today only Australian citizens will be eligible for a weapons licence, and non-citizens will need exemptions for sport or work.

Industry and experts say uncertainty about future restrictions is among a mix of factors driving demand, with women leading the charge.

Uncertainty spikes demand

Aaron Lemphers runs one of Queensland's largest firearms training services, providing accredited safety courses in almost 70 locations across the state.

Aaron Lemphers has been a firearms instructor since 2018. (Supplied)

He said enquiries spiked almost immediately after the December attack.

New Qld guns law restrict weapons ownership The laws aim to crack down on rising gun crime and include tougher penalties for drive-by shootings.

"Literally the weekend after it happened … the phone didn't stop," Mr Lemphers said.

"They would say, 'I want to get one before the government makes it harder. I want to get my wife a licence before they can take them.'"

Applicants must complete a safety course approved by Queensland Police before they can apply for a gun licence.

In the past six months, Mr Lemphers said he had hired four additional training contractors to meet the rising demand.

A firearms safety course Statement of Attainment certificate is needed before applying for a weapons licence in Queensland. (ABC Tropical North: Aimee Mitchell)

Figures to the end of May show there were 234,732 issued weapons licences and 1,171,717 registered weapons in Queensland.

In March, there were 2,387 new firearm licence applications, up from 1,971 the year before, a rise of 21 per cent.

Between January and April, applications were up 19 per cent, with more than 1,200 additional applications lodged compared with the same period in 2025.

New applications received YEAR APPLICATIONS 2021 17,353 2022 15,701 2023 18,086 2024 19,797 2025 19,320

In North Queensland, Bowen Sporting Shooters Association president Marty Duggan said a growing number of women were applying for gun licences and joining the sport.

"The last 18 months has seen an influx in women joining the club," he said.

"Husbands are getting their wives to join clubs so they can share the weapons if the Queensland government do put a limit on them."

While the reforms have influenced some of his members to consider new licences, experts who study legal gun owners say there were several factors at play.

The broader picture

University of Queensland criminologist associate professor Suzanna Fay has spent years researching Australia's legal firearms community.

Suzanna Fay says the firearm community have been concerned about what policy changes were going to follow the Bondi Beach attack. (Supplied)

She said while it was unlikely there was a single explanation for the increase in licence applications, concerns over the reforms were a factor.

"I do think that the Bondi incident is probably playing into people's concerns about what might happen to legislation," she said.

"It's hard for me to tell exactly what is driving that trend and it's probably more than just one thing."

She said nationally there was a longer-term trend of more women becoming involved in recreational shooting and shooting sports, as both clubs and family members increased recruitment.

Qld government won't support gun buyback, ABC understands The ABC understands Queensland will join the Northern Territory and Tasmania in rejecting a national gun buyback scheme.

Dr Fay said firearm ownership often served a different purpose in rural Australia than in metropolitan areas.

"The reasons for rural ownership are a bit different to city ownership of firearms. It's really around farm work that's intrinsic to their livelihood," she said.

She said public debate after high-profile incidents such as the Bondi attack needed to be evidence-based.

"I understand that there are emotions in play, and the fear is very real," she said.

"But we need to make sure we have those discussions without driving everybody to extremes."

Concerns over future law changes

The last of the reforms introduced by the state government are due to come into effect in 2027.

Graham Park says Shooters Union Australia members are concerned more restrictions may be on the way. (ABC News: Lawrence Jeffcoat)

But advocacy group Shooters Union Australia president Graham Park said gun owners were worried more restrictions could come, especially as the federal government pursued a buyback.

"I just think that spending billions of dollars on buying back farmers' and target shooters' legal guns and destroying them when we're in the midst of a cost-of-living crisis isn't the answer," he said.

He said some members had encouraged spouses or adult family members to obtain firearm licences while they could.

"People respond," he said. "Family members will get a licence … which is perfectly sensible behaviour when you're trying to keep family heirlooms and work tools."

World.title: Quick hits: Delta stuns with Aussie classic, 76yo claims history-making gold
World.content:
Delta Goodrem belts out an Aussie classic, a 76-year-old makes Commonwealth Games history and a cycling star is proud to have not thrown up on the podium.

Here are the quick hits from day nine of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Delta makes it a hat-trick with Aussie classic

Delta Goodrem produced a breathtaking performance in the closing ceremony. (Getty Images: Mattia Ozbot)

It was a closing ceremony featuring some serious Australian star power, with Delta Goodrem headlining proceedings.

It was the third time, after Melbourne 2006 and Gold Coast 2018, that Goodrem had performed at a Commonwealth Games, and the Australian icon was in fine form at the Hydro indoor arena in Glasgow.

Goodrem was revealed to the crowd in dramatic fashion, lit by a spotlight and sitting at a grand piano, belting out her classic Born To Try, before rising from her seat and welcoming the athletes into the venue with an inspired medley of her hits.

And the performance reached a real crescendo when she welcomed Scottish pop star Cammy Barnes to the stage for a rendition of the most classic of Aussie classics, John Farnham's You're the Voice.

Goosebumps in Glasgow.

2. 76-year-old creates Games history

Louise Hoskins made history on the final day of competition. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Louise Hoskins, 76, made history on the final day of competition in Glasgow, becoming the oldest medal winner in Commonwealth Games history.

She, along with partner Serena Bonnell, won gold in the women's Para bowls, defeating New Zealand in a classic.

It was Bonnell who provided the winning moment for the Aussies, conjuring a sublime shot late in the second set to secure the win.

The oldest competitor in Glasgow, Hoskins was struggling to wrap her head around the enormity of the achievement.

"It is incredible. I'm still pinching myself," she said.

"I never thought I'd ever get [a gold medal] at my age. Get out there and have a go, and never give up."

Asked how she planned to celebrate, Hoskins noted Bonnell still owed her a few drinks.

What will it be then?

"Whatever Serena's going to give me," Hoskins laughed.

3. Cycling star proud not to spew on podium

Leigh Hoffman looked far from comfortable on the podium. (Getty Images: Rob Casey/SNS Group)

Australian Leigh Hoffman won four medals in a packed track cycling program, including a gold on the final day of competition.

He was the second-last rider in the men's 1,000m time trial, so had a truncated warm-down before climbing onto the podium to receive his gold medal.

And he looked far from comfortable on the top step.

"You don't feel human," he says.

"You're just so cooked, my legs are still burning right now, I think it's been a solid hour. There's no pain like it for sprint and endurance – 1 kilometre all-out sprint, 58 seconds of pure pain. I'm still feeling it.

"I made sure to eat about four hours out so my stomach was pretty empty. I'm proud I didn't spew."

This is the sprint and keirin specialist's first 1km time trial in six years, but he says he has no plans to keep riding them at world titles, although he may go again in Amdavad in four years' time.

4. Aussie chef de mission gets ink

Loading...

Australia's chef de mission Petria Thomas loves the Friendly Games — and understandably so.

She was a nine-time Commonwealth gold medallist during her decorated swimming career and has just overseen a Games in which Australia claimed 70 golds, 41 more than the next best nation, England.

On the final day of competition, Thomas was seen out in Glasgow getting herself a permanent testament to the event for which she has so much affection.

She said the Games have a special place in her heart, and now a special place on her body.

"I've thought about it for a long time and the Commonwealth Games has been such a big part of my life, as big a part as the Olympics. So I thought why not get the Commonwealth Sport mark as well, and I'll wear it very proudly," Thomas said.

"The Commonwealth Games has played such an important part of my life and I wanted to get something to remember that."

5. Scottish athletes win fashion stakes

Scottish athletes had some fun at the closing ceremony. (AP: Kin Cheung)

Scottish athletes were hard to miss at the closing ceremony.

The host nation's contingent wore traffic cones on their heads as they took part in the festivities inside The Hydro.

Loading Instagram content

It's common practice for Glaswegians to put traffic cones on the heads of statues around the city.

Arguably the most famous example is the Duke of Wellington statue outside the Gallery of Modern Art.

A statue in Boston could not escape the Glaswegian tradition during the FIFA World Cup. (Getty Images: Craig Williamson/SNS Group)

The ritual was celebrated at the recent FIFA World Cup, with Scottish fans decorating statues in Boston in their customary way.

You can never suggest Scots don't know how to poke fun at themselves.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Blues pay tribute to 'hero' Daley as he stands down as coach
World.content:
Laurie Daley has ended speculation about his future by stepping down as NSW State of Origin coach after a series victory over Queensland.

After much speculation about his future, Daley took the expected step and announced the move in a statement from the NSWRL.

"I've always considered it an absolute honour and privilege to be involved with the NSW Blues State of Origin team, whether that was as a player or a coach, and I've always been ready to answer the call for my state whenever they needed me," Daley said.

Daley slams 'hidden agendas' after NSW Origin win Laurie Daley has the last laugh over critics who hounded him ahead of the State of Origin decider at Lang Park.

"We faced plenty of challenges in the 2026 series and I'm proud of the way the players banded together to overcome them and save their best performance for Game Three in Brisbane to secure a memorable series win.

"I thank the fans for their passion and their support, and I can't think of a better way to move on with the Shield back where it belongs in NSW."

The NSWRL paid tribute to Daley for his time with the team.

"NSWRL owes a massive debt of gratitude to Laurie for the service he has given to his state as both a player and a coach," NSWRL chief executive David Trodden said.

"He is widely regarded as one of the greatest players to have ever pulled on a sky blue jumper, becoming the first NSW captain to lead his state to three consecutive series wins in 1992-94.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"He has also led NSW to arguably two of the greatest Origin series wins of all time as a coach, after ending Queensland's eight-year winning streak in 2014 and overcoming adversity to steer the Blues home in 2026.

"Those wins transcended football. They lifted and reinvigorated the whole state. He deserves to leave the NSW Origin arena as the hero that he is."

After sealing the State of Origin series win, Daley delivered a scathing rebuke to his critics, suggesting there were "hidden agendas" that attempted to undermine his NSW camp.

Daley, hammered publicly and privately over the Blues' form through the first two games of the series, had the last laugh as NSW secured a 30-12 victory at Lang Park.

World.title: Commonwealth Games don't need to mean anything to you to mean the world
World.content:
You see a lot of Olympic rings tattoos on athletes.

They feature a lot in the pool and the track, as you'd expect, but you'll catch them on NRL and NRLW players too from time to time, thanks to the recent inclusion of rugby sevens.

Petria Thomas got them on her right ankle 30 years ago and, after Glasgow, she's had the 2026 Commonwealth Games logo inked on the other side.

"The Commonwealth Games has been such a big part of my life, as big a part as the Olympics, so I thought why not?" the eight-time Olympic medallist said.

"I'll wear it very proudly."

Loading...

Thomas, who won nine golds across three Commonwealth outings, said the 1994 Games were the springboard for her career, just as they will be for so many athletes in Glasgow.

"For many athletes, this is their first experience in a multi-sport environment and there's nothing that can compare to going into those sorts of environments," she said.

"So to have the opportunity to do it here in Glasgow has been incredible and for so many of our Australian athletes, the Commonwealth Games is their launching pad."

The 2026 Games will forever mark the coming out party for debutant athletes as varied as 14-year-old Mia Hogan, a girl who made the final of the women's 100m freestyle S13 on the first night of the swimming program, and 76-year-old Louise Hoskins, Australia's oldest gold medallist after para pairs bowls victory in the final hours of competition.

At 76, Games debutant Louise Hopkins is Australia's oldest gold medallist. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

For the rising athletics team, this was a combination of a coming of age and a coming out, with the middle-distance, long-distance and field stars reaffirming their brilliance, and the newly minted sprint stars shining at an international meet for the first time.

Even in the swimming team, with so many established stars who regularly speak about the Commonwealth Games as a stepping stone, there were people like Jenna Forrester and Sam Williamson and Meg Harris getting their moments in the sun.

At times it felt like an unfair fight.

Shayna Jack, Meg Harris and Mollie O'Callaghan made just one of the podium sweeps for the Australian team. (Gety Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

In the end, Australia led the overall medal tally by a cool 61 medals, winning more than twice as many golds as England and more than triple Canada's after topping the swimming, cycling and athletics.

It's true that some of the best sporting nations weren't here and of those that were, some of the superstars didn't turn up, but you can only beat the ones who do.

"We're just good at our sport. Everyone likes an underdog. We're the same in Australia," Thomas said.

"Australians really value Commonwealth Games, it's always been an important competition for us and our sports know how important it is for athlete development and career progression. We really have prioritised Commonwealth Games and that's really shown here."

And try telling Peter Bol that these Games don't matter as he cheered on Luke Boyes and Peyton Craig on their way to the 800m final.

It mattered to Peter Bol. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Try telling Paul Trainor not to worry as he processed being battered by Dimeji Shittu in their heavyweight semifinal.

It mattered to Paul Trainor. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Try telling Kiana Elliott to cheer up after her third clean and jerk left her fourth for a second straight Games.

It mattered to Kiana Elliott. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Try telling Georgia Baker her spectacular Games weren't worth anything as she burst into tears when receiving the news she was the closing ceremony flag-bearer.

It mattered to Georgia Baker. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

These Games can mean government waste to Victorians, they can mean occasional traffic inconveniences to Glaswegians, they can mean late nights or early mornings on a blog or stream for many of you.

But they can also mean a new beginning, for athletes young and old, and for the Games as a whole.

Ironically, the event that Thomas credits for kickstarting her international career 32 years ago, was held in Victoria, albeit the one in Canada. This time around, the Australian version's withdrawal led to Glasgow picking up the baton.

Fans gather near Glasgow's Finnieston Crane between Games events. (Getty Images: Euan Cherry)

Limited and imperfect, it was a decision that saved a concept on life support.

"We're just grateful to be here," Thomas said, getting choked up.

"After what occurred, there was a time where we didn't know whether there would ever be another Commonwealth Games."

Commonwealth Sport has pledged to keep the Games alive.

It wants to engage with athletes to make them fit for purpose and sustainable, economically and environmentally.

Amdavad in India has pledged to deliver a full slate of events in 2030, with prospective hosts allegedly expressing interest in taking on 2034.

Who knows if that will come to fruition, but for 10 days of inclement weather and imperfect organisation, we saw a glimpse of Australia's future, and that's got to be worth something.

World.title: Hundreds gather at Harts Range for red dirt racing and rodeo
World.content:
In the desert sand beneath the towering ranges, more than 1,200 ringers, pastoralists and residents from across the Red Centre gathered on the weekend for the Harts Range Rodeo and Races.

The iconic outback event takes place on Mount Riddock cattle station near the remote community of Atitjere, about a 220-kilometre drive north-east from Alice Springs.

Now in their 79th year, the races have been bringing people together in this remote part of the country for decades.

Riders showcased their steeds to spectators before taking to the track. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

A chance to reconnect

For people living on remote Territory cattle stations, events like the past weekend's are rare opportunities to spend time with friends face-to-face.

The future of rodeo was in safe hands at Harts Range. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

This year, many stations in the region are celebrating their best season in recent memory due to significant rainfall.

But others are still recovering from damaging historic flooding from the start of the year.

Harts Range Races life member Jo Fogarty is from Lucy Creek Station, which is still working through repairs.

Jo Fogarty says it has been nice to see everyone after a particularly heavy wet season. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

"Especially this area with all the rain people have had, it's good just to get together and have a yarn," Ms Fogarty said.

"When you're [at] the beginning of the year when everyone's talking about the floods [and] now it's like, oh, let's just have a good time," she said.

"We're a pretty good community and everyone is very caring."

Will Weir and Alan Brown helped organise the bucking stock on the day. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

Good-natured competition

As well as lots of racing, the weekend hosts fashion on the field events, family activities and a Saturday night bush dance.

The rodeo events attract seasoned competitors as well as more recently arrived young ringers living and working in the region.

Anthony and Danyelle Haigh took out one of the Fashions on the Field events at the Central Australian race meet. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

Jacob Portelli is from Sydney, and is a first-year ringer at Huckitta Station, where his brother is the station manager.

He said local rodeos like these will keep him in the region a little longer.

"I want to give it a crack and try and win meself one of them [trophy belt] buckles," Mr Portelli said.

Bronco riders were assisted by pickup men from local cattle stations. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

"[It] might not be next year, but I think I'm stuck here until I get one of them."

In the horse racing, Jake Dallaglio took out the feature Stockman's Cup, having struggled in the earlier races in the afternoon.

Jake Dallaglio took out the feature Stockman’s Cup on Saturday afternoon. (ABC Rural: Charles Geary)

Finishing the race as the sun set over Harts Range, he said it was a good way to end the racing.

"First race didn't go so well, [I] came second last," Mr Dallaglio said.

"[So] to win, that's a pretty cool feeling."

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Former 2GB broadcaster on trial for indecent assault, sexual touching
World.content:
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of day one of Alan Jones’ indecent assault and sexual touching trial. I’ll be keeping you informed of the latest developments with my colleague Clare Sibthorpe.

Jones, a former teacher, political candidate, speechwriter and coach of the Australian national rugby union team, dominated Sydney breakfast radio for decades before he retired from 2GB in May 2020.

Alan Jones leaves Day Street police station in November 2024 after being arrested and charged. James Brickwood

More than four years later, in November 2024, he was arrested and charged over allegations he indecently assaulted, groped or inappropriately touched a number of young men.

His criminal trial starts today in the NSW Local Court in Sydney and centres on allegations by six men, who will give evidence over the coming weeks. Jones has always maintained his innocence and is defending the charges.

Warning: This blog may contain discussion of legal submissions and evidence that is confronting for some readers.

Anyone needing support can contact 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732), National Sexual Abuse and Redress Support Service 1800 211 028, Lifeline 13 11 14, and Kids Helpline 1800 55 1800.

World.title: One Nation unveils Victorian candidates ahead of state election
World.content:
A former high-profile Liberal who quit after suing her own party and the inner-city animator behind Pauline Hanson’s controversial “anti-woke” movie are among eight Victorian upper house candidates One Nation will formally unveil on Monday.

Warren Pickering, One Nation’s Victorian president, will run as the party’s leader in the Victorian upper house. Pickering ran the party’s campaign in the 2022 election, before an unsuccessful tilt as a Victorian senator for One Nation at the federal election last year.

One Nation Victorian president Warren Pickering will run as the party’s leader in the Victorian upper house. Simon Schluter

Colleen Harkin, a former member of the Liberal Party’s administrative committee, is also running for an upper house seat. Harkin led a Supreme Court challenge against the Liberals’ decision to grant John Pesutto a $1.55 million loan after he lost a defamation case against Moira Deeming. The grant spared Pesutto from bankruptcy, which would have forced a byelection in his seat of Hawthorn.

Harkin resigned from the party and quit the administrative council in June. After resigning, she said she would join One Nation and that she would consider standing as a candidate in the election.

World.title: ‘Clarko’ looks exasperated. It’s time for a hard conversation
World.content:
Four Points SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Clarko’ looks exasperated. It’s time for a hard conversation Peter Ryan Updated August 3, 2026 — 9:09am ,first published 7:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Josh Fraser was expected to lay strong foundations for Michael Voss’s replacement. Nothing is as simple as that.

The message to be patient with North Melbourne is wearing thin.

What Nick Watson could achieve that Peter Daicos didn’t.

Essendon are about as deserving of an assistance package as a billionaire seeking tax relief.

North Melbourne are treading water, regardless of what they say In the past five matches, North Melbourne have been sixth in the competition for average age and fifth for games experience. They have been competitive but lost each game. Although there is a big hole in the middle when it comes to age and experience, they should be performing better than they have in the past five matches when a wildcard chance has been up for grabs.



Their inaccuracy has been costly but combined with the overuse of handball and indefensible turnovers in the back half, they have collapsed to 13th on the ladder. Billboards promoting improvement aren’t created from two wins over Essendon and Richmond, Carlton on Good Friday, Port Adelaide, Gold Coast and West Coast. Alastair Clarkson faces his moment of truth this off-season at the Kangaroos. AFL Photos Making mistakes is part of learning but some of the risky kicks their defensive runners take from the back half would be off the table even for defenders at the best, most skilful and experienced teams. It works often enough for their transition numbers to be reasonable but too often mistakes are made at crucial moments when the result is in doubt.



It’s not just Colby McKercher and Caleb Daniel biting off more than they can chew, but that pair need to be accountable so the team learns when to go and when to slow. After 19 wins in 79 matches as North Melbourne coach, Alastair Clarkson looks exasperated on game day, his unrelenting style potentially wearing on his leaders who play with furrowed brows in 2026. He reached that point at the Hawks in his first two seasons before switching gear. Perhaps that’s the conversation the club hierarchy needs to have with him before entering next season. They can’t extend him prematurely but the four-time premiership coach who joined them in their hour of need deserves honesty as to what they are thinking. And if they are considering that a new breed of coach could do for North Melbourne what Steven King has done for Melbourne this season then that argument must be had.



The Kangaroos need to be honest with each other over summer so the alignment necessary for success is maintained. Because the message to be patient is wearing thin. Josh Fraser is a ‘disruptor’. That doesn’t meant he’ll get the job Tasmania went for the mature-aged recruit when they appointed Ken Hinkley as their first coach.



Essendon’s coach recruiters are conducting their coaching search in the equivalent of a compromised draft. That’s because several strong candidates declared themselves off-limits to the Bombers due to both the campaign supporting James Hird as a candidate and the club’s perceived treatment of “outsiders”. Josh Fraser’s record as Blues interim coach is outstanding. AFL Photos By contrast Carlton appeared to have a free run to appoint the best untried coach in the market via a process being managed by experienced operators – chief executive Graham Wright and football boss Chris Davies. A predictable process loomed.



Coffee dates at Brunetti’s and elsewhere, followed by a short list of candidates presenting in the next fortnight would lead to a new polo top being measured up and worn by a new coach declaring at a media conference their excitement at what lay ahead. Meanwhile, Josh Fraser was expected to selflessly take on the interim job for 14 matches and lay strong foundations for Michael Voss’s replacement. Fremantle assistant coach Jaymie Graham is a candidate for both the Carlton and Essendon coaching jobs. AFL Photos Of course, nothing is that simple nowadays. Fraser has the Blues inside the top 10 with three games remaining after their 76-point thrashing of the Brisbane Lions became their ninth win in 11 matches under the hoodie-wearing coach.



Reflecting the times, he has disrupted – by winning rather than campaigning – a coaching selection process that you could argue he should have been considered for before his wins as interim coach. Or has he? Those who joined the “give it to him now” category after the Blues’ massive win over Brisbane think Fraser has done the unthinkable and made the Essendon coaching race more open than Carlton’s. That’s a stretch. What Fraser has done is earn himself an invitation to join the short list of candidates to become Carlton’s next coach. He might even earn himself the right to be in the last two considered.



It would be a surprise if he didn’t accept that invitation this week after consulting family, friends, mentors and the Blues as he has done throughout his time in the chair. Fraser deserves that chance to present, but he also should be respected if he decides the time is not right for him. He coached the Blues on Saturday night as he mourned the death of his father, Bill, who had died on Thursday. As is his way, Fraser went about his work business, notably acknowledging post-game the support of his assistants in preparing for the match. He has been in the coaching business since 2013, coached his own teams at NEAFL and VFL level and has an ability to create genuine relationships with people across all levels of the game. His authenticity, perspective and humility has shone through during his more regular public appearances as interim coach and, unlike some other interim coaches in recent times, he has wanted to divert attention away from himself at every opportunity.



That’s been good to see as Fraser put his coaching reputation on the line when he did the right thing by the Blues in accepting the interim position for 14 matches. His ability as a coach was going to be judged despite his capacity to create the environment he believed necessary for success being limited. But he took it on anyway. From left: Carlton CEO Graham Wright, president Rob Priestley and football manager Chris Davies have a big decision ahead of them. Getty Images Fraser is not silly. He knows enough about coaching and the AFL to understand that nine wins from 11 matches doesn’t automatically make him the best man for the job. The 44-year-old would be as aware as the hard heads responsible for selecting Carlton’s next coach (which also includes the Eagles’ premiership coach Adam Simpson) that the wins/loss record as interim is just one part of the criteria assessed when deciding the best candidate.



The panel wants to know what the candidates stand for as a coach, their use of data and how it informs their decision-making, their management skills, their capacity to cope with pressure, their ability to teach in a range of ways and a range of other qualities that make senior coaches successful. Carlton have been able to see the way Fraser operates as the stand-in coach but will still be making as educated a guess about him in a range of those areas as they will be on the other known candidates which include James Kelly, Corey Enright, Daniel Giansiracusa and Jaymie Graham. Like Fraser, that crew will have strengths and weaknesses and will need the support of experienced leaders if they become a senior coach. Unlike Fraser they won’t have proved themselves as able to coach a winning team at AFL level and their ability to form relationships with the players will be unknown. To many supporters that will be all that matters and, in many ways, it is all that is important.



Choosing an untried coach other than Fraser will be a harder sell and need explanation, but they will be able to do that if they select another person after comparing the candidate’s methods and personality. If they choose Fraser they need to know he impressed them enough to convince them he was the best candidate. A coach who can lead this team to a premiership is what Carlton are chasing. Of the nine interim coaches appointed full-time this century, Paul Roos is the only interim coach to do so. Fraser may, in fact, be the man. The reality is the next fortnight will help inform Carlton’s decision as much if not more than the past 11 matches.



Whatever the Blues’ call, the past three months has convinced everyone that at some point, somewhere, Fraser, if he wishes to, should become a senior coach. And it should also remind Essendon of the job talented coaches working away in the system can do if given the chance. Don’t sell Nick Watson’s achievement short Nick Watson is a star. He can turn a match in a minute, his ability to switch from defensive to attacking transition is unmatched. He is brave, cheeky and skilful. His effort to kick 52 goals with three rounds remaining is meritorious because few small forwards reach the half century before turning 22.



Nick Watson was at his brilliant best yet again for the Hawks. Getty Images Brisbane Lions champion Luke Power kicked 52 goals before turning 21 in 2000, but he is the only one this century to do so at a younger age than Watson. Cyril Rioli never kicked 50 goals in a season, Luke Breust was aged 23 when he passed the milestone. Eddie Betts was even older than Breust. Jeff Farmer and Phil Matera were 23 and Stephen Milne had turned 22. Ty Stengle helped the Cats to a flag with 50 goals in 2022 aged 23. Peter Daicos, a mid-sized forward, had kicked 70 goals before he turned 20 in 1981. Daicos was a goalkicking freak.



If Watson can win the Coleman Medal, he will have done something Daicos didn’t. Pick one is enough of a helping hand for the Bombers Essendon have draft pick number one with three matches remaining after the Tigers’ win over an inaccurate West Coast. Finishing on the bottom will help the AFL justify an assistance package despite the Bombers being about as deserving of one as a billionaire seeking tax relief. Essendon have high hopes for Nate Caddy AFL Photos



Giving them assistance is not only a reward for mediocrity but investing in a club that, part from recent recruiting, is yet to prove they can stack good decision after good decision as yet. Before any assistance package, the Bombers will have pick one, a likely compensation pick early in the second round which is designed to help clubs rebuilding plus any return from trading Zach Merrett who appears set to exit. That will arrive just one season after they added Sullivan Robey, Jacob Farrow and Dyson Sharp with picks 9, 10 and 13, following Isaac Kako in 2024 and Nate Caddy in 2023. Injuries have affected their performance and they missed on a couple of high draft picks. Fair play to Essendon for asking, but there should be resistance to assistance inside AFL House. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Ariana Grande ditches West End debut over ‘public scrutiny’ amid weight loss concerns
World.content:
CultureCelebrityAriana Grande Ariana Grande ditches West End debut over ‘public scrutiny’ amid weight loss concerns Kayla Olaya August 3, 2026 — 9:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ariana Grande has dropped out of her debut role in the West End revival of Stephen Sondheim’s 1984 musical Sunday in the Park with George due to “ongoing public scrutiny” amid growing concerns about her weight loss. Reps for the Wicked star told People on Monday morning (AEST) that the three-time Grammy Award winner “will be taking a step back from visibility after she completes the Eternal Sunshine tour,” in support of Grande’s 2024 album of the same name. A screen shot from the video clip for Ariana Grande’s song Petal. YouTube “She looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny,” the statement said. “This tour has been a beautiful experience for her. She loves her fans and has loved every minute of this tour so much.”



Before the announcement, fans and commentators expressed concerns about Grande’s wellbeing online after a newly released music video for her latest song, Petal, shows her appearing extremely thin. In the music video, a casting director character is seen making notes about Grande’s “audition”, writing “it couldn’t hurt to lose a little”. A screenshot of Ariana Grande’s Petal music video, where a casting director character notes it “couldn’t hurt to lose a little” about Grande’s audition. YouTube British actor and comedian Jameela Jamil was among those who expressed concern about Grande, stating “this poor woman is possibly dying right in front of us”, and arguing that the pop star’s team was responsible for the image being pushed to younger audiences. “This outfit is designed to accentuate the thinness for discourse. Her team are thoroughly irresponsible for not guiding her away from this deeply damaging image for her young fans to see so glamorised,” Jamil commented beneath one of Grande’s Instagram posts promoting the music video.



Jamil later took to her Instagram story to explain that, while uncomfortable, conversations about Grande’s weight should take place amid the broader context of celebrity thinness culture. “The shrinking pop star situation is something of a trolley problem,” Jamil said. “If we comment on [Grande’s] body, we could harm her mental health, which would be awful and nobody wants that. If we don’t comment on her body, we run the risk of normalising that image to hundreds of millions of teenage girls, kids and even impressionable adults, consuming her content. “Content which is pointedly accentuating her bones and tiny frame with belts and corsets. I think it’s worth considering that the pop star in question has access to a lot of mental health care and the best facilities on the planet, whereas the fans watching largely don’t. “Many have no support system equipped to handle the deadly clutches of anorexia. Her most recent images are flooding pro-anorexia websites, and teenage girls are saying ‘goals’.”



Meanwhile, model and author Charli Howard also took to Instagram to share her discomfort with Grande’s music video – particularly after gaining weight in the past few months and the ongoing battle to accept herself despite being an activist for body positivity. “I think it’s vital we discuss imagery/videos/content like these and the damage they can – and will – have on women and girls. WHAT YOU SEE HERE IS NOT NORMAL,” Howard wrote. “Over the past few weeks, as images of Ariana’s concert get plastered around online, I obviously see comments from worried fans, but I also see other people convincing others that she looks ‘healthy’, or that she has simply ‘lost puppy fat’. “I think it is absolutely appalling, from both a moral and capitalistic standpoint, to have released these videos and an album when this person needs psychiatric help and hospitalisation.



“I truly, truly hope she gets the help that she so desperately needs. We do not need a repeat of the early 2000s.” Grande’s latest album, Petal, was released on July 31. Sunday in the Park with George was slated to run in June next year. Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Robert Assaf continues evidence; Liberal MP Damien Tudehope set to appear
World.content:
Good morning and welcome to the Herald’s live coverage of the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s blockbuster Operation Rosny hearings.

I’m state political reporter Jessica McSweeney, and I’ll be bringing you all the latest updates from today’s evidence, along with analysis from the Herald’s senior writers.

Today we’ll continue to hear from former Catholic Schools NSW staffer and founding member of Liberal Party factional group the Reformers, Robert Assaf. This afternoon the commission is expected to call Damien Tudehope, a current Liberal MP who stood down as shadow attorney general when he discovered he would be asked to appear.

Tudehope is not accused of wrongdoing.

Here’s a recap of what we covered last week:

Former Catholic Schools NSW (CSNSW) CEO Dallas McInerney told the commission he wanted to “shake down” Angus Taylor for $10,000 for the Reformers. Text messages from former CSNSW staffer Dylan Whitelaw shown to the commission claimed Taylor agreed to donate $15,000 plus monthly contributions of $3000. Taylor has repeatedly said no payments were made.

The commission heard evidence from Whitelaw and Assaf that they would do work for the Reformers during the day at CSNSW. Whitelaw estimate Assaf’s work was a 60/40 split – 60 per cent on Reformers, 40 per cent on CSNSW duties. Assaf disputed this, and said he would only do political work after his work for CSNSW was completed.

Counsel assisting the commission, Dr Peggy Dwyer SC, played phone taps during her opening statement showing fugitive property developer Jean Nassif bragging about his influence over the then-Liberal state government. He called Dominic Perrottet his “boy”, and boasted that the fair trading minister would be replaced with one of his “girls”. Eleni Petinos was appointed to the role shortly after that phone call.

Michael O’Hara, who the commission has heard provided financial support to the Reformers, withdrew his support after feeling then-premier Dominic Perrottet and prime minister Scott Morrison had gone too “woke”.

Dwyer said in her opening statement she expects the evidence will show that figures in this investigation – Christian Ellis, Charles Perrottet and Jeremy Greenwood – anticipated they would be paid $2 million in total by Nassif, in exchange for furthering his interests.

A “shit sheet” was prepared against factional enemy of the Reformers David Elliott, which included the false claim he was having an affair. Elliott strongly denies this, and said he is a devoted husband of 30 years.

Today’s hearing kicks off at 9.30am, and you can follow the live stream here.

World.title: Forget the Sydney bubble for a moment. This is the best NRL story of 2026
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 Forget the Sydney bubble for a moment. This is the best NRL story of 2026 Dan Walsh August 3, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With nine Sydney clubs and a pair of powerhouses at either end of the eastern seaboard, it’s easy to spend an entire season navel-gazing. Fun too. See a week of Wests Tigers headlines that ranged from vaping to their halfback walking out, then back in, busting up and making up with his coach and teammates along the way. Loading The Tigers, Eels and Dragons boast three of the game’s largest fan bases and most recognisable brands, and occupy two of the three bottom rungs of the ladder, bringing all the scrutiny that deserves. The Panthers have flexed their post-Origin muscles at the top of the ladder again and the Roosters are flying – with the latter’s small galaxy of stars putting 82 points on North Queensland, becoming the first team to outscore the clock in 91 years.



The drums are beating once more out of Belmore too. The game’s loudest supporters are cautiously finding voice again as Canterbury push back into the top eight with six wins from their last seven games. Meanwhile, the Broncos and Storm will both miss the finals – just the second time in the NRL era that both grand finalists become September spectators without a salary cap punishment involved (2006 – Tigers and Cowboys, and 2005 – Roosters and Bulldogs). And quietly doing their thing among the usual suspects that dominate rugby league’s news cycle is Newcastle, spinning one of the game’s more remarkable revivals. Justin Holbrook is surely now a firm favourite to claim Dally M coach of the year honours after taking last year’s wooden spooners to the brink of a finals return.



His nearest competitors – Kristian Woolf lifting the Dolphins to within touching distance of their own maiden top-eight finish, and Andrew Webster’s Warriors harnessing serious momentum across the ditch – tell the other under-told tales of 2026. So too, the extra gear Cronulla is finding under Craig Fitzgibbon this season as Sydney’s smallest club. But right now, the Knights are our narrative. Especially with three straight losses by two points or less against the Rabbitohs, Sharks and Roosters accompanied by brutal, season-ending injuries to Dylans Brown and Lucas. Kalyn Ponga’s future is no longer a talking point, and it shows. Getty Images The shift in Kalyn Ponga’s body language all season was particularly noticeable in Saturday’s thumping win over Brisbane. With a last-round bye, one more victory from their last four games will have Ponga and Newcastle deservedly back in the mix come September. Figures at the club privately acknowledge that if not for Holbrook’s arrival and sweeping changes this time last year, then the long-running fear Ponga was destined to move on was going to be realised.



Instead, the playmaking shake-up bringing in Brown and Sandon Smith has been more successful than anyone imagined. Just as talk about Ponga’s future, rugby union and the Roosters started to fire up again earlier this year, the Knights buried it by announcing a three-year extension. All the hype, hoopla and endless speculation that has accompanied Ponga’s previous career moves was sidestepped as easily as the headgeared No.1 taking on a backpedalling defender. Knights coach Justin Holbrook has worked wonders in the Hunter. Getty Images Along with Fletcher Sharpe, Newcastle’s playmaking quartet has steered an enterprising, entertaining style well-suited to the game’s latest high-octane officiating, and even without Brown at the scrumbase, they put Brisbane to bed. Sharpe’s second try against the Broncos was their 25th try from inside their own half this year – the most of any side in the NRL. Holbrook’s easy-going outlook and coaxing of career-best form from forwards Jacob Saifiti, Trey Mooney, Lucas and Jermaine McEwen, among others, has revitalised an attack that this time last year simply hurt to watch.



The Dolphins are even easier on the eye, even with moments of brilliance against St George Illawarra outnumbered by bumbling and fumbling in an unconvincing 28-22 win. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Laurie Daley confirms Origin departure – and nominates the coach who should succeed him Isaiya Katoa will be better for his cautious return from a broken wrist. Just in time for Saturday’s latest Battle of Brisbane, with little doubt over the city’s new pecking order. Webster’s Warriors, meanwhile, host Penrith having already produced the best game of 2026 when they clashed in late May. The Kiwi side are the closest this competition has to the Panthers in so many ways – be it game-play, consistency or unflappable coach helming the whole show. After a month of indifferent mid-season form from both front-runners, the Warriors warmed up by pummelling the Gold Coast with eight tries. Penrith beat up Canberra in similar fashion. A top-tier clash is just reward for the stunning surge rugby league is enjoying in New Zealand. A Warriors home final too wouldn’t go astray if they can jag a top-two finish. Auckland’s Eden Park can seat 50,000 fans (an extra 20,000 on the club’s usual Mt Smart haunt) and it would still be well short of fitting everyone in. Just another story worth telling really.

World.title: The Eagles’ performance brought one player to tears. Fans would have felt the same
World.content:
NationalWAAFL 2026 Opinion The Eagles’ performance brought one player to tears. Fans would have felt the same Paddy Sweeney Nine Sports Presenter August 3, 2026 — 8:59am

August 3, 2026 — 8:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to the Western Watercooler, where we digest the talking points from the weekend’s games – and the highlights, frustrations and silver linings WA footy fans can cling to as the season progresses. The Dockers were resolute in their 37-point win over the Bulldogs. Josh Treacy celebrates a goal as Fremantle power past the Bulldogs on Friday. Getty Images They had to navigate a defensively minded opponent who did their very best to stifle and strangle the ladder leaders, but yet again Justin Longmuir and his team maintained their composure and held their nerve. Meanwhile, the Eagles result was enough to bring young gun Willem Duursma to tears post-game and many fans would have been the same.



If you were a West Coast supporter who paid to go to the MCG, you would have every right to contact the club seeking a refund. Related Article AFL 2026 Dan Gorringe was a battling ruckman. He’s now a social media star and might even become an AFL rights holder The poor skills and woeful goalkicking meant the Eagles were humbled by Richmond for a second time this season – both when the Tigers were at the bottom of the table. Fremantle Dockers What went right? The Dockers were able to secure a crucial piece of the premiership puzzle.



By cementing a top-two finish, two home finals are now in their keeping, meaning if things go to plan, they will only need to travel once in the finals series – for the grand final. And there’s reason to be confident. Optus Stadium is officially “Fortress Fremantle”. Abandon hope, all ye who enter here. Daniel Carson/AFL Photos via Getty Images Optus Stadium has been transformed into “Freo’s Fortress” in 2026 – the Dockers have won all 11 games at the venue. What went wrong? An area which remains a work in progress and where improvement can be made is in contested ball and around stoppage.



The Bulldogs won these key statistics, with Ed Richards and Tom Liberatore setting the tone. The positive was the Dockers were able to restrict the Dogs damage, even outscoring them from stoppage. Silver lining? Oscar McDonald. Should either Alex Pearce or Brennan Cox go down at the business end of the season, McDonald has shown he is a more than capable key defender replacement. The 30 year-old played just his seventh game for the season on Friday night, but played easily the best he has in a Fremantle jumper.



He intercepted, was calm and used the ball well. An added bonus is McDonald can also be used forward – booting five goals in his most recent WAFL performance when played in attack. Jake Waterman’s performance in front of goal highlighted the Eagles’ challenges on Sunday. Graham Denholm/AFL Photos via Getty Images West Coast Eagles What went right? The Eagles created enough chances, but couldn’t finish them.



They managed seven more inside-50s, took four more inside-50 marks, more than doubled the Tigers for tackles laid inside 50 and won the clearances. It only highlights how poor their finishing was. Loading What went wrong? The inaccurate goalkicking would have been enough to send fans watching, turn the TV off and go outside to catch some winter sunshine. Time after time, after time, the Eagles blew golden opportunities, some which had to be seen to be believed.



Jake Waterman was the chief offender, booting 2.6, including a miss from two metres out in the goalsquare. At one stage, West Coast were 3.17 in the third term, finishing with 9.19. Ill discipline also played it’s part, Rhett Bazzo’s 50-metre penalty for dissent turned a difficult Tom Lynch shot on goal into a formality at a crucial time. Silver lining? It’s one less away game to play. The 11-point defeat now has the Eagles with just four wins from their past 51 interstate games – a winning percentage of less than eight.



It’s a damning statistic for any side, but even more so for a team which travels every second week and has been doing so for 40 years.

World.title: Tolls cut on Sydney’s motorways following long-running negotiations
World.content:
Tolls will be cut on four motorways in Sydney including the M7 and M2 from as early as July next year while two-way tolling will be introduced on the Eastern Distributor as part of largest shake up of pricing in years.

Less than eight months out from the state election, 10 per cent will be cut from tolls on the Lane Cove Tunnel, while the same reduction will apply to longer journeys on the M2 motorway from July 1 next year.

The changes to toll prices follows two years of direct negotiations between the NSW government and Transurban. Janie Barrett

The cap on distance-based trips on the M7 will be cut by 10 per cent from January 2028, subject to a widening of the motorway.

Tolls on the Cross City Tunnel will be reduced by 20 per cent when the Western Harbour Tunnel opens in 2028.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Former 2GB broadcaster on trial for indecent assault, sexual touching
World.content:
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of day one of Alan Jones’ indecent assault and sexual touching trial. I’ll be keeping you informed of the latest developments with my colleague Clare Sibthorpe.

Jones, a former teacher, political candidate, speechwriter and coach of the Australian national rugby union team, dominated Sydney breakfast radio for decades before he retired from 2GB in May 2020.

Alan Jones leaves Day Street police station in November 2024 after being arrested and charged. James Brickwood

More than four years later, in November 2024, he was arrested and charged over allegations he indecently assaulted, groped or inappropriately touched a number of young men.

His criminal trial starts today in the NSW Local Court in Sydney and centres on allegations by six men, who will give evidence over the coming weeks. Jones has always maintained his innocence and is defending the charges.

Warning: This blog may contain discussion of legal submissions and evidence that is confronting for some readers.

Anyone needing support can contact 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732), National Sexual Abuse and Redress Support Service 1800 211 028, Lifeline 13 11 14, and Kids Helpline 1800 55 1800.

World.title: One Nation unveils Victorian candidates ahead of state election
World.content:
A former high-profile Liberal who quit after suing her own party and the inner-city animator behind Pauline Hanson’s controversial “anti-woke” movie are among eight Victorian upper house candidates One Nation will formally unveil on Monday.

Warren Pickering, One Nation’s Victorian president, will run as the party’s leader in the Victorian upper house. Pickering ran the party’s campaign in the 2022 election, before an unsuccessful tilt as a Victorian senator for One Nation at the federal election last year.

One Nation Victorian president Warren Pickering will run as the party’s leader in the Victorian upper house. Simon Schluter

Colleen Harkin, a former member of the Liberal Party’s administrative committee, is also running for an upper house seat. Harkin led a Supreme Court challenge against the Liberals’ decision to grant John Pesutto a $1.55 million loan after he lost a defamation case against Moira Deeming. The grant spared Pesutto from bankruptcy, which would have forced a byelection in his seat of Hawthorn.

Harkin resigned from the party and quit the administrative council in June. After resigning, she said she would join One Nation and that she would consider standing as a candidate in the election.

World.title: ‘Clarko’ looks exasperated. It’s time for a hard conversation
World.content:
Four Points SportAFLAFL 2026 ‘Clarko’ looks exasperated. It’s time for a hard conversation Peter Ryan Updated August 3, 2026 — 9:09am ,first published 7:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Key points Josh Fraser was expected to lay strong foundations for Michael Voss’s replacement. Nothing is as simple as that.

The message to be patient with North Melbourne is wearing thin.

What Nick Watson could achieve that Peter Daicos didn’t.

Essendon are about as deserving of an assistance package as a billionaire seeking tax relief.

North Melbourne are treading water, regardless of what they say In the past five matches, North Melbourne have been sixth in the competition for average age and fifth for games experience. They have been competitive but lost each game. Although there is a big hole in the middle when it comes to age and experience, they should be performing better than they have in the past five matches when a wildcard chance has been up for grabs.



Their inaccuracy has been costly but combined with the overuse of handball and indefensible turnovers in the back half, they have collapsed to 13th on the ladder. Billboards promoting improvement aren’t created from two wins over Essendon and Richmond, Carlton on Good Friday, Port Adelaide, Gold Coast and West Coast. Alastair Clarkson faces his moment of truth this off-season at the Kangaroos. AFL Photos Making mistakes is part of learning but some of the risky kicks their defensive runners take from the back half would be off the table even for defenders at the best, most skilful and experienced teams. It works often enough for their transition numbers to be reasonable but too often mistakes are made at crucial moments when the result is in doubt.



It’s not just Colby McKercher and Caleb Daniel biting off more than they can chew, but that pair need to be accountable so the team learns when to go and when to slow. After 19 wins in 79 matches as North Melbourne coach, Alastair Clarkson looks exasperated on game day, his unrelenting style potentially wearing on his leaders who play with furrowed brows in 2026. He reached that point at the Hawks in his first two seasons before switching gear. Perhaps that’s the conversation the club hierarchy needs to have with him before entering next season. They can’t extend him prematurely but the four-time premiership coach who joined them in their hour of need deserves honesty as to what they are thinking. And if they are considering that a new breed of coach could do for North Melbourne what Steven King has done for Melbourne this season then that argument must be had.



The Kangaroos need to be honest with each other over summer so the alignment necessary for success is maintained. Because the message to be patient is wearing thin. Josh Fraser is a ‘disruptor’. That doesn’t meant he’ll get the job Tasmania went for the mature-aged recruit when they appointed Ken Hinkley as their first coach.



Essendon’s coach recruiters are conducting their coaching search in the equivalent of a compromised draft. That’s because several strong candidates declared themselves off-limits to the Bombers due to both the campaign supporting James Hird as a candidate and the club’s perceived treatment of “outsiders”. Josh Fraser’s record as Blues interim coach is outstanding. AFL Photos By contrast Carlton appeared to have a free run to appoint the best untried coach in the market via a process being managed by experienced operators – chief executive Graham Wright and football boss Chris Davies. A predictable process loomed.



Coffee dates at Brunetti’s and elsewhere, followed by a short list of candidates presenting in the next fortnight would lead to a new polo top being measured up and worn by a new coach declaring at a media conference their excitement at what lay ahead. Meanwhile, Josh Fraser was expected to selflessly take on the interim job for 14 matches and lay strong foundations for Michael Voss’s replacement. Fremantle assistant coach Jaymie Graham is a candidate for both the Carlton and Essendon coaching jobs. AFL Photos Of course, nothing is that simple nowadays. Fraser has the Blues inside the top 10 with three games remaining after their 76-point thrashing of the Brisbane Lions became their ninth win in 11 matches under the hoodie-wearing coach.



Reflecting the times, he has disrupted – by winning rather than campaigning – a coaching selection process that you could argue he should have been considered for before his wins as interim coach. Or has he? Those who joined the “give it to him now” category after the Blues’ massive win over Brisbane think Fraser has done the unthinkable and made the Essendon coaching race more open than Carlton’s. That’s a stretch. What Fraser has done is earn himself an invitation to join the short list of candidates to become Carlton’s next coach. He might even earn himself the right to be in the last two considered.



It would be a surprise if he didn’t accept that invitation this week after consulting family, friends, mentors and the Blues as he has done throughout his time in the chair. Fraser deserves that chance to present, but he also should be respected if he decides the time is not right for him. He coached the Blues on Saturday night as he mourned the death of his father, Bill, who had died on Thursday. As is his way, Fraser went about his work business, notably acknowledging post-game the support of his assistants in preparing for the match. He has been in the coaching business since 2013, coached his own teams at NEAFL and VFL level and has an ability to create genuine relationships with people across all levels of the game. His authenticity, perspective and humility has shone through during his more regular public appearances as interim coach and, unlike some other interim coaches in recent times, he has wanted to divert attention away from himself at every opportunity.



That’s been good to see as Fraser put his coaching reputation on the line when he did the right thing by the Blues in accepting the interim position for 14 matches. His ability as a coach was going to be judged despite his capacity to create the environment he believed necessary for success being limited. But he took it on anyway. From left: Carlton CEO Graham Wright, president Rob Priestley and football manager Chris Davies have a big decision ahead of them. Getty Images Fraser is not silly. He knows enough about coaching and the AFL to understand that nine wins from 11 matches doesn’t automatically make him the best man for the job. The 44-year-old would be as aware as the hard heads responsible for selecting Carlton’s next coach (which also includes the Eagles’ premiership coach Adam Simpson) that the wins/loss record as interim is just one part of the criteria assessed when deciding the best candidate.



The panel wants to know what the candidates stand for as a coach, their use of data and how it informs their decision-making, their management skills, their capacity to cope with pressure, their ability to teach in a range of ways and a range of other qualities that make senior coaches successful. Carlton have been able to see the way Fraser operates as the stand-in coach but will still be making as educated a guess about him in a range of those areas as they will be on the other known candidates which include James Kelly, Corey Enright, Daniel Giansiracusa and Jaymie Graham. Like Fraser, that crew will have strengths and weaknesses and will need the support of experienced leaders if they become a senior coach. Unlike Fraser they won’t have proved themselves as able to coach a winning team at AFL level and their ability to form relationships with the players will be unknown. To many supporters that will be all that matters and, in many ways, it is all that is important.



Choosing an untried coach other than Fraser will be a harder sell and need explanation, but they will be able to do that if they select another person after comparing the candidate’s methods and personality. If they choose Fraser they need to know he impressed them enough to convince them he was the best candidate. A coach who can lead this team to a premiership is what Carlton are chasing. Of the nine interim coaches appointed full-time this century, Paul Roos is the only interim coach to do so. Fraser may, in fact, be the man. The reality is the next fortnight will help inform Carlton’s decision as much if not more than the past 11 matches.



Whatever the Blues’ call, the past three months has convinced everyone that at some point, somewhere, Fraser, if he wishes to, should become a senior coach. And it should also remind Essendon of the job talented coaches working away in the system can do if given the chance. Don’t sell Nick Watson’s achievement short Nick Watson is a star. He can turn a match in a minute, his ability to switch from defensive to attacking transition is unmatched. He is brave, cheeky and skilful. His effort to kick 52 goals with three rounds remaining is meritorious because few small forwards reach the half century before turning 22.



Nick Watson was at his brilliant best yet again for the Hawks. Getty Images Brisbane Lions champion Luke Power kicked 52 goals before turning 21 in 2000, but he is the only one this century to do so at a younger age than Watson. Cyril Rioli never kicked 50 goals in a season, Luke Breust was aged 23 when he passed the milestone. Eddie Betts was even older than Breust.
