Jeff Farmer and Phil Matera were 23 and Stephen Milne had turned 22. Ty Stengle helped the Cats to a flag with 50 goals in 2022 aged 23. Peter Daicos, a mid-sized forward, had kicked 70 goals before he turned 20 in 1981. Daicos was a goalkicking freak.



If Watson can win the Coleman Medal, he will have done something Daicos didn’t. Pick one is enough of a helping hand for the Bombers Essendon have draft pick number one with three matches remaining after the Tigers’ win over an inaccurate West Coast. Finishing on the bottom will help the AFL justify an assistance package despite the Bombers being about as deserving of one as a billionaire seeking tax relief. Essendon have high hopes for Nate Caddy AFL Photos



Giving them assistance is not only a reward for mediocrity but investing in a club that, part from recent recruiting, is yet to prove they can stack good decision after good decision as yet. Before any assistance package, the Bombers will have pick one, a likely compensation pick early in the second round which is designed to help clubs rebuilding plus any return from trading Zach Merrett who appears set to exit. That will arrive just one season after they added Sullivan Robey, Jacob Farrow and Dyson Sharp with picks 9, 10 and 13, following Isaac Kako in 2024 and Nate Caddy in 2023. Injuries have affected their performance and they missed on a couple of high draft picks. Fair play to Essendon for asking, but there should be resistance to assistance inside AFL House. Keep up to date with the best AFL coverage in the country.

World.title: Ariana Grande ditches West End debut over ‘public scrutiny’ amid weight loss concerns
World.content:
CultureCelebrityAriana Grande Ariana Grande ditches West End debut over ‘public scrutiny’ amid weight loss concerns Kayla Olaya August 3, 2026 — 9:09am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Ariana Grande has dropped out of her debut role in the West End revival of Stephen Sondheim’s 1984 musical Sunday in the Park with George due to “ongoing public scrutiny” amid growing concerns about her weight loss. Reps for the Wicked star told People on Monday morning (AEST) that the three-time Grammy Award winner “will be taking a step back from visibility after she completes the Eternal Sunshine tour,” in support of Grande’s 2024 album of the same name. A screen shot from the video clip for Ariana Grande’s song Petal. YouTube “She looks forward to finishing the tour and ending it on a high note, both healthily and happily, and then taking a much-deserved break from public-facing work and appearances, which has led to endless, ongoing public scrutiny,” the statement said. “This tour has been a beautiful experience for her. She loves her fans and has loved every minute of this tour so much.”



Before the announcement, fans and commentators expressed concerns about Grande’s wellbeing online after a newly released music video for her latest song, Petal, shows her appearing extremely thin. In the music video, a casting director character is seen making notes about Grande’s “audition”, writing “it couldn’t hurt to lose a little”. A screenshot of Ariana Grande’s Petal music video, where a casting director character notes it “couldn’t hurt to lose a little” about Grande’s audition. YouTube British actor and comedian Jameela Jamil was among those who expressed concern about Grande, stating “this poor woman is possibly dying right in front of us”, and arguing that the pop star’s team was responsible for the image being pushed to younger audiences. “This outfit is designed to accentuate the thinness for discourse. Her team are thoroughly irresponsible for not guiding her away from this deeply damaging image for her young fans to see so glamorised,” Jamil commented beneath one of Grande’s Instagram posts promoting the music video.



Jamil later took to her Instagram story to explain that, while uncomfortable, conversations about Grande’s weight should take place amid the broader context of celebrity thinness culture. “The shrinking pop star situation is something of a trolley problem,” Jamil said. “If we comment on [Grande’s] body, we could harm her mental health, which would be awful and nobody wants that. If we don’t comment on her body, we run the risk of normalising that image to hundreds of millions of teenage girls, kids and even impressionable adults, consuming her content. “Content which is pointedly accentuating her bones and tiny frame with belts and corsets. I think it’s worth considering that the pop star in question has access to a lot of mental health care and the best facilities on the planet, whereas the fans watching largely don’t. “Many have no support system equipped to handle the deadly clutches of anorexia. Her most recent images are flooding pro-anorexia websites, and teenage girls are saying ‘goals’.”



Meanwhile, model and author Charli Howard also took to Instagram to share her discomfort with Grande’s music video – particularly after gaining weight in the past few months and the ongoing battle to accept herself despite being an activist for body positivity. “I think it’s vital we discuss imagery/videos/content like these and the damage they can – and will – have on women and girls. WHAT YOU SEE HERE IS NOT NORMAL,” Howard wrote. “Over the past few weeks, as images of Ariana’s concert get plastered around online, I obviously see comments from worried fans, but I also see other people convincing others that she looks ‘healthy’, or that she has simply ‘lost puppy fat’. “I think it is absolutely appalling, from both a moral and capitalistic standpoint, to have released these videos and an album when this person needs psychiatric help and hospitalisation.



“I truly, truly hope she gets the help that she so desperately needs. We do not need a repeat of the early 2000s.” Grande’s latest album, Petal, was released on July 31. Sunday in the Park with George was slated to run in June next year. Find out the next TV, streaming series and movies to add to your must-sees. Get The Watchlist delivered every Thursday.

World.title: ICAC Operation Rosny LIVE updates: Robert Assaf continues evidence; Liberal MP Damien Tudehope set to appear
World.content:
Good morning and welcome to the Herald’s live coverage of the Independent Commission Against Corruption’s blockbuster Operation Rosny hearings.

I’m state political reporter Jessica McSweeney, and I’ll be bringing you all the latest updates from today’s evidence, along with analysis from the Herald’s senior writers.

Today we’ll continue to hear from former Catholic Schools NSW staffer and founding member of Liberal Party factional group the Reformers, Robert Assaf. This afternoon the commission is expected to call Damien Tudehope, a current Liberal MP who stood down as shadow attorney general when he discovered he would be asked to appear.

Tudehope is not accused of wrongdoing.

Here’s a recap of what we covered last week:

Former Catholic Schools NSW (CSNSW) CEO Dallas McInerney told the commission he wanted to “shake down” Angus Taylor for $10,000 for the Reformers. Text messages from former CSNSW staffer Dylan Whitelaw shown to the commission claimed Taylor agreed to donate $15,000 plus monthly contributions of $3000. Taylor has repeatedly said no payments were made.

The commission heard evidence from Whitelaw and Assaf that they would do work for the Reformers during the day at CSNSW. Whitelaw estimate Assaf’s work was a 60/40 split – 60 per cent on Reformers, 40 per cent on CSNSW duties. Assaf disputed this, and said he would only do political work after his work for CSNSW was completed.

Counsel assisting the commission, Dr Peggy Dwyer SC, played phone taps during her opening statement showing fugitive property developer Jean Nassif bragging about his influence over the then-Liberal state government. He called Dominic Perrottet his “boy”, and boasted that the fair trading minister would be replaced with one of his “girls”. Eleni Petinos was appointed to the role shortly after that phone call.

Michael O’Hara, who the commission has heard provided financial support to the Reformers, withdrew his support after feeling then-premier Dominic Perrottet and prime minister Scott Morrison had gone too “woke”.

Dwyer said in her opening statement she expects the evidence will show that figures in this investigation – Christian Ellis, Charles Perrottet and Jeremy Greenwood – anticipated they would be paid $2 million in total by Nassif, in exchange for furthering his interests.

A “shit sheet” was prepared against factional enemy of the Reformers David Elliott, which included the false claim he was having an affair. Elliott strongly denies this, and said he is a devoted husband of 30 years.

Today’s hearing kicks off at 9.30am, and you can follow the live stream here.

World.title: Forget the Sydney bubble for a moment. This is the best NRL story of 2026
World.content:
Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 Forget the Sydney bubble for a moment. This is the best NRL story of 2026 Dan Walsh August 3, 2026 — 9:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

With nine Sydney clubs and a pair of powerhouses at either end of the eastern seaboard, it’s easy to spend an entire season navel-gazing. Fun too. See a week of Wests Tigers headlines that ranged from vaping to their halfback walking out, then back in, busting up and making up with his coach and teammates along the way. Loading The Tigers, Eels and Dragons boast three of the game’s largest fan bases and most recognisable brands, and occupy two of the three bottom rungs of the ladder, bringing all the scrutiny that deserves. The Panthers have flexed their post-Origin muscles at the top of the ladder again and the Roosters are flying – with the latter’s small galaxy of stars putting 82 points on North Queensland, becoming the first team to outscore the clock in 91 years.



The drums are beating once more out of Belmore too. The game’s loudest supporters are cautiously finding voice again as Canterbury push back into the top eight with six wins from their last seven games. Meanwhile, the Broncos and Storm will both miss the finals – just the second time in the NRL era that both grand finalists become September spectators without a salary cap punishment involved (2006 – Tigers and Cowboys, and 2005 – Roosters and Bulldogs). And quietly doing their thing among the usual suspects that dominate rugby league’s news cycle is Newcastle, spinning one of the game’s more remarkable revivals. Justin Holbrook is surely now a firm favourite to claim Dally M coach of the year honours after taking last year’s wooden spooners to the brink of a finals return.



His nearest competitors – Kristian Woolf lifting the Dolphins to within touching distance of their own maiden top-eight finish, and Andrew Webster’s Warriors harnessing serious momentum across the ditch – tell the other under-told tales of 2026. So too, the extra gear Cronulla is finding under Craig Fitzgibbon this season as Sydney’s smallest club. But right now, the Knights are our narrative. Especially with three straight losses by two points or less against the Rabbitohs, Sharks and Roosters accompanied by brutal, season-ending injuries to Dylans Brown and Lucas. Kalyn Ponga’s future is no longer a talking point, and it shows. Getty Images The shift in Kalyn Ponga’s body language all season was particularly noticeable in Saturday’s thumping win over Brisbane. With a last-round bye, one more victory from their last four games will have Ponga and Newcastle deservedly back in the mix come September. Figures at the club privately acknowledge that if not for Holbrook’s arrival and sweeping changes this time last year, then the long-running fear Ponga was destined to move on was going to be realised.



Instead, the playmaking shake-up bringing in Brown and Sandon Smith has been more successful than anyone imagined. Just as talk about Ponga’s future, rugby union and the Roosters started to fire up again earlier this year, the Knights buried it by announcing a three-year extension. All the hype, hoopla and endless speculation that has accompanied Ponga’s previous career moves was sidestepped as easily as the headgeared No.1 taking on a backpedalling defender. Knights coach Justin Holbrook has worked wonders in the Hunter. Getty Images Along with Fletcher Sharpe, Newcastle’s playmaking quartet has steered an enterprising, entertaining style well-suited to the game’s latest high-octane officiating, and even without Brown at the scrumbase, they put Brisbane to bed. Sharpe’s second try against the Broncos was their 25th try from inside their own half this year – the most of any side in the NRL. Holbrook’s easy-going outlook and coaxing of career-best form from forwards Jacob Saifiti, Trey Mooney, Lucas and Jermaine McEwen, among others, has revitalised an attack that this time last year simply hurt to watch.



The Dolphins are even easier on the eye, even with moments of brilliance against St George Illawarra outnumbered by bumbling and fumbling in an unconvincing 28-22 win. Related Article Updated

NRL 2026 Laurie Daley confirms Origin departure – and nominates the coach who should succeed him Isaiya Katoa will be better for his cautious return from a broken wrist. Just in time for Saturday’s latest Battle of Brisbane, with little doubt over the city’s new pecking order. Webster’s Warriors, meanwhile, host Penrith having already produced the best game of 2026 when they clashed in late May. The Kiwi side are the closest this competition has to the Panthers in so many ways – be it game-play, consistency or unflappable coach helming the whole show. After a month of indifferent mid-season form from both front-runners, the Warriors warmed up by pummelling the Gold Coast with eight tries. Penrith beat up Canberra in similar fashion. A top-tier clash is just reward for the stunning surge rugby league is enjoying in New Zealand. A Warriors home final too wouldn’t go astray if they can jag a top-two finish. Auckland’s Eden Park can seat 50,000 fans (an extra 20,000 on the club’s usual Mt Smart haunt) and it would still be well short of fitting everyone in. Just another story worth telling really.

World.title: The Eagles’ performance brought one player to tears. Fans would have felt the same
World.content:
NationalWAAFL 2026 Opinion The Eagles’ performance brought one player to tears. Fans would have felt the same Paddy Sweeney Nine Sports Presenter August 3, 2026 — 8:59am

August 3, 2026 — 8:59am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Welcome to the Western Watercooler, where we digest the talking points from the weekend’s games – and the highlights, frustrations and silver linings WA footy fans can cling to as the season progresses. The Dockers were resolute in their 37-point win over the Bulldogs. Josh Treacy celebrates a goal as Fremantle power past the Bulldogs on Friday. Getty Images They had to navigate a defensively minded opponent who did their very best to stifle and strangle the ladder leaders, but yet again Justin Longmuir and his team maintained their composure and held their nerve. Meanwhile, the Eagles result was enough to bring young gun Willem Duursma to tears post-game and many fans would have been the same.



If you were a West Coast supporter who paid to go to the MCG, you would have every right to contact the club seeking a refund. Related Article AFL 2026 Dan Gorringe was a battling ruckman. He’s now a social media star and might even become an AFL rights holder The poor skills and woeful goalkicking meant the Eagles were humbled by Richmond for a second time this season – both when the Tigers were at the bottom of the table. Fremantle Dockers What went right? The Dockers were able to secure a crucial piece of the premiership puzzle.



By cementing a top-two finish, two home finals are now in their keeping, meaning if things go to plan, they will only need to travel once in the finals series – for the grand final. And there’s reason to be confident. Optus Stadium is officially “Fortress Fremantle”. Abandon hope, all ye who enter here. Daniel Carson/AFL Photos via Getty Images Optus Stadium has been transformed into “Freo’s Fortress” in 2026 – the Dockers have won all 11 games at the venue. What went wrong? An area which remains a work in progress and where improvement can be made is in contested ball and around stoppage.



The Bulldogs won these key statistics, with Ed Richards and Tom Liberatore setting the tone. The positive was the Dockers were able to restrict the Dogs damage, even outscoring them from stoppage. Silver lining? Oscar McDonald. Should either Alex Pearce or Brennan Cox go down at the business end of the season, McDonald has shown he is a more than capable key defender replacement. The 30 year-old played just his seventh game for the season on Friday night, but played easily the best he has in a Fremantle jumper.



He intercepted, was calm and used the ball well. An added bonus is McDonald can also be used forward – booting five goals in his most recent WAFL performance when played in attack. Jake Waterman’s performance in front of goal highlighted the Eagles’ challenges on Sunday. Graham Denholm/AFL Photos via Getty Images West Coast Eagles What went right? The Eagles created enough chances, but couldn’t finish them.



They managed seven more inside-50s, took four more inside-50 marks, more than doubled the Tigers for tackles laid inside 50 and won the clearances. It only highlights how poor their finishing was. Loading What went wrong? The inaccurate goalkicking would have been enough to send fans watching, turn the TV off and go outside to catch some winter sunshine. Time after time, after time, the Eagles blew golden opportunities, some which had to be seen to be believed.



Jake Waterman was the chief offender, booting 2.6, including a miss from two metres out in the goalsquare. At one stage, West Coast were 3.17 in the third term, finishing with 9.19. Ill discipline also played it’s part, Rhett Bazzo’s 50-metre penalty for dissent turned a difficult Tom Lynch shot on goal into a formality at a crucial time. Silver lining? It’s one less away game to play. The 11-point defeat now has the Eagles with just four wins from their past 51 interstate games – a winning percentage of less than eight.



It’s a damning statistic for any side, but even more so for a team which travels every second week and has been doing so for 40 years.

World.title: Tolls cut on Sydney’s motorways following long-running negotiations
World.content:
Tolls will be cut on four motorways in Sydney including the M7 and M2 from as early as July next year while two-way tolling will be introduced on the Eastern Distributor as part of largest shake up of pricing in years.

Less than eight months out from the state election, 10 per cent will be cut from tolls on the Lane Cove Tunnel, while the same reduction will apply to longer journeys on the M2 motorway from July 1 next year.

The changes to toll prices follows two years of direct negotiations between the NSW government and Transurban. Janie Barrett

The cap on distance-based trips on the M7 will be cut by 10 per cent from January 2028, subject to a widening of the motorway.

Tolls on the Cross City Tunnel will be reduced by 20 per cent when the Western Harbour Tunnel opens in 2028.

World.title: Business leaders equal to government, Christopher Luxon says, days after 'parent-child mentality' comments
World.content:
Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon Morning Report Download MP3 9m

The prime minister says the government and business owners are equal players, and must work together to drive economic growth.

At a Rotorua Business Chamber event last week, its chief executive Melanie Short told Christopher Luxon some were questioning how long they could hang on as they grappled with escalating costs.

Luxon told the audience some businesses had a "parent-child mentality" and too often looked to the government for help.

Labour finance spokesperson Barbara Edmonds labelled that a patronising lecture, and said businesses were asking for an "economy that works", not a handout.

Luxon's office said Edmonds has mischaracterised his comments.

The prime minister told Morning Report on Monday he acknowledged businesses were doing it tough, but his point to the Rotorua audience was that they and the government needed to work together.

"I believe very strongly that government, business, community leaders actually are equal in our society," he said.

"They do different things, but they need to work together on the challenges and the obstacles, and also the opportunities that we have."

They each played a part in driving economic growth, Luxon said.

"As a business owner, your job is to make sure that you actually have great commercial returns, build an awesome culture, have a great customer experience.

"And the government's job is to make sure we get the settings right: employment law, RMA (Resource Management Act), investment boosts, trade agreements, those things."

World.title: Trained neurologists quitting NZ due to lack of jobs and funding, experts say
World.content:
Leading brain health and neurological organisations are warning the country is training specialists, only to lose them due to a lack of funded hospital positions.

But health officials say their attempts to grow the workforce are not "exclusive to neurology".

The Neurological Alliance is calling on the government to fund two additional public hospital neurology positions every year and commit to developing a national neurological workforce strategy to plan for the future.

The Alliance represents 20 New Zealand organisations focused on stroke, dementia, Parkinson's and epilepsy, which advocate collectively for the interests of the estimated 1.5 million people living with neurological conditions.

Neurological Alliance chair Rich Easton told Nine to Noon the shortage of neurologists was already causing significant consequences across the health system, including "exceedingly long and very frustrating" wait times and declined referrals.

"Every year at the moment we train five neurologists to enter into the workforce. The resource planning has availability for three of those trainees to enter as neurologists in the public health system, which means the other two either end up going into private health or in many, many cases going overseas as a loss to New Zealand.

"So really we're calling on the government… to train five and keep five in our public health system and also to make a commitment to building a longer-term workforce strategy that meets our future needs as well."

Workforce aging alongside population

At present New Zealand had about 68 full- and part-time neurologists, when it needed at least 100 to meet current demand and 120 by 2036, with an ageing population, Easton said.

The current workforce was also aging according to Dr James Cleland, chair of the Neurological Association, which represents neurologists.

"We have been wanting to make noise in this space for a number of years, but as neurologists, sometimes we find it hard to engage with the political parties…

"We need to rapidly expand our neurology workforce - partly by immediately recruiting the remaining two neurologists that are not funded, but also increasing the number of neurologists in the country probably by at least 10 - if not 15 - to bring us up to even close to parity with our closest neighbor Australia."

He said recent research had shown "neurologic diseases have actually surpassed cancer and cardiovascular disease" in terms of disability-adjusted life years, which Ministry of Health documents describe as "the loss of one year of life lived in good health" - so not just years lost of life, but of good, healthy life.

"We have tended to focus on health outcomes in terms of death rates perhaps at the expense of looking at the chronic diseases."

Cleland said neurology covered a lot of conditions that do not show up in mortality statistics, such as migraines and epilepsy, that "lead to a lot of disability, but that disability is not being met with provision of neurologic care".

Dementia was also a growing problem.

"One of the critical problems… is that we are actually training these people currently, but we are not actually giving them jobs to come back to. So we are spending the resources to do it, but losing the output… We have an aging population that is expanding, neurologic burden, if you like… And if we're not meeting that rate of expansion, then we will continue to fall behind."

Easton said patients often needed multiple appointments, over time, as specialists tried different treatments and the patient's condition changed. Cleland said any delays could dramatically reduce a patient's chances of living without burden.

"In the case of motor neurone disease… if it takes 12 months to get a diagnosis after the onset of symptoms, that's potentially more than a third of the patient's remaining life, and to be uncertain of the diagnosis in that time and to be able to plan is really a huge lost opportunity."

In some parts of the country there were no neurologists, Easton said, relying on specialists from elsewhere.

"[Patients] have to wait and hope they can get access to one of those visiting clinics or travel to one of the main centres, and in particular for some people and their neuro conditions… they're not always able to travel on their own, so they need a support person with them.

"And travelling into a major city, that can be a whole day which can be really tiring and stressful alongside living with the condition that they have as well".

Hands tied

Cleland said while it was the "best job", he often felt he was "practicing with one hand tied behind my back".

While improving wait-times for first specialist appointments was great, he said if follow-ups were delayed, it made it difficult to provide the level of care needed - which in turn piled pressure back on the person's GP.

"We're all aware that the care is not ideal, but we are really hamstrung in how to fix it because the resources are not there to do it."

In a statement, National Chief Medical Officer Dame Helen Stokes-Lampard said Health New Zealand was "committed to giving New Zealanders timely access to the health care they need".

"We know that as part of this we need to grow our healthcare workforce, and this is not exclusive to neurology."

She said healthcare targets - such as shorter wait times for first specialist assessments - also applied to neurology.

World.title: Wife of patient who died at Waikato Hospital says staffing levels and experience remain a concern
World.content:
A widow of a diabetic and cardiac patient who collapsed and later died while searching for food in Waikato Hospital says he was coherent, talking and comfortable when she'd last seen him just hours earlier.

But somehow, Colin John Clarkson's blood glucose levels [BGL] had managed to drop to a dangerously low level, a couple of hours after having his hospital dinner.

Lois Clarkson told NZME her husband was an independent man, and didn't like to be a bother to anyone, so would have gone to look for food himself but was instead found unconscious in a stairwell near the Cardiac Care Unit [CCU] he had been admitted into on the night of 30 December 2019.

The 79-year-old had been missing from the ward for nearly an hour before the alarm was raised, and soon after he was found, he died.

That sparked a tenacious fight for answers by his wife, and a damning report from the Health and Disability Commissioner [HDC], which found Health New Zealand Te Whatu Ora breached the Code of Health and Disability Services Consumers' Rights in its handling of his medical needs.

Coroner Donna Llewell on Monday announced she had also closed the six-year-old inquiry into Clarkson's death, citing the HDC's thorough investigation, stating she was satisfied it was not necessary.

The coroner found that Clarkson's death was preventable, while Lois Clarkson said she appreciated the numerous recommendations that had already been enacted; it was the hospital's staffing levels that still left her concerned.

Lois Clarkson holds a drawing that her grandson, Thomas Clarkson, created of his grandfather, and diabetic, Colin Clarkson. NZ Herald / Belinda Feek

'I'm worried about my blood glucose level'

Clarkson, 79, had multiple health conditions, including an extensive cardiac history, longstanding memory loss and dementia, a mild cognitive impairment, and type 2 diabetes.

However, Lois Clarkson was a retired registered physiotherapist and was diligent with her husband's care and monitoring his diabetes.

About 3.10am, on 29 December 2019, he went to Waikato Hospital's emergency department with chest pain, accompanied by his wife.

During triaging, the nurse recorded he had diabetes, but not whether he was on insulin or other medications.

While his blood glucose level was initially measured, there was no further testing while he was in the emergency department [ED].

Lois had brought her husband's diabetic kit, record book, and medications, so she administered his insulin herself.

At 2.30pm, later that day, he was transferred to the CCU.

The next day he had blood glucose testing and insulin administered, but after dinner, at 9.30pm, he returned blood glucose levels [BGL] of 4.4mmol/L.

Clarkson told the CCU nurse he was concerned about his level, and the nurse went to get him a drink and a sandwich.

But there were no sandwiches in the unit's fridge, so the nurse went elsewhere.

When she returned, at 9.44pm, he wasn't in his bed, so she left his food on his bedside table.

She went back 10 minutes later, and he still wasn't there.

She assumed he was in the toilet, so she resumed other duties.

However, CCTV revealed Clarkson had left his room and was trying to get food from a vending machine in the ward hallway at 10.27pm before he got into a nearby lift.

The footage also showed 11 people, including seven hospital staff, walked straight past him without checking on him.

At 11.01pm, he was found unconscious on a stairwell past fire doors and was bleeding from a cut to his head.

He died 21 minutes later, after unsuccessful attempts to revive him.

A coronial inquiry was opened on 9 January 2020, but was adjourned 12 months later for an investigation to be carried out by the Health and Disability Commissioner [HDC].

The HDC found Te Whatu Ora failed to provide Clarkson with a reasonable standard of care, was critical of the care in Waikato Hospital's ED, and the CCU nurse for not checking whether he'd eaten his food or re-checking his BGL levels.

There were also failures by Te Whatu Ora in having inadequate food and systems in place to alert staff to wandering patients.

A number of recommendations were made, and Te Whatu Ora has already instigated many changes.

However, in deciding against resuming her inquiry, Coroner Llewell said the HDC had given an undertaking to Clarkson's family they would be alerted once all of the recommendations had been completed by Te Whatu Ora.

Of particular interest to the family was the outstanding recommendation that they carry out a random audit of 15 diabetic patients admitted into the CCU in the last 12 months.

'He was coherent, he was talking, he was comfortable'

Clarkson's widow told NZME that she was grateful that the result of the HDC and coroner investigations was how she saw it.

"Because I was convinced that the care he received [was poor].

"They have done some staff training and other things, and that's a really good step forward."

However, she felt the problem ran deeper.

"I don't think the hospital has got enough staff and I don't think the hospital has enough appropriately trained and experienced staff."

She had worked at the hospital as a physiotherapist many years ago, so knew how to care for her husband.

Ironically, it was when she left her husband's care in the hands of professionals that he died.

"I had an idea of what should have been happening in relation to the care of my husband.

"Unfortunately, the night it all happened, I had gone back home, and so I just felt terrible about being [home] because if I had been with him, that wouldn't have happened.

"He would not have died at that time if I had been in the hospital with him."

She had previously spoken to her husband's GP who said if his BGL level got below 7mmol/L, he would need urgent assistance.

She said the quickest thing to do when her husband had a low BGL level was to mix up two heaped teaspoons of sugar and half a glass of water, or juice.

"And the recovery time is really quick.

"However, the nurse toddled off to get sandwiches and a drink.

"That all took time, and time was something that my husband didn't have on his side."

She believed the "whole thing was dealt with inappropriately".

"The nurse did not have the understanding or knowledge in order to do something quick, and that was the whole thing.

"He didn't get the aid he needed."

Lois noted evidence in the HDC investigation from an expert, independent nurse, who said someone should have been with her husband to witness him eating the sandwich because, given his condition, that was considered a medicine.

"But of course, he never ate it."

Lois said she and her son visited Colin the evening he died, leaving around dinner time.

"He was coherent, he was talking, he was comfortable.

"Everything looked fine."

But she was shocked how her husband's BGL level was able to drop so low by 9.30pm, especially after having dinner.

"Having that low blood sugar at that time of night was very unusual.

"I don't know what happened, but that was another red flag."

Lois said the family was aware of his health issues, and wondered if he was going to pull through after his suspected heart attack, but for him to get into such a poor state so quickly, and then die, had left her in shock.

"To hear that he had died was a terrible thing, but then to hear how he died, I was very, very angry about that."

She said the fact Waikato Hospital had thrown out her book she'd used to record her husband's BGL levels was unfortunate, as it might have given the family a better idea about how he was doing that night.

Overall, she was grateful for the help from the HDC, the coroner, and her four sons, but hoped that no other family would ever have to go through what they did.

'I acknowledge Lois Clarkson's determination'

Coroner Llewell said Clarkson's death was preventable.

"Had the proper standards of medical care, treatment and services been afforded to him and management of his diabetic condition, it is probable he would have had more time with his family," she said.

She also paid tribute to Lois Clarkson and two of her sons, who had provided her with well-articulated submissions.

"I acknowledge the determination and advocacy of Mrs Clarkson with the support of two of her sons in my inquiry.

"Mr Clarkson's death could be said to be a prime example of the principle that the provision of the appropriate food is in fact a form of medical treatment during a diabetic crisis."

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Five Pacific states face permanent US visa bond requirement
World.content:
Five Pacific Islands Forum member states are set to be permanently included in a United States visa bond programme that will require nationals from those countries to post up to US$20,000 to be able to travel to America as a temporary visitor.

This is after the US State Department confirmed it will make permanent its 'Visa Bond Pilot Program', as first reported by Reuters news agency over the weekend.

The Trump administration's visa bond programme, which includes 50-odd nations mostly from Africa, was initiated in late August 2025, to crack down on illegal visa overstayers in the US.

Fiji, Papua New Guinea, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu were the five Pacific Island nations on the list.

According to the federal notice, nationals from the 50-identified countries will remain subject to the visa bond requirement under the finalised rule.

"Under the Program ... visa bonds may be required from certain business/pleasure (B1/B-2) visa applicants who are nationals of countries with high overstay rates, deficient information sharing, insufficient identity verification and criminal records, and that need improvement in the area of screening and vetting and the security of travel and civil documents, including in the granting of citizenship," the federal notice states.

The pilot programme required bonds of $5000, $10,000 or up to $15,000, but the final rule eliminates the $5000 option and raises the maximum bond to $20,000.

The bonds have proved to be "an effective tool for reducing overstayers", the US government says.

World.title: 'SaaSpocalypse' avoided as software catches angel investors' eyes again
World.content:
Software has regained its position as the largest angel investment category despite first quarter predictions of a looming 'SaaSpocalypse'.

The second quarter (Q2) Catalist New Zealand Angel Market report (PDF) indicated software investments rose 48 percent on a punishing first quarter, and 42 percent on the year earlier period.

Female-led startups also bounced back, capturing one-third of angel investment.

The data also indicated Angel investors were doubling down on proven businesses, with 75 percent of capital and 83 percent of investments in follow-on rounds rather than in new startups.

A total of $2.7 million was invested into 33 businesses, supported by 132 active angels, suggesting renewed confidence despite ongoing economic uncertainty.

"The conversation appears to be evolving," Catalist chief executive Colin Magee said.

"Earlier this year there was a lot of discussion about whether AI would undermine software business models."

However, software attracted 43 percent of capital deployed during Q2.

Angel Association chief executive Bridget Unsworth said it was too soon to call it a trend, though software's share of the investment was double the previous quarter and was moving back above its longer-term trend.

"And we're seeing some really phenomenal companies that have really nailed exactly what they're offering, exactly what the problem is that they're solving, and they are raising good rounds of capital, and that is really great to see," she said.

World.title: Man allegedly robs Auckland restaurant armed with machete
World.content:
Police say another investigation is underway on Auckland's North Shore after an aggravated robbery last night.

Waitematā CIB's acting detective inspector Megan Goldie said a man entered a restaurant in Hinemoa Street, Birkenhead, at about 8.45pm on Sunday with what appeared to be a machete.

Goldie said the man threatened staff and demanded money.

He left before police arrived.

She said inquiries are underway to identify and find the person.

World.title: Government spending $21.7m to expand teacher training in classrooms
World.content:
The government's striving to curb persistent teacher shortages by spending more than $20 million to expand a classroom-based training scheme.

The $21.7 million over five years will also bolster a fund which keeps teachers working at schools that are hard to staff.

Education Minister Erica Stanford said the School Onsite Training Programme - which allows trainee teachers to spend up to three days a week in classrooms while completing their formal study - has grown from 147 places in 2024 to 528 places in 2026.

The expansion will allow for 660 places next year and 704 training places every year from 2028.

"We have been able to use onsite teacher training to deliberately target trainee teachers to where they are needed most," Stanford said.

"We opened the programme to primary teacher training in 2025 in response to shortages across both primary and secondary schools. Now that workforce data is beginning to show a small oversupply of primary teachers, we are weighting more of the available places towards secondary teacher training."

In future, the government would also be able to target places towards secondary subjects suffering shortages, she said.

"We have also targeted places to rural and isolated communities by enabling providers to offer online programmes, allowing people to train as teachers while remaining in the communities where they are needed," she said.

In 2027, participants would receive a stipend of $20,660 to help cover course fees and living costs.

An Education Review Office report found only one in five principals considered new teacher graduates ready for the classroom, Stanford said.

"Giving trainee teachers more time in schools, supported by experienced teachers, helps them develop the practical skills and confidence they need from day one."

The money will also fund an extra 50 places in the Teacher Bonding Scheme, increasing the 2026/27 cohort from 185 to 235.

The scheme pays eligible teachers $40,000 over five years to stay working at schools that struggle with staffing.

Funding for the classroom training scheme was reprioritised from the Overseas Relocation Grant, which reimbursed early childhood teachers relocating to New Zealand.

Demand for the grant had fallen substantially, the government said, so it reduced the budget and changed the eligibility criteria.

World.title: Cronulla coach's belief grows as Sharks surge towards NRL finals
World.content:
Cronulla is promising no let-up after extending its league-best winning streak to five matches, sparking talk that an elusive second NRL premiership is in the offing for the surging Sharks.

Rarely has understated coach Craig Fitzgibbon been more bullish about his belief in the team than after Sunday's dazzling 32-16 dispatch of South Sydney.

"I've never felt any different about the group in the last five years, to be honest, but maybe I believe in them more than they believe in themselves," he said.

With Nicho Hynes back to the vintage form that earned him the Dally M Medal and the Sharks a top-two finish in 2022, and his halves partner, Braydon Trindall, in career-best touch, the Sharks are flying with nine wins from their past 10 outings.

Michael Ennis, the club's 2016 grand final-winning hooker-turned-analyst, believes the Sharks will go all the way again a decade on from breaking the longest and most infamous title drought in premiership history.

It's 10 years since the Sharks beat the Storm in the NRL grand final and the club is shaping up to scale the heights again. (Getty Images: Mark Kolbe)

"We're working hard towards something and we've been building that for a little bit," Fitzgibbon said.

"And then sometimes you get things go your way, sometimes they don't. But at the moment, it's going our way.

"There's still plenty more. We'll have a hiccup here and there and there'll be turbulence, but you won't challenge me on how much I believe in them."

Sitting fourth and certain not to face any more top-eight opposition until the finals, the Sharks are well placed to snatch an all-important top-two spot.

But skipper Blayke Brailey says the Sharks won't be taking their foot off the pedal, with the side's immediate focus on Sunday's derby with St George Illawarra.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The Dragons may be wooden spoon-bound but the Sharks won't be taking their arch rivals lightly, especially with points differential between the top teams looking increasingly important.

"A derby clash, no matter where you're sitting on the table, it's a tough contest," Brailey said.

"Those derby games are tough, no matter the form you're in."

After the Dragons at Kogarah, the Sharks face Canberra at home, the Titans on the Gold Coast, Parramatta away and Melbourne in a potentially crucial last-round battle at Shark Park.

World.title: Lorena Wiebes sprints to second straight win at Tour de France Femmes
World.content:
Lorena Wiebes again sprinted to victory in the second stage of the Women’s Tour de France.

The Dutch rider of SD Worx-Protime won the flat 147.9-kilometre stage from Aigle to Geneva, the second on Swiss territory, in 3 hours, 42 minutes, 8 seconds on Sunday.

Wiebes went ahead with some 250 metres to go and claimed her seventh overall victory at the tour.

Wiebes also won the opening stage on Saturday in the same dominant fashion.

Lidl-Trek rider Elisa Balsamo finished second and Marianne Vos of Team Visma-Lease a Bike was third.

Wiebes leads Kim Le Court Pienaar by 14 seconds overall, with the 2023 Tour champion Demi Vollering another two seconds back in third.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Monday's 156.5km (97.2-mile) hilly stage starts in Geneva before the riders cross the border to France to finish in Poligny.

This edition of the race, the fifth of the Women’s Tour, covers 1,175km (730 miles) over nine days.

Amanda Spratt is the leading Australian in the race, in 68th place, 3 minutes and 20 seconds behind Wiebes.

Tadej Pogacar won his fifth men's Tour de France title last weekend.

AP/ABC

World.title: Diamonds win bronze medal with an eye to greater things for netball
World.content:
There's a sentiment in team sports at multi-sport events like the Commonwealth Games that you lose silver and win bronze.

The bronze medallists get to climb on the podium having won their last match, while second place is coming off a heartbreaking loss, having let gold slip through their grasp.

For the Diamonds, bronze at the 2026 Commonwealth Games is a complicated celebration.

Less than 20 hours after Jamaica ripped their hearts out in the semifinal, the Aussie netballers were back on court at 9am in Glasgow for the first centre pass of their first-ever bronze-medal match.

Diamonds fumble Australia's most anticipated gold medal The Diamonds will miss the Commonwealth Games gold medal match for the first time after a shock semifinal loss to Jamaica in front of a crowd baying for Australia's downfall.

It was hard to bounce back from the loss but they did so against England, winning 65-80.

"We had such a quick time to process what happened, I think a lot of us still feel quite numb," defender Jo Weston said.

"Then you go out and have a game like we did, we're so proud and we know all of Australia have been behind us, so it's been a real rollercoaster of emotions in a very short time frame. But I think the overwhelming feeling is pride and a lot of love for each other.

"It's immensely challenging for us having that mental fortitude to come back out. We have very high expectations of ourselves and we want to do our country proud.

The Diamonds rediscovered their flow to keep their medal-winning streak alive. (AP: Andrew Milligan/PA)

"They always say Diamonds are made under pressure and I think that really showed in us today. Although it's not the colour we were after we're really proud about it."

Coach Stacey Marinkovich said the night between the games was about leaving space for team members to "be vulnerable".

There was no point pretending they weren't gutted, that the loss was anything other than gut-wrenching, but once they left the meeting room it was about moving forward.

"It was very emotional last night, it was still probably lingering today a little bit, so to be able to mentally switch in showed our culture isn't words on a wall," she said.

There were complicated emotions for Australia's bronze medallists. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

"That took a lot of grit to be able to go out there and get that result."

Adding another layer of emotion for these stewards of the game, constantly fighting for eyeballs and recognition, is the more objective flip-side of the loss.

That is those celebrations of the Sunshine Girls after the semifinal.

For the first five Commonwealth Games, only Australia and New Zealand won gold and silver. In 2018, England stunned the Diamonds on their home patch for the Gold Coast title. Four years ago Jamaica beat the Aussies in their group match and made their first final. And in Glasgow, they went even better to take the Diamonds down in a knockout match to fight New Zealand for gold.

"International netball is the best it's ever been, which is so good for the sport, it's what we want to see," Weston said.

Four countries is not an enormous range of winners or even contenders, but in every event around the world there are dominant forces.

It wasn't the colour they wanted or expected, but a medal's a medal. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

With six years to the Brisbane Olympics and a push for the sport's inclusion, the Diamonds' bronze may have been the best thing for game.

"It's great for the sport because we always want the game to grow. Gone are the days where it's just one or two nations really dominating," Kiera Austin said.

"It's disappointing for us to have not gotten to that point ... but Jamaica were far too good on the day and that's great going into Brisbane hopefully getting netball into the Olympics.

"It's a sport we absolutely love, a sport we think deserves a great platform on the international stage and if it means a greater competition, then winning that gold medal whenever we get the chance to again is going to be all that much sweeter."

World.title: Delta Goodrem brings Australia's golden Commonwealth Games to a close
World.content:
Delta Goodrem shone on a saltire-shaped stage as Glasgow waved farewell to the Commonwealth Games in spectacular style by the banks of the River Clyde.

As a packed Hydro crowd roared with Scottish rock band Simple Minds and fireworks lit up the River Clyde waterfront, lingering fears were momentarily set aside.

The Commonwealth Games, having been on life support, are alive and kicking.

It came as Australian athletes were led out by Georgia Baker, who earned flag bearer honours by adding two gold medals in Glasgow to take her record-equalling cycling tally to five.

Glasgow's cut-price "Friendly Games" were inescapably cheerful, and run with good humour throughout, even through persistent summer rain, in tribute to a proud city that picked up the pieces when Victoria pulled out.

Delta Goodrem brought the house down at the Hydro for the closing ceremony. (Getty: Euan Cherry)

Eleven days of competition — which produced 171 medals for table-topping Australia — came to a close in a celebration of athlete performances as Glasgow 2026 formally passed the baton to Amdavad 2030.

It came with an unmistakable message from Scotland's gritty cultural hub, its people and the headline act: Don't you forget about me.

Scottish singer-songwriter Sandi Thom, shimmering in a sequined saltire dress, kicked off the closing ceremony with her reworked football anthem Proud to Be from Scotland.

Australian pop princess Delta Goodrem also shone on the saltire-shaped stage, opening with Born To Try and belting out a cover of John Farnham's You're the Voice with Scottish country and folk singer-songwriter Cammy Barnes.

Goodrem's presence was designed as a metaphor for an extension of Scotland's hand of friendship to the country that was originally set to have staged the Games.

Australian chef de mission Petria Thomas expressed gratitude to Glasgow for taking on hosting duties after Victoria pulled out.

"The Commonwealth Games is a really critically important event," Thomas said.

"If this had not been on it would have left a huge hole in our in the calendar, and for many athletes this is their first experience in a multi-sport environment.

"There's nothing that can compare to going into those sort of environments, so to give them the opportunity to do it here in Glasgow has been incredible.

"For so many of our Australian athletes the Commonwealth Games is their launching pad."

What the Commonwealth Games mean is up to you Australian chef de mission and eight-time Olympic medallist Petria Thomas cried as she spoke about the importance of the Commonwealth Games to her, so it doesn't really matter if it felt too easy for Australia at times.

Goodrem's medley led into a "festival of connection", supported by musicians in Highland dress, and the appearances of Glasgow-based rapper Bemz and neo-traditional folk band Elephant Sessions.

Scotland's dual gold medallist Melanie Woods — who won the 400m T54 and 1500m T54 races — was handed the David Dixon Award for fair play and contribution to the Games.

Glasgow 2026 organising committee chair George Black hailed the city for putting on an "unforgettable" event.

"Together we have achieved something extraordinary and I am extremely proud of Glasgow," Black said in his address.

" Once again this city has shown the world who we are. "

The 2030 hosts, Amdavad, also known as Ahmedabad, gave a vision of the celebration to expect in four years' time.

The colourful and extravagant showcase was dubbed "The world is one family", and included performances by Indian artists Rashmika Mandanna and Shankar Mahadevan, amid a cast of about 200 dancers.

The Glasgow crowd was given a taste of Amdavad at the closing ceremony. (Getty: Mattia Ozbot)

Prince Edward, Duke of Edinburgh, formally closed the event, thanking athletes for their efforts.

"You have brought the spirit and values of the Commonwealth to life," the Duke said.

"You have inspired us, and hopefully future generations. You have also demonstrated what unites us."

UK street dance group Diversity lit up the stage, bringing the crowd to their feet, and another troupe performed a traditional Gaelic ceilidh with a modern twist.

But local lads Simple Minds had the final say, bringing down the curtain on Glasgow 2026 as fireworks lit up the sky from the Finnieston Crane to Govan Docks.

Catch up on the action of the final day of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in our blog below.

World.title: Australia's Rhiannan Iffland becomes greatest cliff diver of all time
World.content:
Australia's Rhiannan Iffland has officially become the greatest cliff diver of all time after winning the penultimate event of the season in Mostar, in southern Bosnia and Herzegovina.

The 34-year-old from Newcastle arrived at the historic bridge knowing that victory on Saturday local time from the 21m platform would seal her 10th World Series title in a row and 48th victory of her career.

An estimated 23,000 fans turned out across three days of competition to see Iffland tally 363.20 points, finishing ahead of Canada's Molly Carlson (361.60) and Australian Xantheia Pennisi (345.80) to again lift the King Kahekili Trophy.

Pennisi's 10th career podium came thanks to a personal best total score, while Stella Forsyth (276.15), the third Australian participating, came 10th in the 12-woman field.

Rhiannan Iffland is now a commanding 27 points ahead of her nearest rival in the standings. (Getty Images: Dean Treml)

"I'm super stoked, and I guess it's time to process and then celebrate," said Iffland, who entered the final round just 1.6 points ahead of Carlson in sweltering conditions.

"I knew deep down in my heart that it wasn't going to be an easy one today. I knew Molly wasn't going to leave without putting up a good fight."

Iffland's triumph — her 48th in 59 stops — moved her to 77 points after four of the five stops on tour, an unassailable 27 clear of Carlson, with compatriot Pennisi (35) fifth.

The win — thanks to a stunning inward three somersaults half twist tuck dive into the Neretva River — also moved Iffland ahead of Englishman Gary Hunt on the all-time wins list.

It is the third time she has wrapped up the title with a stop to spare.

Romania's Constantin Popovici (right) joined Australia's Rhiannon Iffland in celebrations after winning the men's event in Mostar. (Getty Images: Romina Amato)

"Forty-eight out of 50-something starts, it's nuts," the five-time high diving world champion added.

"But I guess the recipe really comes down to passion, and drive and hard work. There is no secret recipe to being so consistent. Practice, practice, practice, and it paid off for me."

The men's event was won by Romania's Constantin Popovici, who edged out Britain's Aidan Heslop and James Lichenstein of the United States.

Heslop leads the standings on 68 points, followed by Lichtenstein (57) and Popovici (55).

Divers now have an extended two-month break before the final event of the 2026 calendar takes place in Polignano a Mare, Italy — the home of European cliff diving — from September 27.

World.title: 'Rubbish' costs Rabbitohs as Hynes chases NRL record, Eels beat Tigers
World.content:
South Sydney coach Wayne Bennett has said "rubbish" from his team continues to cost them chances to win games, as the Rabbitohs were beaten by the Cronulla Sharks.

The Rabbitohs started Sunday's top-eight battle brightly, scoring first and then playing against 12 men when Cronulla's Teig Wilton was sin-binned for a high shot on Jack Wighton.

But the Sharks would bounce back with 18 unanswered points before half-time, before kicking on in the second half for a 32-16 win.

Souths were their own worst enemy at times, missing more than 50 tackles as well as conceding six penalties and three six-again restarts.

The loss leaves the Rabbitohs seventh on the NRL ladder with 10 wins and nine losses, just one win ahead of 10th place Manly in the tight race for the top-eight.

After Sunday's 16-point loss to Cronulla, Bennett told reporters Souths' repeated errors were costing them the chance of competing with the best team in the league.

"Our Achilles heel is when we don't execute and then we pay a bit of a price for it," Bennett said.

"We can run deep (in the premiership) any day of the week if we can just get over the rubbish that gets in our game.

"If we can get that right, we can hold our own with most teams in the competition."

Meanwhile, Sharks halfback Nicho Hynes set a new club record by successfully kicking his 32nd consecutive goal.

Entering the day with a streak of 26, Hynes was perfect from his six attempts on Sunday to extend his run and close within three of the all-time record.

Canterbury Bulldogs great Hazem El Masri holds the record when he converted 35 consecutive goals in 2003.

In the final match on Sunday, Parramatta broke the hearts of Wests Tigers fans with a late try to Isaiah Iongi, snatching a 16-13 win.

The Eels led 12-0 at half-time before suffering a shocking second half, camped in their own end thanks to repeated errors, while two defence lapses allowed the Tigers to level the score.

Tigers halfback Adam Doueihi, who returned to the side after refusing to play last week, scored the try to level the scores, and kicked the Tigers ahead with a 72nd-minute field goal.

But a late try to Iongi in the 76th minute sealed an unconvincing win for the blue and gold.

World.title: Glorious athletics campaign ends in an empty stadium near midnight
World.content:
The final moment of celebration in Australia's glorious athletics campaign at the 2026 Glasgow Commonwealth Games was hilariously understated.

Approaching midnight, Lachlan Kennedy, Calab Law, Josh Azzopardi, Rohan Browning and Chris Ius finally walked onto the podium to receive their gold medals for the men's 4x100-metre relay.

The crowd had long since filed out of Scotstoun Stadium when the medal ceremony, which was supposed to happen two and a half hours earlier, kicked off.

The track and field that had hosted seven golds, five silvers and five bronze medals for Australia on a jam-packed day, had been leaf-blown, cleaned and stripped of most of its Games paraphernalia.

The stadium was empty when the medal ceremony took place. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Only a handful of volunteers, family, stadium crew, media members and team support staff remained to applaud the historic relay winners, Australia's first since 1974.

A protest by the initially disqualified Canadian team had finally succeeded, reinstating the Olympic champions to the silver medal spot and cutting short Ghanaian celebrations of bronze deep in the bowels of the Glasgow Warriors' rugby club home ground.

In a credit to organisers, the pyrotechnics still fired, the flags were still raised by military personnel in full regalia, and the anthem still played over the stadium PA.

Lachlan Kennedy, Josh Azzopardi, Calab Law, Rohan Browning and Chris Ius eventually got their moment. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

Advance Australia Fair was sung even more drone-fully than usual without the safety of a crowd to hide the nasal tones of the Aussie accent, before the small gathering shuffled off the track.

It was a bizarrely low-key moment for one of the crowning achievements of this breakout meet for Team Australia, equalling the most medals won by the track and field team at a Commonwealth Games on foreign soil.

Of the 12 gold medals, 11 silver, and 11 bronzes, none sums up what the team has and can become more than this relay triumph.

Administrators, cheerleaders and athletes alike have been spruiking this new golden generation for Australian Athletics, which has pumped countless hours and very countable dollars into the nation's relays program in recent years.

Team Australia athletes pose for a photo after the women's and men's 4x100 metres relay finals on day nine of the Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium. (Getty Images: Paul Harding)

In the past four years, Commonwealth Games Australia invested $11.6 million into the Green2Gold2Great program.

That covered a wide range of athletes, with $500,000 dedicated to relays specifically.

In that time, Australia's teams have found some phenomenal success across a number of events.

In 2025, there were green and gold teams in all six events at the World Athletics Relays for the first time ever and the mixed 4x400m team won silver.

At this year's World Relays, the men's 4x400m picked up an Australian record and bronze.

Calab Law handed over to final runner Rohan Browning with Australia in first place. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

So well drilled are these teams that when it came time for the heats on the final morning of the athletics program, both the men's and women's teams could rest individual 100m medallists Kennedy and Torrie Lewis.

Azzopardi put aside his bitter disappointment at only being brought to Glasgow as a relay runner to contribute to the cause, describing the heats as "a training run".

That is a far cry from the team that missed out in Birmingham because Browning took a tumble in the heats.

They missed the 2024 Olympic final despite running faster heat times than the top three in the opposite heat, mucked up the final change in last year's world championships final, and missed a medal by just 0.24 of a second at World Relays in May.

This gold medal puts the world on notice, and there is still more room to grow.

Lachlan Kennedy, Joshua Azzopardi, Calab Law and Rohan Browning celebrate victory in the men's 4x100m relay final at Scotstoun Stadium. (Getty Images: Ross MacDonald/SNS Group)

It is a credit to the system and their confidence in it that they didn't rush Glasgow 100m finalist Eddie Nketia into the team, even for the heats, opting instead for quick-start specialist Ius to lead off.

Kennedy replaced him for the final, playing his role to perfection, handing off cleanly to Azzopardi deep in the box, before Law and Browning came home in 38.07.

"We knew what we had in us, we're training well, we compete domestically all year against each other, [so] we're pretty used to each other. I think it's a big part of why we're so successful. Train together all year, camps all year," Kennedy said.

Kennedy said there is no first and second squad in their team, but 1A and 1B, described as "green and gold" by Browning, who flagged the looming arrivals of Gout Gout and Nketia once they have more time to train with the team that now carries a golden aura.

"I hope there are kids at home tonight watching this who aspire to grow up and be part of this team," Browning said.

"Not just aspire to the baggy green or the Wallabies or the Australian AFL team, aspire to be part of the Australian relay team."

We have already seen glimpses of it, with former Cronulla Sharks under-17 player Zavier Peacock opting for the track and finishing second behind Gout at this year's junior Australian titles.

Aussies on fire on a night when that should've been impossible Australian athletics lives up to the immense hype on a night of glorious culmination for Lachie Kennedy, Torrie Lewis and their team of track stars.

And veteran Kurtis Marschall was spurred on by their performance.

The back-to-back-to-back Commonwealth Games pole vault champion started his competition first and finished last on a frigid summer's night in Glasgow, getting the chance to watch his teammates pick up medals as he made his way up to a Games record of 5.85m, claiming the last Aussie gold of the program.

"The system is working. The boys' relay tonight was just phenomenal. They inspired me to get over the line," he said.

"We just want to keep pushing this sport along more and more and more. It's the best sport in the world and deserves more eyes, so we're just doing our part."

The whole stadium was watching his crowning moment and while no-one saw "the boys" get theirs, they weren't there to see the work it took to get there either.

World.title: Eagles star in tears after loss, Crows into top four after downing Dons
World.content:
Melbourne captain Max Gawn was inspirational in his team's nine-point win over Gold Coast. (Getty Images)

Melbourne has cemented its top six status ahead of next weekend's clash with ladder leaders Fremantle, defeating Gold Coast by nine points at Carrara Stadium.

In a contest featuring several lead changes, the Demons did just enough in the fourth quarter to claim an 18.6 (114) to 16.9 (105) victory.

After a four-goal display against Geelong last week, Harrison Petty kicked three majors including a crucial after-the-siren effort at the end of the third quarter, while Jacob van Rooyen also kicked three for the visitors.

Melbourne captain Max Gawn was huge for the Demons, notching 25 disposals, 10 marks, 33 hit-outs and nine clearances.

After last weekend's loss to the Cats, Demons coach Steven King was thrilled by his team's ability to find a way to victory ahead of the clash with the Dockers.

"We've already played them once earlier this year, and we got taught a lesson," King said.

"This time we'll be at the MCG and we love playing there but I'm sure they'll come over as a full dress rehearsal for what's in front of them as a footy club.

"It's a privilege to play in big games that count, and we're lucky we grabbed our opportunity today and can still be relevant in this competition for what's ahead."

Jed Walter kicked three for the Suns, all in the first half, as Gold Coast was unable to prevent slumping to its 10th straight defeat in what was Christian Petracca's first match against his former club.

Petracca, whose impact at the Suns had been under the spotlight throughout the week following an on-field argument with young gun Leo Lombard in the loss to Carlton, had minimal impact on the contest with 16 disposals and two clearances.

Instead it was John Noble (34 disposals, seven tackles, 10 marks) and Matt Rowell (30 disposals, nine tackles, eight clearances) who led the way for the Suns, with coach Damien Hardwick lamenting a similar display to previous defeats.

"It's just frustrating because a lot of those things are absolutely within our control, and it's the stuff that we need to eradicate," Hardwick said.

Gold Coast slumped to its 10th straight loss, a feat unthinkable at the start of the season. (Getty Images)

"I've got to coach harder and tougher because otherwise we don't move forward.

"So we've learned a lot of lessons like that this year, unfortunately, but not getting the result we're after."

Both teams had injury worries with Sam Collins (ribs) and Blake Howes (wrist) sent to hospital for X-rays after coming off in separate incidents.

Melbourne set the template for their accuracy in front of goal early, kicking five straight in the opening term to hold a three-point lead at the first break.

Bailey Humphrey's goal after the siren at the end of the second quarter, despite a question mark over whether he ran off the line of the mark as he came into kick, had the hosts in front heading into the main break.

And the Suns extended that lead to three goals during a high-scoring third term, kicking four goals alone from free kicks.

The Demons, however, kicked two goals in the last 30 seconds including another after-the-siren major to Petty to snatch a one-point lead heading into the final quarter.

Howes' nasty looking fall early in the last term didn't deter the Demons, who kicked four goals to three to secure the points.

While the Demons host the Dockers next weekend, the Suns will aim to snap their losing run in Canberra against GWS.

AAP

Tech.title: Rachika Nayar’s Heaven Come Crashing is an instrumental epic of desperate longing
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Two minutes and thirty seconds into the title track of Rachika Nayar’s Heaven Come Crashing, an absolutely massive drum and bass beat drops. As a fan of Nayar’s debut record Our Hands Against The Dusk, it caught me off guard. That album has no percussion on it at all. Heaven Comes Crashing is almost entirely drum-free, too. There are some rapid-fire mechanical hi-hats on the second track, “Tetramorph,” and the back half of track six, “Gayatri,” has what sounds like a snare buried deep in the mix. But it isn’t until track seven that Nayar delivers an unexpected drum explosion, before immediately retreating to the soothing wash of “Sleepless,” just one song later.

Nayar’s unique brand of guitar-heavy ambient-adjacent music plays almost like a version of M83 from an alternate universe. One where instead of turning to ‘80s pop music for inspiration, Anthony Gonzalez mined his instrumental epics for every last drop of emotion. Heaven Comes Crashing is as emotionally heavy as the title would imply but uses surprisingly few words to get there. The only vocals come courtesy of Maria BC, who floats over the title track and the stunning album closer “Our Wretched Fate,” where she worldlessly belts out her laments.

There are lyrics on “Heaven Comes Crashing,” but they’re almost indecipherable as Maria BC whispers beneath an ocean of flailing guitar lines and sparkling drones:

Is it morning? I don’t remember going to sleep How can we face the day Like this? You throw down your arms and count to see How deep it is

Instead of words, Nayar turns to heavily processed guitar, lonesome textures, and the occasional burst of trance chords to capture the desperate longing at the album’s core. But the album is also an indictment of the sort of abandon that often accompanies unbridled passion. It’s bookended by “Our Wretched Fantasy” and “Our Wretched Fate,” betraying a certain disgust for its own emotional recklessness. Track three isn’t “Death and Love”; it’s “Death and Limerence” — opting to spotlight unhealthy romantic obsession rather than fulfilling emotional partnership, through U2-esque guitar lines that eventually drown beneath heavily reverbed and out-of-tune tremolo-picked notes.

That’s followed by the unease of “Nausea,” which builds from an unsteady drone to maximalist panic of ‘90s synths and one of the simplest and prettiest guitar melodies on the record. The ambient emo of “Promises” follows, leading into “Gayatri,” which ratchets up the energy and serves as a bridge to the explosive title track.

Rachika Nayar’s Heaven Comes Crashing is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, Qobuz, and Deezer.

Tech.title: Fender’s CEO seems to think your bandmates are just analog AI
Tech.content:
Cole’s philosophy is that AI in music is nothing new. “I think AI has existed in music as long as there’s been recorded music,” he says. While the biggest barrier to playing guitar is the time it takes to learn the instrument, it’s the second barrier, writing songs, where he believes AI plays a part.

“I actually believe cover music has been sort of analog AI for a long time,” says Cole. Those that don’t yet have the skills to write their own songs can play the songs written by their favourite artists instead. “I listened a lot to REM, U2, The Smiths and The Cure, and at some point I got sick of just listening to them. I wanted to play it, so I learned to play guitar.”

Those taking their first steps into writing, according to Cole, can also lean on a second analogue form of AI: their band mates. You might just have a chorus or a riff to start with but then the drummer or bassist can add to it, and a song is born. AI can also play this role. “I actually think that we are in the brink of freeing up people to move beyond the same old covers and to really get into working like they do with their bands,” says Cole.

Tech.title: Xbox prices are increasing by up to €200 or £170
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

When Microsoft announced its latest round of Xbox price bumps in June, it only gave US pricing. Now we know the pricing increases for the EU and UK, and they’re dramatic. Depending on the model, Xbox prices are increasing by up to €200 or £170. The 1TB Xbox Series X with a disc drive is going up by over 30 percent from £499.99 / €599.99 to £669.99 / €799.99. The 512GB Xbox Series S is getting a price increase of over 43 percent, jumping from £299.99 / €349.99 to £429.99 / €499.99.

While other consoles have received price bumps as RAM and storage prices skyrocket due to demand from the AI industry, none have been quite as dramatic as Microsoft’s. This is the third round of price increases since May of 2025, with the highest-end model now costing $300 more than its launch price of $499.99 in 2020. The 2TB model is also being retired in the face of the storage crunch. Here’s the full list of price changes:

Tech.title: Skylight’s smart calendars are up to $90 off during its back-to-school sale
Tech.content:
The start of a new school year can feel hectic, as parents juggle their kids’ classes, extracurriculars and sports on top of work, appointments, and other responsibilities. It’s easy for things to slip through the cracks, but Skylight’s shared smart calendars can help keep everyone on track, and from August 2nd through August 9th they’re up to $90 off.

The sale includes the 10-inch Skylight Calendar for $119.99 ($50 off), the 15-inch Skylight Calendar 2 for $259.99 ($20 off), and the 27-inch Skylight Calendar Max for $479.99 ($90 off). The 10-inch model takes up the least amount of space, though the newer, larger 15-inch Calendar 2 features faster performance, a brighter display, and swappable magnetic frames. The 27-inch Calendar Max, meanwhile, offers the sharpest and largest screen and must be mounted to the wall (the other models can stand on a table or be mounted), making it the easiest option for large families to view from across the room.

Regardless of which model you choose, every Skylight Calendar includes the same set of organizational features. Each member of your household can have their own color-coded profile, and each can sync events from Google, Outlook, Apple, Cozi, or Yahoo calendars. You can also create shared lists for groceries, chores, and other to-dos that everyone can access from the calendar or the companion mobile app, and even send your grocery list to Instacart with a couple of taps. Built-in weather forecasts also can help you plan around upcoming events, and you can also share calendar access with family members and trusted contacts.

You get even more perks if you subscribe to the $79 per year Plus Plan (the first month of the service is free to try). Skylight uses AI to automatically turn emails, photos, flyers, and spreadsheets into calendar entries. It also adds meal planning, tools for assigning and rewarding completed chores, and a mode that displays your photos like a digital picture frame.

Tech.title: HP’s HyperX Omen 15 isn’t quite the budget-friendly gaming laptop its predecessor was
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

The HP HyperX Omen 15, which I first saw at CES, replaces the HP Victus 15, a longtime bestselling budget gaming laptop. The Victus cost just $800, or less when on sale, and was a good entry point to decent laptop gaming.

The Omen 15 has nice little upgrades over the Victus. Its RTX 5050 Laptop GPU can play 2026’s latest games, albeit on low-ish settings. But it’s also got a brighter 16:10 aspect ratio display with higher refresh rate, and a 1080p webcam to make it a little better for non-gaming stuff.

I’d call it a working-class gaming laptop, but thanks to RAMageddon, the Omen 15 starts at $1,200 — a far cry from the $800 that made its predecessor so appealing. But laptop prices are way up across the board, and if you want current-gen gaming hardware, this is about as cheap as you’re going to find it.
